LOUIS HAROLD ANDERSON
GRAND MASTER

L. HAROLD ANDERSON
Grand Master
September 21, 1956 - September 27, 1957

There are very few who will recognize the 91 st Grand Master of
the Grand Lodge of California by that name. His signature designates
him as L. Harold Anderson, but in the hearts of all Masons wheresoever dispersed, and in the wide circle of his friends and acquaintances,
he is affectionately known as "Pete."
Brother "Pete" was born March 29, 1900 in St. Cloud, Minnesota,
the son of Anna Louise and Peter H. Anderson. He attended public
schools in the elementary, secondary and high school grades. Self
supporting since he was 1i years of age, he continued his studies,. :6.rst
at St. Cloud State Teachers College, then the University of Minnesota,
and finally matriculated at Stanford University in 1921, where he
gi:aduated in engineering in 1923-1924.
On August 5, 1925, he married Edna Mae Parsons in the Memorial
Chapel of Stanford University. They have two daughters, Anna Louise
Ashford and Nona Lucile Ring. "Pete" and Edna Mae proudly boast
o1 their five grandchildren.
His Masonic record shows that he was raised in Palo Alto Lodge
No. 346 on October 28, 1924. He served as master of his Lodge in 1932.
He was ;president of the Masters and Wardens Association of the 52nd
Masonic District in 1932, and has been vice president of the Palo Alto
Masonic Temple Association since 1932. He is a charter member of
the Northern California Research Lodge.
His first Grand Lodge appointment was as Grand Sword Bearer in
1945. The following year he was appointed to the Board of Control. on
which he served for two years. Other important Grand Lodge committee appointments include the Special Committee of Investigation of
Masonic Homes in 1947; the Grand Lodge Centennial Committee, 1949
and 1950; Board of Trustees, Masonic Homes, 1948 through 1956;
and the Masonic Homes Committee on Motion Picture, 1951 and 1952.
Elected Junior Grand Warden in 1953, he progressed successively
through the required offices and was elected Grand Master in September, 1956.
Brother "Pete" asserts an active interest in many of the masonically
affiliated groups. He is a member of Palo Alto Chapter No. 93, Royal
Arch Masons; Palo Alto Commandery No. 47, Knights Templar;
Order of Red Cross of Constantine; San Jose Consistory No. 9, Ancient
and Accepted Scottish Rite; Islam Temple of the Ancient Order of
Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, where he served as Potentate in 1953.
His interest in youth groups is reflected by his designation to the Honorary Legion of Honor, Order of De Molay.

2

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

In business life, Brother L. Harold Anderson is Vice President and
Assistant General Manager of the Pacific Gas and Electric Company,
a position which he has held since 1948. His tremendous energy and
ability are emphasized when it is realized that he fulfilled all Grand
Lodge commitments while giving daily attention to the important requirements of his vocation. All of this was done while meeting the
demands made upon him as a member of the Advisory Board of the
Bank of America, Palo Alto Branch; Director and Vice President of
the San Francisco Down Town Association; member of the Pacific
Coast Electrical Association, Pacific Coast Gas Association, American
Water Works Association, and both the United States and the San
Francisco Chambers of Commerce.
His business career began as a part time employee of Washburn
Crosby Co., ( General Mills), while still in college. Shortly after
graduation he became Chief Building Inspector of Palo Alto, and
successively Deputy City Engineer and Director of Utilities, 1933-1941:
City Engineer from 1941 to 1945, when he was appointed by the governor of the State as a member of the California State Railroad Commission. He resigned as President of the commission to accept the Vice
Presidency of the Pacific Gas and Electric Company in 1946. ·
Club Affiliations include The Engineers' Club of San Francisco, The
Family of San Francisco, Press and Union League Club, Palo Alto
Kiwanis Club, Palo Alto Elks, the Delta Chi 'Fraternity, and the
Commonwealth Club of California. He is a member of the All Saints
Episcopal Church of Palo Alto.
History is a record of the deeds of men and their times, and the
Masonic History of the Grand Jurisdiction of California will record the
deeds and the courage of the 91 st Grand Master of Masons in California. During the 108 years of its existence, Grand Lodge of California
has been blessed and nourished by an unbroken succession of worthy
and well qualified Grand Masters. Each, according to his opportunity,
has met the necessities of his time, each has carefully preserved our
traditions, reaffirmed our aims and purposes, and enriched our heritage.
Brother "~Pete" is a strong link in that chain of succession.
His Grand Master's message is perhaps the best description of the
man. The visitations reflect his energy and strength: the opinions and
decisions, his wisdom and prudence: the edicts, his principles, convictions and courage; and the proclamations, his P'hilosophies and humility.
L. Harold "Pete" Anderson, the 91st Grand Master, the Master
Mason and the man are the same entity and inseparable. Freemasonry
and Freemasons in California will always have cause to remember his
successful administration by his far reaching declarations and his defense of the dignity and sovereignty of the Master Mason.

DR.

J. RICHARD SNEED, GRAND CHAPLAIN

Most Worshipful Sir,
Members of the Grand Lodge of California.
Delegates to the 108th Annual Convention of the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F . & A. M. of California.
Visiting Brethren of Districts.
Today I acknowledge with deep humility the privilege which you
have entrusted to me to bring the devotional service at the beginning of
this 1957 annual communication. Representing, as you do, nearly a
quarter million Masons of California. with nearly that many more residing here who hold membership elsewhere, you hold a responsibility for
these almost half million residing within our State boundary, making a
total of about one-eighth of the Masons of America our neighbors. Yet.
we are to be measured not by our size. but by our quality; not by our
history, but by our foture; not by our accomplishments today. hut by
what we are building for tomorrow.

1

ENDURING SYMBOL

No one knows all about Masonry, no one ever can. Each of us, however, has some over-all symbol which in his mind represents this ancient
and honorable craft more than any other, and for me that symbol is the
BUILDER. Whatever else Masonry is, always it is the science and
art of building. •I have twice visited Solomon's quarries under old
Jerusalem where the lodge of Jerusalem holds its meetings, and I have
made two trips in the past decade to the place where Solomon's Temple
proudly stood. Always I am impressed by the fact that the temple was
built with special care because it was the dwelling place of Jehovah.
"What/ the Builder?" is an ancient phrase which should identify any
man today who serves in this craft. Therefore let us now think together
during these devotions on the topic, THE MASTER BUILDER.
As a Master Builder, therefore, join me in focusing some defi nitions
of Masonry. like these three which are the most meaningful to me.
selected from Brother Charles Clyde Hunt's Masonic Symbolism.

A science which is engaged in the search after
Divine truth.
An institution. founded upon the purest principles of
Morality and Virtue, teaching the Fatherhood of
God and the Brotherhood of Man.
Friendship. Love, and Integrity.
Whenever was there a more vital time to be alive and to become a
living example of these definitions than now?

No TIME To D1E!
Some years ago an old Mason and Methodi st Preacher , Dr. John
Norris Hall. at the age of 94 wrote me a letter describing his daily routine
of study, writing, and servi·ce, and concludi ng. "This is no time to die!"
The sentence carried a punch all its own-on e which so deeply impressed me that I decided to use it as a sermon subject on the fourth
Sunday in Octobe r-a month which we in First Methodi st Church of
Los Angeles designat e as "Rally Month." I •had postal cards printed, to
be mailed each week during the month , listing the sermon subject for the
coming Sunday, and addresse d to each member of the church. But little
did I realize the trouble I was inviting.
During the fourth week in October I entered the Church at 9:30
one morning to learn that an irate man had been telephon ing me and
had, in fact , called nine times. Just then the phone rang again and there
he was.
"Did you know that my mother-i n-law had died?" he shouted.
" No. I didn't even know you were married, " I answered .
"Well, I am!" he replied furiously, "and what's more, my mother-i nlaw just died!"
Then his tone became more exaspera ted. "I want to talk to you right
here and now. for I don't like what happened . My mother-i n-law died.
We had the funeral at the house. We returned from the cemetery after
burying her. and I myself met the postman at the door. He handed me
a card addresse d, mind you, to her, my mother-i n-law. And what do you
think the card had on the other side? Only the words: "Really, This
Is No Time To Die!" I want to tell you most emphatic ally that I just
don't like it!"
Well, for all I know, this man still may be talking, for he was really
all wound up.
But notwiths tanding even the type of embarras sment which provoked such wrath, I still think that 94-year- old Dr. Hall had a note of
comman d to every Master Builder when he declared , "Really This Is
No Time To Die!"
In spite of life's disasters , of wars and rumors of wars, and of "man's
inhuman ity to man," this is the most vital time in history to be vibrantly ,
significantly alive. This is the hour to become a Master Builder!
NEw MEN FoR NEW WoRLD
Fifteen years ago when the world had been wrecked by the bombs
of angered destroye rs. Warsaw 93 per cent demolished, and 59 of
Germany 's 60 cities of I 00,000 or more populati on almost complete ly
wrecked , as well as much of Free Europe, I went back to Grinnell
College in Iowa to talk with my old teacher. the wisest counselo r I had
known, Dr. Edward A . Steiner. "Tell me, Dr. Steiner," ·I asked, "out
of this world of wreckag e, where the embers are still hot, can we build

a better world?" Then I focused my query still sharper: "I know we
must build a new world because the old one is gone, but will it now
be a better world?"
As if it were yesterda y, I remember Dr. Steiner's able, practical
reply: "Well. you see, that is not only my question , but .. also your

looked at me searchin gly.-"A re you- am I-the new man for the nev.'
world?"
Master Builder? That is my question to you now, here today: Are
you the new man for the new world? As has often bee~ suggeste d, the
supreme issue of our time is not whether we can make life small enough
for us, but whether we can make ourselves big enough for life. Are you
one of the "strong nails" which holds the new world together?
The challeng e comes to today's Master Builder to witness his
effectiveness in the craft by his competen ce to build on a three dimensional pattern : INWAR D. OUTW ARD. UPWAR D.
BUILD INWARD CHARACT ER!

Can you prove that you are a new man for the new world by your
recognized ability to build inwardly . resulting in a HEALT HY PERSONAL ITY?
Here is another definition by Hunt who declares :
Freemas onry is an organize d society of men symbolically_ applying the principle s of operativ e masonry
and ar~ hitecture to the science and the art of
characte r building.
Now. a man who utilizes the ancient a nd accepted principles of the
craft to build inwardly the temple of his personal ity discovers "really
this is no time to die." In fact, this is the best time that a man making
himself big enough for life could ever hope to live!
But not only must a Mason build his own supportin g characte r
inwardly . he must also inspire and encourag e all others to do the same.
And here one comes to face one of the great necessities and conflicts of
our time.
In The Argonau t. a paper publishe d here in San Francisc o, the issue
of July 12, 1957 contains an editorial on page four entitled, "The City
of the Dreadfu l Night." The contentio n is that 59,000 out of San
Francisc o's populatio n of 736,900 are under treatmen t for what we call
"mental illness." And tens of thousand s of others. for whom there
are no precise statistics , are s till denied the treatmen t they need. "Something is gravely wrong with a way of life that incapaci tates one in ten
among us," declares the editorial. lamenting that so many are lost to
anything approach ing a useful life.

Every Master Builder must come face to face with his task of inward
building. for as the editorial concludes, " Various mental health societies
rightly concentrate on rescuing those who are floundering . . . but they
leave to some other agency the task of finding out just what there is in
life as we now live it that so many people find insupportable: for no one
descends into the terrible world of insanity voluntarily."
Now~here in the realm of personal character~very Master
Builder is called to the dual task outlined in those words of St. Paul
who commanded :
Every man shall bear his own burden. (Galatians 6 :5)
and also.
Bear ye one another's burdens. (Galatians 6:2)
This is saying that we must build inwardly, making ourselves strong
for life; also tha t we are to help others who need the support of strong
hands and hearts to relieve their distress.
BUILD 0U1WARD SOCIETY!

Can you prove that you are a new man for the new world by your
recognized ability to build outwardly- resulting in 1happy SOCIAL
RELATIONSHIPS?
Here, for the man who keeps alive and alert comes the application
of the principles: "Friendship. Love and Integrity."
Friendship which rises superior to the fictitious distinctions of society. the prejudices of religion and the
pecuniary conditions of life.
Life, which knows no limit, nor inequality. nor
decay.
Integrity. which binds men to eternal law of duty.
Each of these describes some social purpose of Freemasonry: all of
these combine to add qualities to make the Master Builder strong
enough for life. rather than letting life become limited, and small enough
for him.
Years ago, after World War I, I saw a cartoon by McCutchan in
the Chicago Tribune designed to lead us to a better tomorrow. The
"Big Four" were around a table. These included Woodrow Wilson,
Lloyd George. Orlando, and Clemenceau. At one end of the table was
Mars; on his brief case was written "God of War." At the other end
of the table sat Jesus, as represented by Leonardo Da Vinci's portrayal
of Him at the Last Supper. His portfolio was inscribed, "Secretary of
Human Relations."
Today's Master Builder, by employing every art, ethic, and science
of human relationship, exemplifying those principles which Jesus
enumerated in the Sermon on the Mount, builds not only a house that

:t~:ic warfare, but he extends outwardly this Friendship. Love'. In·t to others that they, too, may become free men in a free society.

ded for the rebuilding of the world? Were they intended objects of

Her answer was far ahead of my question:-"Really. sir, the bombs

How better can you say it? Honestly but cleverly she was .forc~fu11y

THE HIDDEN DIPPERE N CE

It was in Moscow. I asked my Soviet guide. a brilliant Moscow
Uni versity graduate , if she would drive me to the cemetery . At first
she refused, though finally she reluctant ly consente d. but declared she
would not go in. As I needed her to read the names on the tombston es
of the philosoph ers, compose rs, and poets, I pressed her for her reason.
Dejected ly, she remarked that her father, an explorer , teacher, and
gifted geograph er. had suddenly died in his early forties, and was
buried there. Expressi ng my sympath y. I added that I, too. had lost my
father, but the plot of ground where he was buried was, to me. a sacred
spot, one I liked to visit often.
"But don't you believe this adventur ing mind and spirit of your
fa th er lives on?" I asked.
"No!" she replied harshly.
"When you buried your father, did a clergyma n, a priest, or a rabbi
officiate and pay tribute to his accompli shments? "
"No." s he replied in a hard, taunting tone. "We just opened up the
ground and put him in-that was all!"
"Doesn't your mother. a generatio n older , believe that your father
has an immortal spirit which lives on?"
With a derisive, hollow, almost rhythmic sort of laughter. she replied,
" N o! Ho-Ho! S he does NOT!"
Anyone. hearing this strange. pressure d tone, and watching her
sitting outside in the car. could detect the tragic emptines s w hich the
earthbou nd, materiali stic, secular teaching of Karl Marx ("Religio n
is an opiate of the people" ) produces after two generatio ns of exploitation .

LET THE PEOPLE R1sE

I close with this poem, God Prays, the best poem. I'm told. that
came out of World War I. written by Angela Morgan. a frequent
worshipp er in my congrega tion :
What is Thy will for the people, God?
Thy will for the people, tell it me!
For War is swallowi ng up the sod
And still no help from Thee.
Thou, who are mighty. hast forgot:
And art Thou God. or Art Thou not?
When wilt Thou come to sa ve the earth
Where death has conquere d birth?
And the Lord God whispere d and said to me.
"These things shall be, these things shall be .
Nor help shall come from the scarlet skies
Till the people rise!
Till the people rise, My arm is wea k;
I cannot speak till the people speak:
When men are dumb. My voice is dumb-..
•
I cannot come till the peop Ie come.
"Blazing systems of s un and star
Are not so great as My people are.
Nor chanting angels so sweet to hear
As the Voice c:;f the nations, freed from fear .
They are My mouth . My breath. My soul!
I wait their summon s to make Me whole."

CHANGE OF MEETING PLACE

La Puente Lodge No. 446 has changed its meeting place from Puente
to La Puente. Hammonton Lodge No. 433 has changed its meeting place
from Hammonton to Sutter. Ascot Lodge No. 538 has changed its meeting place from Los Angeles to Gardena. La Canada Lodge No. 739 has
changed its meeting place from La Canada to La Crescenta. These have
all been officially approved under the authority of the Grand Master.
and the Grand Secretary now requests authority to properly endorse
their Charters.
Waikiki Lodge U.D. has removed its meeting place from Wahaiwa
to Honolulu, and San Dieguito Lodge U .D . has changed its meeting
place from Oceanside to Cardiff-by-the-Sea, but there is no change in
the Charter involved.

REVISION OF DUES AND FEES

Many Masters and Wardens have asked the question, "What are
the Lodges doing about increasing dues and fees?" To furnish accurate
information we have analyzed what has been done in the past four
years, and we present that tabulation herewith.
In these days of rising prices and mounting costs Lodges are finding
it increasingly difficult to get along on low dues the same as individuals
flnd it difficult to get along on low income. In relation to fees it must
be borne in mind that to the indicated amount there must be added
$25.00 for the Masonic Homes, $9.00 for the Memorial Temple and
$1.00 for the George Washington Memorial Endowment Fund. Where
the amount of fee is shown as, for example, $50.00 the actual amount
paid by the Candidate is $85.00.
It is noteworthy that more and more Lodges are moving upward
from the minimum dues, and $15.00 and $18.00 are the figure to which
the advance is most customarily made.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is my fifth annual report, covering my activities as Grand Lecturer and those of the Committee on Ritual.
Early this year.we were saddened by loss of our Brother Clark H.
Shaw, Assistant Grand Lecturer for Division Six. This brother served
in the ritual for more than 45 years, and more than 42 of these years as
an Inspector of this Grand Lodge. He was a good and kindly friend to
each member of our Committee, and he was revered by the Inspectors
under his charge. In his iplace, the Grand Master, on my recommendation, appointed Brother W. Ben Sorrells of Laguna Bea{:h, an Inspector
with six years of service.
The usual Spring Conferences of Inspectors were held as follows:
Divisions 1 and 2 at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 21-23, 1957, conducted
jointly by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell and Worshipful Ralph M.
Foote, Assistant Grand Lecturers.
Division 3, at Guerneville, May 17-19, 1957, conducted by Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 4, at Yosemite, June 7-9, 1957, conducted by the Grand
Lecturer, in the absence of Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor.
Division 5, at Ventura, April 5~7, 1957, conducted by Worshipful
Donald G. Campbell, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 6, at Riverside, March 22-24, 1957, conducted by the Grand
Lecturer.
At each of tpese conferences the work was fully and well done by
the Inspectors of the respective divisions. The Inspectors of Divisions
Four and Six had ,perfect attendance at their Conferences.
At each of the Conferences, the Inspectors were addressed by the
Grand Master and Grand Secretary, or by the Deputy Grand Master,
on matters of interest and importance to the Craft.
At several of the Conferences, meetings of the Ritual Committee were
held to consider various matters pertaining to the ritual. iln addition, a
special meeting of the Committee was held at San Francisco, on December 1st and 2nd, 1956, with all members of t he Committee present, at
Which meeting the entire work of the three degrees was reviewed and
performed.
The annual reports received by me from the Inspectors of the jurisdh:tion, as required by section 161 of the Masonic Code, show that our
lodges, for the most part, are in good working condition, and that most
of them are actively at work. The few weak spots disclosed by the
reports are receiving the special attention of the Inspectors.
More than a year ago, I objected to the use of the small, so-called
"Masonic edition" of the Holman Bible, because of the collateral material appearing in the book, violating our rule of secrecy by disclosing
1

45

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

the contents of our degrees and by making references to esoteric matters.
Similar objections to the larger edition of the Holman Bible were pointed
out by Grand Master Clausen in a decision in 1955. (Proceedings, 1955,
pp. 64-65.) The smaller edition was, in my opinion, subject to prac..
tically the same objections as the larger one. After some discussion and
correspondence between the publishers, the Grand Master and myself,
the publishers have eliminated all of the objectionable matter, including
the phrase "Masonic edition" and have discontinued use of the square
and compass on the cover. I see no further objection to the presentation
of such Bibles in their modified .form. However, the small edition still
cannot conform to our ritual if intended to be used on the Altar.

by all Lodges and Masons in this Jurisdiction," with certain express
exceptions. ( C.M.C., sec. 554.) Section 555 of the Ordinances specifically provides that Grand Lodge alone has power to authorize any
changes in the ritual, "for the purpose of having it remain as it was
handed down from time immemorial." Despite this restrictive provision,
each year we have to defend the ritual against proposed changes which
do not even >purport to meet this required purpose. For instance, there is
presented this year a resolution containing a proposal which this Grand
Lodge has twice declared illegal and contrary to our Masonic obligations. It is our contention that any proposal to change the ritual must
show that it is for the purpose of restoring it to what was handed down
to us, the custodians of the ritual. It is therefore my recommendation that
the Committee on Jurisprudence interpret this provision c>f our law, and
if necessary present legislation which will implement or clarify section
555, so that the Ritual Committee shall not have the burden of continually defending the ritual we have received from our predecessors.
At the invitation of the Most Worshipful Conrad H. Baldwin,
Grand Master of Masons in Arizona, and with the direction and
approval of our own Grand Master, I attended the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arizona, April 21st and 22nd, 1957, as
representative of our Grand Master. The brethren of Arizona were most
cordial and hospitable to me, and I appreciated the opportunity of visiting them and becoming acquainted with them.
In closing, may I ex.press to our Grand Master my personal thanks
for his courtesies during the past year, and to the Grand Secretary and
Assistant Grand Secretary my appreciation for their help during the
year, and my thanks to you brethren for the opportunity c>f serving you.
Respectfully submitted,

One of our Inspectors inquired if he had authority to require conformity to the ritual on the part of Past Masters conferring a degree.
I assured ·him he had full authority to require anyone so to conform and
could report infractions to the Grand Master for disciplinary action,
if necessary. '1t is well to remind the Masters that they themselves are
responsible for the conferring of all degrees in strict accordance with
the ritual, and the Past Masters are not to be regarded as exceptions.
We have insisted that the adopted Installation Service be strictly
complied with, without any additions or deviations in the public cere..
mony. This has resulted in a number of resolutions :proposing additions
to the ceremony, such as a prayer and a Flag presentation. Your Committee on Ritual is neutral on all these proposals, except we suggest that
the Installation Service should be kept definite and uniform, and perhaps,
therefore, there should be a revision to consider all these proposals.

In order Jo secure uniformity in the ritual and to reconcile differing
practices in various parts of the jurisdiction, the Ritual Committee has
adopted the rule that any officer who vacates his station or place shall
surrender to the brother occupying the same not only the jewel of the
office but also the apron, if it bears insignia indicating the office. The
apron does not, o'f course, belong to the elective or appointive officer,
any more than does the jewel; each is merely a symbol of the station or
place. The temporary occupant of the station or place, in the con'ferring
of a degree, is, for all the purposes of that degree, the officer selected to
occupy it. The requirement is not new to most parts of the jurisdiction.
The practice must be uni.form in all parts.
As I have reported in previous years, the Committee has no suggestions for any changes in the esoteric work.
Under the Ordinances of Grand Lodge, the Ritual Committee has
been made the custodian of the esoteric work ( C.M.C., sec. 159). By
section 554, "eac<h degree conferred and all lectures in this jurisdiction
must be in conformity with the ritual now taught by the Grand Lecturer and recognized by the Grand Lodge, and such must be adhered to

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
The following resolution, passed at the Stated Meeting for April.
1957, is respectfulJy submitted by Tyre Lodge No. 741 of Downey:
WHEREAS. Masonry, although not a religion, has at its roots an
unfeigned piety for God; and
WHEREAS. this characteristic is recognized by the public so that
it expects Masons to be reverent in their behavior: and
WHEREAS, Masons are enjoined in their teachings to conduct
themselves in a manner which will reflect ·honor on the .fraternity: and
WHEREAS. the annual installation of officers affords the public
one of its few opportunities to observe Masons at work: and
WHEREAS, the absence of any appeal to God in the public c1tremony of as important an event as the annual installation of officers
must surely seem to be out of C'haracter to the uninitiated: and
WHEREAS, a prayer at any point in the public ritual would not
only be consistent with other Masonic rituals and with Masonic teachings in general. but would, in fact, have ample precedent upon which
to be based:
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED. that a suitable invocation
be added to the ritual for the public instalJation of officers. at the point
in the ceremony when the officers elect have been conducted to their
seats, but before they ·h ave been seated.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
We, the undersigned, members of Grand Lodge, respectfully present
the .following resolution:
WHEREAS, one of the first lessons we are taught in Masonry
is that before entering upon any great or important undertaking, we
should first invoke the blessing of God. Certainly the installation of
officers of a consistent Lodge is a great and important undertaking.
WHEREAS, a prayer, delivered by a brother, asking the Supreme
Architect of the Universe for guidance of these brethern during their
term of office, is bound to add solemnity to the occasion, and to inspire
these brethern to discharge their duties with fidelity and with honor.
WHEREAS, this resolution is not inconsi'Stent with the ceremonies
used by our Grand Lodge. such as the Laying of Cornerstones, Constitution of Newly Chartered Lodges, Dedication of Masonic Halls,
etc.
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge Committee on Policy and General
Purposes of the One Hundred Seventh Annual Communication approved this resolution as being wholly consistent with Masonic ritual
concerning prayer as an integral part of all important undertakings
and would carry into practice in the constituent Lodges the practice of
Grand Lodge.
· THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED: That the Installation
Services for Constituent Lodges be amended to include an appropriate
prayer immediately prior to the presentation of the Master-elect for
installation.
Respectfully and Fraternally submitted by

USE OF SAILING SHIP MODELS AND PICTURES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it ·h as been the custom of our Lodge and many other
Lodges in this Jurisdiction, throughout the history of California Masonry.
to use sailing ship models or ·pictures as ornaments on the walls ot
the Lodge Rooms, and
WHEREAS, the removal of these models and pictures is the
change--something new to a great many of our older Lodges and some
of the "young" ones, and which has resulted in attracting much
unusual attention and comment by the Brethern and the uninitiated,
and
WHEREAS, they have the same meaning to the Master Mason
whether they be in the Lodge Room or the Foyer or Tiler's Room,
(they have been approved for these locations), and
WHEREAS, these models or pictures have not been used as
"props" to augment the ritual or the lectures, as does the Second
Degree Carpet, and
WHEREAS, it is well beyond our understanding to see how the
existence of a mere simple ship model or pkture could .possibly convey
even in the most vague way, any of the meaning of our esoteric work,
and
WHEREAS. all explanations pointed out by our Grand Lecturer
have been used by Inspectors and Masters with the same result: Confusion and bitterness among the Brethren, and inability to understand
how present Law applies,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: that the sailing shf.p
models or pictures be allowed as optional ornaments or furnishings on
the walls of a Regular Lodge Room.

POINT WITHIN CIRCLE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, it has been ruled by the Grand Lecturer that "a certain
Point within a Circle" will no longer ~e permitted to be displayed in
Lodge Rooms, citing CMC sec. 554v as authority for this decision,
and
WHEREAS, page 12 of the "Monitor and Officers' Manual,"
issued by Grand Lodge, states in part, quote. "and since their time
there is, or should be, represented in every regular Lodge a certain
point within a circle," unquote, and
WHEREAS, it is our sincere belief that the use of "a certain
point within a circle" does not conflict with the intent of the ruling
in CMC, sec 554v as it is not a costume, chart, slide or film but a
physical, three dimensional object more like the middle chamber columns
and floor carpet authorized for use by CMC, sec. 554b, tihey too are
purely symbolic but quite important visual aids to teaching the wonderful
lessons they symbolize, and
WHEREAS, enough thinking along these lines to modernize could
lead to making illegal the use of all so-called "props" or visual aids
and no longer allow the use of the pillars, middle C'hamber carpet,
suspended, even the square and
the working tools, the letter
compass and Holy Bible. Masonry is old and honorable, our teachings
are old and honorable and our props are old and honorable: they have
stood the test of centuries, let us not destroy all this in one generation.
NOW. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: that the use of
this ancient and accepted visual aid be authorized in this Grand
Jurisdiction at the discretion of the Lodge.
E. 1F. !MOHR, Past Master

PERMITTING OFFICERS COACHES TO ATTEND
GRAND LECTURERS SCHOOL OF INSTRUCTION
AT GRAND LODGE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
WHEREAS, the Officers' Coach in a Lodge does the actual
coaching of the officers and who in turn has to receive his coaching
from the Inspector of the district, who attends the School of Instruction
held by the Grand Lecturer during Grand Lodge.
AND, as the Inspector does not coach the officers of the Lodge-only inspects them as to their proficiency at the end of the year before

SECOND MONDAY OF OCTOBER FOR

NUMBER OF CHARTER MEMBERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
WHEREAS, the present regulation limiting the charter membership
of ne\V lodges to fifty automatically imposes financial limitations, and
WHEREAS, the limitation often causes bitter disappointment and
resentment which sometimes leads to dissension and embarrassment,
and
WHEREAS. as a result of this limitation, new lodges are often
deprived of the services of many excellent Brethren who do not learn
of the formation of said lodges in time to become charter members. and
WHEREAS, existing lodges are adequately protected against
"raiding" or divisive tactics by the forty ...flve {45) day notice provision
and by the diligence of the Inspectors:
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED: That Part 2, Article
1, Section 301 of the Ordinances be, and the same hereby is, amended
by deleting from the second line thereof the words "and not more
than fl•fty" and substituting therefor the words "or more."
Respectfully submitted,

ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
PROPOSED RESOLUTION RE
DATE OP ANNUAL COMMUNICATIONS
WHEREAS, the fourth Monday in September ·has been designated
as the starting date for Grand Lodge. Should the flrst of September
fall on Tuesday, as it will in 1959 and approximately every 6th year
thereafter, it would force every Lodge in the state that meets on
Thursday or Friday to change its By Laws. By not doing so they would
be unable to hold a Stated Meeting in October, which would be in
violation of Sec. 321, California Masonic Code, since the Grand
Master does not have the power to issue a special dispensation to
change a stated meeting date. See C.M.C. 18a, 12lg, 323a and 343c.
Note: Any Lodge meeting on Friday would be
similarly affected when September 1st is
on Wednesday, and
WHEREAS, the fourth Monday in September as the starting date
in any case would leave very little time to correlate notes for a report

on Grand Lodge activities to the constituent Lodges, we deem it
advisable to change the permanent date prescribed for commencement
of the Annual Communications.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 101,
Article 1, Part 1 of the Ordinances o-f the Grand Lodge of California,
be amended to read as follows:
101, Annual, Eac<h annual communication shall be held in the City
of 'San Francisco, commencing on the second Monday of October at
10 o'clock A.M.: 1provided, however, that any Annual Communication
may be held at any other place in the State of California upon adoption
by the Grand Lodge at any previous ANNUAL Communication by
a flve-sixth vote of a resolution so providing.
E. F. MOHR, Past Master
Lawndale Lodge No. 753
HowARD H. ARNOLD, Past Master
Lawndale Lodge No. 753
W. 0. NASH, Worshipful Master

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

A Mason can be charged and tried for an offense committed before
his initiation if it consists of some act involving great moral turpitude,
but if said offense was one for whicli he was convicted in the courts of
the land 1he shall be charged with said offense only if he had been
convicted of a .felony in the federal or state courts, either of this or any
other state, and had been imprisoned in a state prison or in any such
place of imprisonment for a federal felony offense as provided for by

offense for which he was placed on probation without imprisonment in
a state prison or federal place of detention for felonies as above set
out or was imprisoned only in the county jail or road or farm cam.p
he cannot be tried for said offense committed before his initiation.

No person who has ever been convicted of a felony in any federal
court of the United States or in any state, county or municipal court
of this or any other state of the United States, and ·who has suffered
imprisonment therefor in a state prison or reformatory, or, in the case
of a federal offense, in any place of imprisonment provided for by the
laws of the United States, is eligible to receive the degrees of Masonry.
A person convicted of a felony as above stated but who was placed on
probation or sentenced to a jail commitment only is not ineligible for
said degrees by that reason alone but must be judged as to 'his moral
fitness at the time of his application for the degrees.

SUMMER SCHOOL EXCHANGE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
WHEREAS, the spectacular advances in the sciences and other
flelds :have greatly narrowed the distances bet~een the peoples of the
world and Masonic Lodges in the many countries of the world: and
WHEREAS it has become vitally im1portant to our very existence
that the peoples' of the world learn to know each other better with
respect to customs, traditions, beliefs and language: and
WHEREAS, the best program for a better understanding among
the ,peoples of the world is the exchange of youth: and
WHEREAS, the youth of today who will be leaders of the worl~
in the future are those belonging to affiliated Masonic Youth Organizations and who are indirectly learning how Free Masons work and act.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that the Grand Lodge of
Masons in the State of California formally sponsor a summer exchange
program for yoting boys and girls of Masonic fa?1ilies ~?d affiliated
organizations in California with youth of Masonic families the free
world over so that each may bring to his or her own country and
family a knowledge of the way in which the other peoples of the world
live and also how Free Masonry in California works and acts.

RESOLUTIO N

BE IT RESOLV ED, that the decision of Grand Master Clausen,
1955, ipp. 51, 353, and cited in California Masonic Code Annotated as
sub-parag raph "s" to Section 412 be reversed.
REASONS POR RESOLUTIO N

Adoption of the resolution would allow constituent lodges to expend
monies from the refreshment .fund in support of lodge athletic events.
It is of vital interest to constituent lodges to keep and maintain the
interest of its younger members, for they are the life blood of every
lodge. The reason given by the Most Worshiipful Grand Master for
his ruling was that, in view of the limited amount of members involved,
it could be held to be a matter of fraternal intercourse. It is respectfully
submitted that this reason is not persuasive from a practical viewpoint.
The real question should be: Does a member have the right to participate in the activity? In almost every lodge, only a small percentage
of the members actually tum out for the conferring of a degtee. May
it then be said that refreshments following a degree should not be
deemed to be fraternal intercourse because only a limited number of
members participate? Of course not, because all ·have the right to
participate. The same is true of athletic events, as all have the right to
participate. lf because of age or infirmities a member cannot participate
directly, he may still vicariously enjoy the activity as a spectator. This
has been done by members of Charter Rock Lodge. It is our respectful
opinion that athletic events of a lodge are important matters o.f fraternal
intercourse and should .be encouraged.
Respectfully submitted,
LEWIS F. SHERMAN , Master
Charter Rock Lodge No. 410

Referred

PUBLIC RELATIONS COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A wise man once remarked that, given the truth people will always
resolve a problem aright.
A situation now faces Masonry in the form of a force inimical to
our aims, our beliefs and our ·principles. A force that because it cannot
rule us, must therefore bend every effort to discredit and destroy us.
The primary tenet of its belief is that the end justiJles the means. Halftruths, misstatements and innuendos are but the mildest approach
regularly employed on its own adherents and any others who will listen.
It goes about its self-assigned task with complete and intentional disr~ard for the legal and moral code it shatters.
Masonry •has the ·gravest responsibility to use all means which
wise and moral men can afford to the end of combating the insidious
effects of this attack.
Let us publicize the truth, not men, not the Craft, but the tenets
we know to be just, the causes we espouse for the good of man, and
die doctrines under which it •has been proven free men may live and
prosper.
BE IT THEREFORE NOW RESOLVED, that this Grand
Lodge adopt the policy of militantly combating untruths and misconceptions concerning our fraternity, its aims, its rules for admission
and its stand concerning religion, government and man's freedom for
self-determination; to spread the truth wherever the attack of false
premise is encountered.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED. that to implement this policy
the Grand Master of Masons in California, in due time after his

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

65

fllstallation. appoint a committee to be known as the Public Relations
Committee for Masonry in California and to be composed of members
of this Grand Lodge in such number as will be consistent with the
Law of this Grand Lodge, the will of the Grand Master and the
objective herein stated.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that it shall be the duty of
this Committee to accomplish the dissemination of information to the
general public by use of newsprint, magazine, radio, television, direct
mail and all other such media available: to em'Ploy public relations
counsel as need may warrant.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED. that a sum not to exceed
$50,000.00 be budgeted for the use of this Committee in its endeavor
to diseharge its assigned duty.
Respectfully submitted,
PETER F. PHILLIPS, Worshipful Master

GRAN D MAST ER'S MESSA GE
L. HAROLD ANDERS ON, Grand Master
Brethren of the Grand Lodge of California . . . .
All of my life adds up to this moment. ... It is quite appropr iate,
therefore, that my first words should be in conside ration of the Master
Masons and the member s of this Grand Lodge jurisdiction who have
made this moment possible.
Tihere was a very wise man who once said, "A room is always crowded when you are surroun ded with friends, " and perhaps therein lies the
greatest reward of this high office. The awaren ess of brother hood born
of mutual esteem, mutual respons ibility and common interest , becomes
increasi ngly evident as the duties and travel of the year progres s. So, as
I look upon this vast audienc e I see among you the men of Masonr y of
Californ ia who ·have been my greates t strength in times of need, whose
encoura gement has given me comfort in times of stress and tension.
whose support has given me courage in times of grave decision . It is to
you, my brother s and my friends, that I humbly acknow ledge a great
debt of gratitud e and my everlast ing loyalty.
One year ago last week you invested me with the dignity and title
of Grand Master of Masons in Californ ia. On that day the cloak of
Grand Master rested lightly on my shoulde rs. and togethe r w ith the
newly elected and appoint ed Grand Lodge family. we embark ed upon
another Grand Lodge year. The dedicati on of our new Californ ia
Masoni c Memorial Temple was to be the crownin g event at the climax
of Californ ia Grand Lodge's longest year. Howev er. because of delays.
the Temple we planned to dedicat e in Novem ber will not be complet ed
until early in 1958. This has resulted in a Grand Lodge year of normal
length but one of extraor dinary activity . The cloak of Grand Master has
become heavy with the respons ibilities of the office, and during these
last days of this Grand Lodge year I have looked forward to the day
when this mantle would be lifted from my shoulde rs, when I would be
relieved of its burdens by your action at this Communication , and it
would be invested to rest lightly on the shoulde rs of my chosen successor.
To him will go the privileg e and honor of dedicati ng our beautifu l new
home atop Nob Hill. I wish for him every success and pledge to him
the same devoted loyalty he has given me through out the year.
The purpose of my appeara nce here this afterno on is to give to you
a report of my steward ship as Grand Master. This could be a statistical
and detailed report, but in that form would not give sufficient evidenc e
of the problem s that have been presente d for decision and edict. I have
chosen to include many of these detailed items as exhibits, which can
be reviewe d whenev er you desire and at your leisure.

I look upon this Communication as a sort of stockholders meeting,
and you, my brethren, are the proxies for the shareholders. Every Mason
in California has a vital interest in all business that will be conducted
during this Communication, and you, members of Grand Lodge, the
elected representatives of your Lodges, have come here to act in behalf
of the brethren of your Lodge.
Many of the duties of a Grand Master are the same from year to
year. He is required to constitute and institute Lodges, dedicate Masonic
Temples and public buildings, conduct cornerstone ceremonies issue
dispensations, fulfill the requirements of visitations to cent~ials
ins~~toral conferenc~, Masonic Districts, Lodges, and other groups a;
an 1tin~rary and propriety permit. In the interest of reserving full time to
Masomc issues and the consideration of every recommendation that has
as i~s purp?se the welfare of the Craft, I will merely summarize the
routine duties of the Grand Master in this spoken report and for the
printed record, supply supplemental eX'hibits that will give fuil details
of these activities.
. Since the last Communication there have been 29 special communications of Grand ·Lodge which have provided for 8 Masonic dedications,
6 cor?erstone ceremonies, 2 high school dedications, and 11 new lodges
constituted. There have also been 3 special ceremonies, 50 Masonic
breakfasts and receptions by Lodges and Masonic Districts, fl.ve centennial celebrations, two 15th and four 50th anniversaries of lodges, 16
out-of-state visitations, including the Grand Masters' Conference in
Washington, D.C., and the Communication of the United Grand Lodge
of England in London. This visitation was followed by visitations to the
Grand Lodge of Denmark, the Grand Lodge of Finland, the Grand
Lodge of Sweden, the Grand Lodge of Norway, the Grand Lodge of
Scotland. the Grand Lodge of Ireland, the Grand Lodge of France the
National Grand Lodge of France, and the Grand Lodge of Italy, in 'that
order. Five receptions were held in the Territory of Hawaii, and there
have been the usual Inspectors' Conferences, and also a series of
research seminars.
INSPECTORAL DISTRICTS

During the last Grand Lodge year there have been six new Inspectoral Districts created: District 539 in Los Angeles; District 421 comprising San Miguel, Paso Robles and Atascadero; District 333 in San
Francisco; District 637 comprising Escondido, Ramona and Vista; District 639 comprising three San Diego Lodges and Coronado Lodge; and
District 227 comprising Mount Oso Lodge at Tracy and two Stockton
Lodges. Districts 380 and 604 have been discontinued. There have been
20 Inspectors appointed, :fl.ve of whom are the Inspectors of the fl.ve new
Districts.

DECISIONS

In more ways than one this has been a year of decisions. Since the
last Communication there have been 34. The report to the Jurisprudence
Committee contains a foll analysis of the questions that 'have been submitted for opinion and decision.
Several of them relate to questions which have long since been
settled and recorded in our law. Such questions should never have been
propounded and would not have been if the Master had been diligent
in the performance of his duties. Many Masters live by the rule that it
is easier to ask a question than it is to tum a page. It is not my desire
that such questions be reported and recorded. They should, however,
point out to the Masters and Wardens that oftentimes the answers to
their questions can be found in the California Masonic Code.

MASONIC CLUBHOUSES
( BoARD OF DIRECTORS)

Your attention is called to the increasing importance of our Masonic
Clubhouses at the University of California in Berkeley and in Los
Angeles. As the enrollments of these universities continue to assume
larger proportions the use of these Clubhouses and their facilities increases, and they become a focal point of activity for increased numbers
of Masonic sons and daughters.
Over the years the pattern of electing Directors for these Clubhouses
has been for the Grand Master to nominate one and the Directors to
elect him and/ or others to the Board of Directors. I can say generally
the means have accomplished the end of good administration and good
supervision. However, in other Grand Lodge business matters the Grand
Lodge exercises control over every Board and Committee that has the

74

75

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

responsibility of being the custodian of monies budgeted or appropriate d
by Grand Lodge or as Directors or Committeemen administering or
operating property whose title is held by Grand Lodge.
In the case of the Clubhouses the Grand Master exercises little or
no control. I look upon our Masonic Clubhouses in exactly the same light
as I look upon our Masonic Homes and feel that both of these Masonic
facilities should be operated by the same set of rules. These Masonic
Clubhouses have many self-sustaini ng activities which are usually under
the control of Club members and under the supervision of the Director
or Hostess of these Clubhouses, but all the costs of supervision, operation and maintenance are budgeted Grand Lodge expense items, and as
Grand Lodge expense items they should be handled in the exact manner
that Grand Lodge controls its other financial responsibilities.
There is a further matter of principle involved beyond the financial
control, and that is the moral responsibility of title and ownership. Under
Grand Lodge title these Masonic Clubhouses are the property of all the
Masons of California, and whatever happens become the responsibility
of all the Masons of California. While there never has been any occasion in the past that has provoked public criticism, there is always the
possibility that some event of the future could create adverse publidty,
and as presently constituted Grand Lodge would have no direct means
of correcting.
The list of Directors for each of the two Masonic Clubhouses looks
like an honor roll of Masonry. They are men who have served their
Lodges, been active in Masonic, civic and community welfare, and by
their devoted service have established themselves as good citizens, good
Masons, and friends and counselors of our youth. Had I the authority
to appoint any Boards of Directors for our Masonic Clubhouses, I hope
every member of the present Boards would c'hoose to accept, so it is not
because of present personnel or present administrati on that this recommendation is made, but only with the foresight of a possible future day
when a self-perpetu ating Board might create conditions which they
could not-but Grand Lodge and another Grand Master could--corre<:t
by more direct means than are now possible.
It is my recommendation that the subject of Boards of Directors for
our Masonic Clubhouses be explored and referred to the Jurispruden ce
Committee for a report on how our Masonic Clubhouses could come
more directly under the control of Grand Lodge and their Boards of
Directors be governed more like the Board of Trustees of our Masonic
Homes.

MASONIC TEMPLE PROPERTIES

I have been impressed with the unselfish devotion and dedication to
Masonic service of the brethren who are members of the Committee on
Lodge Financing. Although the duties and responsibilities of the members of this Committee require them to delve into the intimate details of
Lodge financial affairs. they have earned the confidence and respect of
a vast majority of the brethren involved.
During this past year numerous violations of Masonic law coming
under the jurisdiction of the Committee on Lodge Financing have come
to my attention. Accordingly, I assigned to this Committee the diflkult
task of resolving complex problems arising from these violations and it
has carried out these assignments in the finest Masonic tradition. As a
result the record has been cleared in all of these cases and harmony
again prevails where once reigned conflict and confusion.
As might he expected the work of the Committee has been subjected
to some harsh criticism and even abuse by a few brethren who, apparently. are inclined to place personal views and actions above the
restraints placed upon them by the ordinances of Grand Lodge. It is
a pleasure to report that such instances are indeed rare and these have
also been satisfactorily adjusted.
The monuments of Masonry are our Masonic Temples. It is in these
Temples that all Masonic Lodges and most Masonic prerequisite membership bodies conduct their meetings and activities. Many of these Temples reflect great credit to the Craft. They need not be new and modern,
but they show exactly the zeal, interest and labors of their proprietors.

PROPERTY MANAGEMENT CONSULTANT

To the end that Masonic Lodges and Masonic Temple Associations
become properly informed and counseled, and in keeping with the modern
methods of property management. there should he a professional land
and property management consultant, whose serv~ces are available to
Masonic Temple Associations in regard to evaluating rental schedules,
operating budgets. and all phases that come within the profttable operation of a Masonic Temple property. There are many examples throughout the state where this neglect has been the cause of tension and discord
between members of the Craft and between Lodges. Investigations this
year into four Temple Association controversies--one in the far no~.
one in the south, and two in central California-lead to the firm conviction that this is a matter of grave concern, requiring immediate attention. I therefore recommend that a Property Management Consulta1!t
be employed by Grand Lodge, to operate from the Grand Secretary s
office and in harmony with the Grand Lodge Committee on Lod~e
Financing and such other Committees as may he proper, who Wtll
consult and advise with all Brethren who have Masonic property under
their direction and control. He will keep an accurate record of his work
and report his ftndings and recommendations at the Annual Communications of Grand Lodge.

CALIFORNIA" FREEMASON

During the past year our publication of the "California Freemason"
has come of age. Due to the increased support of members of the Craft
it has passed from a venture that was operating at a deficit to a Grand
Lodge project that is now paying its own way.
I do not think it necessary to stress the point that as a medium of
Masonic information it provides California Masonry with a source of
informed and responsible news of the Craft, not only of events within
our immediate jurisdiction and interest, but of Masons throughout the
world.
The "California Freemason" is the means of reaching every California Mason, not only those who attend Lodge but, more important,
those thousands of Masons who have vocations or interests which prevent them from attending their Lodges regularly. This publication can
also be the means of stimulating attendance among those who have been
neglecting their Lodges, as here is a Masonic Trestleboard, covering
the state, the nation, yes, even the world, that will make him realize his
brotherhood with all Masons whithersoever dispersed around the globe.
With this knowledge should come the realization of the duty :he owes to
his neighbor and to himself. If all the members of all constituent Lodges
were to subscribe to the "California Freemason" it probably could be
produced and distributed for approximately 60 cents per year, perhaps
less. It would provide California Masonry with a tool that would
strengthen our brotherhood.
I recommend that the Committee on Correspondence report to the
next Annual Communication, after a thorough survey of all phases of
the subject, the approximate per capita cost that would be needed to
supply members of the constituent Lodges with this publication and
that Grand Lodge then consider such action.
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

At the beginnig of this Grand Lodge term, I proclaimed this year
to be "The Year of the Temple." At that time, the progress of the work
on Nob Hill was most encouraging, and everything pointed to the possibility that we would be able to dedicate our $6,000,000 California
Masonic Memorial Temple for this Communication. But our plans could
not anticipate the strike in the carpenter trades, the strike in the steel
industry, and the critical structural problems that delayed us beyond
all hope of meeting the scheduled completion date.
It is of course a great personal disappointment that the "Year of the
Temple" is not an accomplished fact. But in a broader sense, there is a
warming confidence and a sincere hope that this delay will provide
California Freemasonry with ample opportunity to complete their job
of financing this "once-in-a-lifetime" project.

79

In the Masonic tradition, Josephus informs us "that all eyes seemed
directed toward Jerusalem, as if to witness the splendid display of the
wisdom of Solomon." Brethren . . . I can assure you that the eyes of
the Masonic world are now directed toward this jurisdiction . . . to
witness your support and your wisdom in building this modern Temple
of Solomon. It will be to the everlasting glory of this generation of
California Freemasons, if we can complete this Temple without any
outstanding indebtedness . . . and this can be done if every Master
Mason, according to his means, becomes a contributor, and a part of
this sanctum sanctorium.
I urge each of you to take the time to see what is going on at California's "Threshing Floor of Oman." It is a source of amazed interest
to those who are not Masons. To you and to all who are California
Masons, it should be a source of reverent and devout interest . . . an
emotional interest that should inspire you to more participation and
greater effort to fully own this symbol of brotherly love, relief and truth,
that each of us may truly say to the world ... this is my Temple.
Hardly a day has passed since construction was started, that I have
not gone to the top of Nob Hill to watch the workmen at their labors.
I saw it as a mighty steel frame, showing the strength and mighty
sinews of California Freemasonry, . . . then they poured the cement
that united the structure into a common mass ... and finally ..• as you
will now see it they adorned the Temple with beauty by applying the
white Vermont marble slabs that face the building. They use the trowel.
my brethren, and as you watch them spread the cement that unites the
marble, cement and steel into a common mass. be ever mindful that it is
your donation of marble, your brother Mason's donation of cement, and
his brother Mason's donation of steel-that will make this Temple truly
symbolical of the beauty, harmony and strength of California Masonry.
Brethren ... a part of that building is mine ... and even in its unfinished state it is among my most treasured possessions, because it is not
something I have bought ..• but something I have given ..• I hope
every California Master Mason will be able to look upon the California
Masonic Memorial Temple with the same pride and sense of ownership.
I urge every Mason to become a part of this beautiful catihedral of
Freemasonry-a beacon of truth to Masons the world over-the home
of Masonry in California. H you have already subscribed ... give more.
if you have not yet subscribed ... do your part according to your means.
MASONIC HOMES

In my proclamation for Masonic Homes Endowment Month, I stated
that "our Masonic homes are the highest and noblest expression of
brotherly love and affection. They stand as monuments of security ... to
relieve the distresses of our elder brethren. to protect their widows, and
to support and educate the orphan."

80

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

As "ex·pressions of brotherly love and affection,'' they reflect the
devoted and unselfish labors of the board of trustees and the superintendents. These dedicated Masons give generously and untiringly of
their time and abilities to administer and operate our ·homes with kindness and compassion, and at levels of economy and efficiency that have
earned for them and for us an enviable reputation among all the jurisdictions.
As "monuments of security" they reftect the diligent and faithful
labors of the endowment board, and the integrity, fidelity and generosity
of the Masons of California, who year after year share their blessings,
to relieve the distresses of worthy Master Masons, their widows and
orphans, with increasing endowments and contributions to the fund.
'Phere is nothing I can say that could add to the stature of the men
of the board of trustees, t!he endowment board, or those who serve us as
superintendents of our homes. Our landmarks at Decoto and Covina,
and the comfort and well being of the residents at these homes offer
eloquent testimony that all of their acts are done with a tenderness of
heart and generosity of spirit •.. that is born of love.
But I do wish to take this moment to thank the chairmen and members of the Masonic ·homes endowment committees in the Lodges, who
... year after year, continue to sow t!he seeds of Masonic responsibility,
that allows a greater harvest of homes endowment funds. Each year, we
successively and successfully reflect any increasing interest and support
of these monuments of security.
Your continued faithfulness and zeal can hasten that day, when we
hope that the endowment fund will be sufBcient to carry the cost of
operating our homes to ·perpetuity. Your efforts to "aid and assist" in
achieving this goal, is an outstanding Masonic service.
CEMETERIES

As time and neglect exact their tolls, the importance of a Masonic
Cemetery Committee becomes increasingly apparent. This is not only
a safeguard to the resting places of the Brethren who have gone this
way before us, but it is a guarantee by California Masonry of today
to .future generations of Masons that they, too, may rest in peace until
time is no more. There are many examples of Masonic cemeteries that
reftect great discredit to our Craft. There are others that reftect great
credit.
Imagine, if you will, your own reaction to the experience of the
descendants of a departed grandfather on their Brst visit to his resting
place in a Masonic cemetery, to ftnd that the Masonic burial place was
surrounded by a dilapidated six-foot board fence which concealed a
more dilapidated burial ground. This plot had no direct entrance, it
being necessary to climb a ladder to gain access. W 'hile I cite this as
a flagrant example of neglect, there are many more examples throug'hout
the state that warrant a careful and continuing vigilance that the ground

DE MoLAY

At the 1956 Communication a resolution was adopted declaring it
to be the policy of Grand Lodge that constituent Lodges be permitted
to sponsor De Molay Chapters, but prohibiting the use of Lodge funds
for such purpose. An amendment (Section 159.1 ), designed to provide
the law for such sponsorship, failed of adoption. The Grand Master
ruled that permission to sponsor Chapters of De Molay would be the
policy of Grand Lodge. I have not supplemented the policy referred to
by either proclamation or ruling, as it is my sincere conviction that in
so doing confusion would be the result.
Masonry is an ancient and honorable institution, having its origin
in antiquity. Down through the ages it has adhered to certain fundamental principles. Among these is one that leaves to each individual
Mason the discliarge of his civic and personal responsibilities. This has
proved to be a sound fundamental concept, for it has insured peace and
harmony among our Lodges and the Craft generally.
There are many who believe that Lodges should ofHcially sponsor
the Order of De Molay and its Chapters. However, there are just as
many, or more, who sincerely believe that Lodges should not sponsor
such Order or its Chapters. Since the matter is, to say the least, controversial, it could threaten the peace and harmony of our Lodges and
the Craft.
The Order of De Molay is a separate and distinct organization,
having its own laws, rules and regulations, and its own international,
national and local officers, who are not and could not be subject to
control either by Grand Lodge or the constituent Lodges. Further, at
no time within the history of the Grand Lodge of California has it or
its constituent Lodges ever sponsored any organization, even though
that organization may require direct Masonic affiliation. To so sponsor
such an organization would constitute an innovation in Masonic fundamental law and could not be done by a mere declaration of policy, but
would require an amendment to our law. But the Order of De Molay

cannot even qualify under direct Masonic affiliation, as its membership
is open to relatives and non-relatives, requiring the sponsorship only df

I do not mean to imply that the Order of De Malay is not a worthy

personal responsibility, will insure the continued preservation of that
"peace and harmony" that is so essential if Masonry is to fulfill its
mission in our lives and in the world.
As evidence of my interest in the youth of our State, I caused to be

individual civic and personal responsibilities to the end that they would

Order of De Malay, Job's Daughters, the Rainbow Girls, and the many

sincere in their service to youth as those who apply themselves to De
Molay, and therein lies part of die controversy.

exists, and I sincerely believe that the policy adopted by Grand Lodge
in the last Communication should be rescinded.

declaring the Royal Order of Caritas and the Amaranth Foundation,
Inc., as un-Masonic. The flrst-named order was the outgrowth of dissension and a lawsuit. Included in the many Orders requiring Masonic

Court of Amaranth, State of California." For many years the prerequisite of membership in that body was membership in the Order of the
Eastern Star. In more recent years they modifled this requirement and
made it the same as the Order of the Eastern Star. Within the membership of the Grand Court of Amaranth, State of California, a group
of dissidents withdrew from the Grand Court, formed a board of 16
directors, formed a corporation, and filed Articles of lnco!lporation for
another Masonically related body to be called the Order of Amaranth,
Incorporated. T,he Grand Court of Amaranth immediately asked for
statutory relief and the matter was taken to court, where the evidence
established that the original Grand Court of Amaranth was a legally
and duly incorporated organization with a proprietorship in the name
"Amaranth," and the courts of this state considered t'he formation and
the name of the Order of Amaranth, lncoriporated, to be an unlawful
infringement and so entered a judgment. The next event was the flling
of papers by a new corporation with the same directors, using all
the
previously adjudged Articles of Incorporation, except ~he name 1tse.lf
changed wherever it appeared to Royal Order of Cantas, and again
preserving the Masonic prerequisite for membership eligibility.
The judgment in favor of the Grand Court of Amaranth, State of
California, permanently enjoined the dissidents from doing the acts and
things complained of in the proceedings and is flnal. Yet this same group,
among whom are many members of the Craft, persisted in their designs
which had been judged improper and thereby injurious to the Grand
Lodge of California and the Craft generally. My investigation revealed

SHRINE CIRCUSES

A full story surrounding the activities of the so-called Shrine Circuses is contained in the Report of the Committee on Commercialism at
the 1956 Communication of Grand Lodge (Pages 164-167, 1956 Proceedings). This subject has also been discussed on many previous
occasions.
To my personal knowledge, many officers of the various Temples in
California had been cautioned many times to conduct these affairs in a
Masonic manner. At the 1956 Communication of Grand Lodge. your
Grand Master was directed to take whatever action he deemed necessary
to force any organization to cease and desist any such enterprise (Page
321, 1956 Proceedings). This was done. Your Grand Master and the
Committee on Commercialism met with the heads of the Shrine Temples
and reviewed the rather unsavory record of the Circuses. It became the
duty of your Grand Master to issue an edict, a copy of which is contained in the Exhibits of this message, which erased the association of
·a strictly private commercial enterprise from the philosophical and fraternal escutcheon of our Craft.
While the action may have seemed precipitate to some, it was done
only after long and careful deliberation. There had been many complaints over the recent years of the increasing high pressure by the
promoters of the Shrine Circus in their solicitation of advertising and
the sale of block seats. These solicitations used the Shriners Hospitals
for Crippled Children and often inferred that they were the beneficiaries
of the support of the so-called Shrine Circus. As evidence of the objections to this type of solicitation began to accumulate, it became immediately apparent that the commercial aspect of the Shrine Circus had gone
out o·f bounds and was sufficient reason to declare the association unMasonic. But added to that were investigations by Better Business
Bureaus, inquiries from bunco squads of police departments and complaints within our Fraternity as well, not only from Masons who were
members of our constituent Lodges only, but from Masons who were
Shriners as well.
This was perhaps the most far-reaching edict that had ever been
issued by any Grand Lodge jurisdiction. It is needless to say that the
immediate effect of this edict was echoed in the halls of Masonry and
the prerequisite groups with the roll of thunder. Pressure of every kind
was applied that would have given a liberalizing interpretation to the
edict, but your Grand Master, backed up by members of the Fraternity,
who are Masons first, last and always, stood ·firm and the edict rode
out the storm.

SAN JosE SITUATION

Which brings me now to one of the most trying and troublesome
incidents of the year...• In and around San Jose there has been what
is known as a "Santa Clara Valley Shrine Club." Many of its members,
together with members from other Shrine Clubs in the area, have been
preparing for the day when a petition would be granted by the Shrine
of North America for a charter to form their own Temple. During the
past Jew years such a petition has been circulated under the leadership
of a steering committee, whose efforts exceeded all bounds of Masonry
and propriety and created a condition that aroused much bitterness,
Masonic unrest, and discredit to our Cra ft.
Ample evidence was presented to me that in the desire to form a
new Temple, members o'f the group had inaugurated a program of
coercion, economic reprisals, boycotts and other injury, not merely
1

With the issuance of this edict much pressure was brought to bear
and there was muC'h frantic maneuvering of the so-called steering committee, which explored every avenue of approach that might relieve.
modify or revoke the edict. But the Grand •Master held his ground and
at the last session of the Imperial Council of the Shrine of North
America the San Jose petition was denied, and the area must now wait
for a period o'f three years before a new petition may be circulated.

•

My purpose was to dissolve the group and thereby bar the unMasonic practices used in its formation. I did not intend to bar another
movement to form a Shrine Temple in the San Jose area at some future
date by means which are consonant wit'h Masonic principles. I have so
advised the Lodges under date of August 21st.
All of these matters which I have reported are matters which I report
with some reluctance and regret that they have happened. Each action
was taken at the time of necessity with the sole purpose of maintaining
the integrity of the Craft. A Grand Master cannot make decisions for
the good of Masonry that are always going to be met with immediate
and unanimous approval of the membership. Each one of the issues I
have presented here has friends in this session. You, as an individual.
have the right to deal with any one or all of them subjectively. Grand
Lodge, the coordinating body that considers only the welfare of all the
Lodges and all the Masons in California, must deal with these problems
objectively.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
CONDITION OF THE CRAFT

In February of this year it was my privilege to attend the Conference
of Grand Masters in Washington, D.C. It was my great honor to represent the sixth largest jurisdiction in the United States-the Grand
Lodge of California. During the Conference of Grand Masters the
Masons of California presented to The George Washington Masonic
National Memorial Association the second of the two great murals
which now adorn the Memorial Hall, and it was my proud duty to make
that presentation on behalf of all the Masons of California. It is not
my intent to take this opportunity to describe the ceremony or the pictures, but I believe it is worthy of the time required to tell you of the
importance of California in the national 'Picture of Freemasonry in the
United States.
My brethren, days of tremendous responsibility lie immediately
ahead. Today. with an estimated population of fifteen million people,
California is the second largest state in the Union. Every day marks a
higher migration to our state, and it is predicted with confidence that
California is destined to become the most heavily populated commonwealth years ahead of what the experts tell us. Even the most conservative Masonic estimate would give California a Masonic population of
sojourners from other jurisdictions equal at least to the membership in
our constituent Lodges, and every passing day adds to that figure.
In the Conference of Grand Masters in Washington, all of the
Grand Masters were very much aware of this western migration and
they manifested a great interest. not only in our growth but in our
handling of matters of Masonic influence and importance.
The history and traditions of the human race show that the course
of civilization has been from east to west. From the Far East of antiquity
it moved to the Middle East and across the Near East, and then to
Europe. It spanned the Atlantic and moved westward to form the thirteen colonies. Still the migration westward continued and spread over
the western continent until today it crowds the most western shore of
the farthest western frontier. From here the course is eastward-from
where the sun sets toward where the sun rises.
At present there are more than four million Masons with membership
in the Lodges of the United States. If the estimate of the number of
sojourners in this state is correct and is added to the number of Masons
in California Lodges, we have a total of approximately 500,000 Masons
within our borders, or 12,!.1% of all the Masons in the United States
now reside in the California jurisdiction.
These comparative figures should offer California Lodges a very
optimistic outlook by merely drawing on the number of sojourners as
potentials of increase for further strengthening our Lodges. Our laws
permit dual membership, so that if, for reasons of sentiment, the sojourn-

GENERAL ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

As the events of this Grand Lodge year have :progressed, each day
has given a greater awareness to the structure of California Freemasonry. And now, at the end of our Masonic year, I am faced with
the problem of voicing my appreciation of the help and encouragement
that have been my greatest strength. Without the assistance of the
Officers of Grand Lodge it would have been impossible to fulfill either
the duties or the responsibilities of stewardship. Their readiness to serve
has been the means of meeting every demand made upon Grand Lodge
for official representation. The tireless devotion of the Deputy Grand
Master, the Rig'ht Worshipful Leo E. Anderson, an~ of the G~and
Wardens, the Right Worshipful Phil Myers and the Right Worshipful
Joe Shell, as well as the Most Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilso?· Gra?d
Secretary, have been an inspiration and example of Masonic service
we11 worthy of imitation. And all of the other Officers of the Grand
Lodge family, according to their authority and opportunity, have been
equally diligent. I have thanked all of them personally, and I now thank
them publicly.
And to the members of the many permanent and special Grand
Lodge Committees who are charged with the responsibility of maintaining the wise and efficient administration of the many Grand Lodge functions, California Freemasonry owes to them a great debt of gratitude.
From a Grand Master's point of view there are no obscure Grand Lodge
Committees. Each has an important part in the control of Masonic
welfare, and all the members of these Committees have fulBlled their
offices with credit to themselves and with distinction to the Craft. So to
you, on b~half of a11 California Freemasonry, and with my personal
appreciation, may I say. "Well done, good and faithful servants of
. Masonry!"
Brethren, we are living in the highest civilization that the world has
ever known. Mankind is no longer earthbound-he is probing the secrets
of the universe, the unknown atmosphere of the heavens, the darkness
and depths of the seas. We no longer measure great distances in miles--
