London is overnight from San Francisco or Los Angeles-and within
the last few weeks man flew from coast to coast at a speed that almost
matched the course of the sun through the heavens. Every day science
seeks further penetration into the great storehouse of nature's secrets,
so that nations are ready to meet the challenges that a nervous and
troubled world may visit upon us.
Masonry must continue to 'furnish the leadership required of it or
become subservient to organizations it has spawned.
Masonry cannot meet in the future any greater challenges t'han it
has survived in the past. Our ancient landmarks are more secure today
than they have ever been in the entire history and tradition of Masonic
philosophy. While nations strive to become stronger than each other,
Masons strive only to be better than themselves-and therein lies a
strength greater than the most powerful weapons.

good which it has exerted through the ages. It has been my firm and
steadfast purpose that in all matters pertaining to fundamental Masonic
morality, that there would be no compromises between expediency and
principle.
California Freemasonry has a proud and rich inheritance. It was born
a little over a century ago. when California was the .farthest and fiercest
frontier in the world. It was nursed by our early Masons through the
perilous days and lawless nights of the gold rush. It was trained in the
manly virtues by Masonic forefathers whom history proudly records as
early pioneers, and for 108 years has continuously labored in the interest
of brotherly love, relief and truth.
Albert Pike, the philosopher, statesman, general, and Master Mason
said this: "Everything that exists ... every movement in nature •••
every counsel of providence, •.. every interposition of God, centers on
one point-the fidelity of man."
And I say to you men of :California Masonry . . . everything that
here exists centers on one point-your fidelity. That which is given to
every Master Mason, strictly in charge is the only true wealth of
Masonry. It is the symbol of our wisdom, strength and beauty, the purpose o·f all Freemasonry.
One year ago. I uttered my first words as Grand Master •.. and they
expressed my gratitude and appreciation for the high honor that the
Fraternity 'h ad bestowed upon me. I dedicated myself to a foll year of
unselfish service in the labors you had entrusted to my care. In these
closing days of that term, I can only reiterate my deep sense of obligation
to the Brotherhood of California Freemasonry who have paid me this
high tribute of confidence and trust. The memories of your warm friendships and many acts of kindness and personal consideration will survive
far beyond transitory honors and ceremonies.
So in closing ... my brethren ..• let us ever remember •.. that we
travel from West to East, in search of that which was lost. From West
to East toward the source of light. May the Great Architect of the
Universe cause the Light of His Wisdom to illumine our pathway so that
we may ful611 our earthly purpose in the duty we owe to Him •.• to our
country ••• to our neighbor ... and to ourselves.

MASONRY IN A CHANGING WORLD

My brethren, we are gathered here in the twilight hours of another
Grand Lodge year, to reflect on the events of the past year, and where
they have taken us. It is fitting therefore, that we contemplate-not
only upon the Masonic world within our ancient and venerated Craft,
but also that we project and orient our Masonic concepts into the changing world without.
The course of Masonry throughout the centuri~s of our Fraternity.
and throughout the ages of our traditions and philosophies • . . is one
straight line ... leading directly 'from where we stand as Masons today.
back into the darkest and most remote corridors of antiquity. It has had
many challenges from the left and from the right . . • and there is
evidence that opposing philosophies have attempted to cut across its
path, but the course has ever been ..• onward and upward, and what
might have become obstacles, disappeared when confronted with Masonic ,patience, determination, and perseverance.
The course of Masonry into the future is one straight line, leading
directly from where we stand as Masons today-carefully posted with
our ancient landmarks that have been severely tested in the crucible of
time, and leads into eternity. Our aims and purposes today, are exactly
the same as they were in the beginning, and should temain exactly as
they are until time is no more. I cannot subscribe to any school of thought
that would change any of these fundamental principles of Freemasonry,
and with a "changing world" as an excuse, involve ·Masons or Masonry
in any project, subsidy, or enterprise that alters these fundamental
Masonic truths.
iif Masons of every age had yielded to their temporal influences, and
changed our ritual and usages to conform to their changing world, our
ancient Craft Masonry would have lost much of the potent influence for

EXHIBIT "E"

NUMBER 3, NOVEMBER 1
A brother was made an Entered Apprentice in May of 1946 and was
Passed to the degree of Fellow Craft in October of the same year, the;n
he disappeared until August 1956, when he requeste d to complete his
Masonry. Had he forfeited his right to continue as he did not present
himself properly qualified for the next degree within a period of Bve
years?
Decision: Provisions of Ross Digest 241, as amended 1953, are to be
followed; then if the brother should present himself for the Third Degree
he could be stopped by proper objection.
NUMBER 4, NOVEMBER 9
A man who had worked in Saudi Arabia for several years and had
maintained his residence address in Californ ia, applied for degrees. He
had used his brother's home as permane nt address for past twenty years;
he was still working in Saudi Arabia when his application was received.
It was learned that While he uses his brother's address for all business
purposes and claims residence there, yet for income tax purposes he
claims non-residence. May his application be received?
Decision: A man cannot be both a resident and a non-resident. lf a
man claims non-residence because of income tax purposes, he cannot be
considered a resident of the community. His application, therefore, cannot be received.
NUMBER 5, NOVEMBER 13
What steps should be taken by Eden Lodge No. 113 for corrective
action requested by the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Fi~ancing to
comply with R.D .. 151 and 152, relating to a Temple corporation?
Decision: This calls for a combined civil and Masonic law study and
requires the services of legal counsel. With that reservation, it appears
that Eden Lodge may amend tihe Articles of Incorporation to eliminate
the provision& of Article Fifth relating to t'he selection of directors.
NUMBER 6, DECEMBER 10
May application be made for a Fifty-Ye ar Button for a brother who
is confined to a State hospital and has little contact with reality?
Decision: No. We do not present a Button posthumously nor do we
present it to relatives. In this case the ceremony would have absolutely
no meaning whatever; therefore, no application should be made for such
a Button.
NUMBER 7, DECEMBER 18
May a Masonic funeral service be held for a deceased Mason who
was lost at sea and his body not recovered?
Decision: Yes. The funeral service is a symbolic one and it is entirely
proper to pay respect to the memory of a departed brother even though
his last earthly remains may be lost at sea.

May a lodge establish a Foundation with the power to administer,

NUMBER 10, JANUARY 11

May. lodges join with the cqncordant bodies and the Eastern Star,
White Shrine, Job's Daughters and De Molay in publishing a bulletin
without advertising?
Decision: No. The lodges may join with concordant bodies in publishing a bulletin without advertising, but the concordant bodies include
only the Scottish and York Rites. (Grand Master Clausen. Decision No.
39, 1955: 355.)
NUMBER 11, JANUARY 11
Is an applicant eligible for tlhe degrees of Masonry when his history
shows that at the age of 19 he was charged with a felony, later reduced
to a misdemeanor, probation granted and the record expunged by dismissal thereafter: and did not serve time in the state or federal prison?
Decision: Yes. (Grand Master Clausen, Decision No. 36, 1955: 59,
353.)
NUMBER 12, JANUARY 11
May an apprentice brother who suffered physical diebility after initiation be advanced?
Decision: Yes. Physical disability is no bar to advancement ( R.D.,
515). In this case, however, the candidate probably can conform sub..
stantially to what is required of :him by the degrees, albeit not be able
to conform to tlhe requirements for preparation. The Lodge may proceed
to confer the remaining degrees and no dispensation for this purpose is
required.
NUMBER 13, JANUARY 11
May a Lodge try a member for unmasonic conduct who answered
"No" to Question 12 in his application for the Degrees and who had

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

103

b~ convicted of a felony and has served three years in the state penitentiary?
Decision: Yes. The member falsely answered the question in his
application as to whether he knew of any moral reason that ~ould prevent :him from becoming a Freemason and also concealed his record.
Consequently he may be tried. {Grand Master Harwell, Decision No.
20, 1954: 83, 270; Grand Master Clausen. Decision No. 36, 1955: 59,

NUMBER 14, JANUARY 29
Is it permissible to work out an agency dea~ witlh the Trust D~
ment of the Citizens National Trust and Savings Bank, under which
that bank would supervise and advise as to investments? Would this be
permitted and, if so, would the •fees charged by the Trust Department
be a proper disbursement?
Decision: Yes. However, in any transaction of the Board of Trustees
or the Trust Department of the Citizens National Bank Building by
authorization of the Board of Trustees, Section 152.1 must be adhered
to. The trustees must consult Moody's Investors Service but may conisder this service advisory. Fees charged by the Trust Department of
tlhe bank would be considered a proper disbursement.
NUMBER 15, FEBRUARY 6
A brother was placed on two years' probation by a Superior Court
for being guilty of passing bad dhecks and heavy drinking: his plea of
guilty made him a felon. He was notified that if he did not reply or seek
trial within sixty days from that date he would stand expelled from all
rights and privileges of Masonry. Subsequentl~. he was picked up
violation of probation: and later he was committed to a State hospital
for alcoholism. He had not replied to his lodge's notice and the sixty days
were up. Could he be ex·pelled?
Decision: Section 332 of Ross Digest requires ( 1) conviction of
felony and ( 2) imprisonment. (See Section 953, R.D., and Section 1OM.
R.D.) The brother should be tried for unmasonic conduct for offenses
of which he was found guilty in civil court.
NUMBER 16, FEBRUARY 14
May the square and compass be used on a calling card of a member
of the Sciots?
Decision: No. This would be contrary to Masonic law and principles.
NUMBER 17, FEBRUARY 27
Must a Master Mason wait one year before he is permitted to join
an organization requiring Masonic membership as a prerequisite, even
though this organization does not confer degrees?
Decision: Yes. If exceptions were allowed there would be no end to
requests of this nature.

NUMBER 18, MARCH 7
What procedure should be taken in respect of a Master Mason,
plural member of two California Lodges, who, when visiting Laurel
Lodge, was asked in open Lodge by the Master the answers to questions
on a petition for affiliation, whereupon he signed the petition, the Master
then signed as a recommender and had a Past Master present sign also
although this Past Master stated that he did not know the petitioner:
and which petition was never read by the Secretary in open Lodge: and,
an investigating committee having been appointed and return of its
report being made at a stated meeting two months later, last August, the
petitioner was declared elected to membership?

Decision: No. The vice, as I see it, in letting the Sciots undertake
this particular project is ( 1 ) that other organizations come up with something different and when told that the particular undertaking is taboo,
they point out the fact that some other organization is engaged in a
public money-raising scheme, hence why can't they: and (2) this particular undertaking does violence to the letter of my edict and certainly
to the spirit of it.
Public money-raising schemes should not be indulged in by prerequisite bodies; if such organizations cannot be supported by their
members they are not worthy of existence. These organizations use their
official name, claim affiliation with Masonry, and so far as the public is
concerned, are believed to be Masonic: hence, the public in buying a
ticket or patronizing the project or event, thinks Masonry is being aided.
It is most unfair to the Blue Lodges which are restrained, whereas
Masonic members in these very same Blue Lodges may band together
in another organization and endeavor to do what their own Blue Lodges
cannot do, and if any onus attaches to the sc·heme, project or undertaking, Masonry suffers.
NUMBER 21, APRIL 2
May a Lodge resolve to set aside annually a sum from its refreshment
funds and thus accumulate a sum certain for a "centennial fund"?
Decision: No. This would be an improper attempt to bind the future
membership of the Lodge.

Decision: No.

May the Koran be used in the ritual of the Masonic order, in place
of the Holy Bible?
Decision: No. Drapeau, 1952: 330 R.D .. Sec. 801 (c): C.M.C. appendix, p. 364, former R.D. Sec. 650. Drapeau, 1952: C.M.C., Sec.
554.
Our law provides that the Holy Bible must be used and it is the only
volume that can be used.
NUMBER 25, APRIL 22
May Napa High Twelve Club set up a non-profit organization that
would take subscriptions or renewals to any magazine or trade journal
and periodical, all profits to go to the Napa De Molay Chapter?

104

Decision: The applicant has not returned to a Lodge meeting, nor
signed the By-Laws, nor paid any dues. T:he purported election of petitioner was void in that the conditions prerequisite to election for affiliation were not followed. (Sections 431, 526, 528, 556 and 557, C.M.C.)
Consequently. the Lodge minutes and records should be corrected
accordingly.
In the event the petitioner desires membership in Laurel Lodge he
should present a new petition and the proper steps looking toward affiliation should be followed. (Section 557r, C.M.C.)
There does not seem to be any demit problem involved, perhaps
because of his multiple membership. (Section 432, C.M.C.)
The attention of the then-Master was called to this matter as being
highly irregular and the Secretary was instructed that the then-Master
be reprimanded before the Lodge for his thoughtless disregard of our
regulations.
NUMBER 19, MARCH 21
Should members of Lomita Lodge No. 644 be encouraged to buy lots
in the proposed Masonic section of a cemetery on the outskirts of
Lomita?
Decision: No. It would appear that the cemetery is having difficulty
in selling lots and the name of Masonry should not be loaned to it for
the purpose of helping its sales. The lodge should not, under any circumstances, encourage its members to buy lots in any so-called Masonic
section; nor should the Master or any other officer or any member thereof do so. Many unfortunate experiences have resulted from similar commercial ventures by cemeteries. We have no way of knowing whether
twenty-five or fifty years from now the situation would not develop in
this particular cemetery.

for one of our lodges and hence it should not be sanctioned for an allied
Masonic organization.

NUMBER 28, JUNE 25
(Deputy Grand Master)
Request that Grand Lodge give clearance to the Department of
Social Service of the City of Los Angeles for solicitations in Los Angeles
on behalf of the Omaha Home for Boys of Omaha, Nebraska.
Decision: Grand Lodge cannot give the clearance requested. Our
Masonic Homes and lodges are not permitted to sanction any solicitation
of funds from the general public for the support of any Masonic activity.
The giving of the clearance requested would be in effect a sanction o.f the
proposed solicitation.

NUMBER 31, JULY 31
Needles Lodge No. 326: May the proposed scholarship program be
financed from refreshment fund of the lodge?
Decision: No. It would not be a proper exipenditure for the refreshment fund ( C.M.C .• Sec. 412).
NUMBER 32, AUGUST 1
Unity Lodge No. 368: Can the lodge, when properly put before it at
a Stated Meeting, approve payment from lodge funds of a bill from a
restaurant for meals of the officers of the lodge incurred in conjunction
with a business meeting of the officers of the lodge called by the Master?
Decision: No. Expenditures are for purposes of refreshments and
for the promotion of fraternal intercourse. (C.M.C .• 409, 410, 411, 412.)
NUMBER 33, AUGUST 5
Oriental Lodge No. 1H: If a Lodge has spent all of its revenue over
a number of years, but in so doing has spent only an average of 10%
for social purposes, is it permissible to spend at a later date, out of the
revenues, an amount equivalent to the unspent 20% of the total revenue
of the respective years for social purposes? (The 20% was not spent on
social purposes, however, it was spent on operating expenses.) It has
been the belief of the Master that the 30% for social purposes must come
out of the current revenue after all other expenses have been met, and
should not come out of the reserves.
Decision: No. No accumulation for refreshment purposes can be
made of funds which the lodge does not have, because it has spent them
once for other purposes and therefore cannot spend them again.
NUMBER 34, SEPTEMBER 9
Clear Lake Lodge No. 183: May an application for degrees be accepted from an applicant who answered "No" to question No. 6: can
he change this answer to "Yes" and resubmit his application for degrees?
Decision: Yes. The applicant has maintained his home in Lower
Lake for nearly three years, at which place his family resides.

NUMBER 29, JuNE 25
(Deputy Grand MasterJ
Request by Mrs. Marilyn J. Mayfield for approval of proposed state
law requiring covering of abandoned water wells, oil wells, holes and
cisterns and covering of other excavations, etc.
Decision: No. Grand Lodge and its lodges are prohibited by our laws
and regulations from engaging in this type of political activity.
NUMBER 30, JuNE 25
(Deputy Grand MasterJ
May lodge refreshment funds be used to contribute to the campaign
being carried on by Californians for Public Schools?
Decision: No. Lodges cannot use ttheir refreshment funds for this
purpose.

NUMBER 26, APRIL 29
Does the Ionic Foundation come within the jurisdiction of the Committee on Lodge Financing or Grand Lodge?
Decision: Yes. The prerequisite requirements which are tied directly
into Ionic Lodge No. 520 and the organizational Masonic pattern call
for Grand Lodge supervision under Section 199, C.M.C., among other
Masonic Laws. Moreover, the Ionic Foundation may be held to be an
agency of the Lodge, civilly.
NUMBER 27, APRIL 19
If a candidate is unable to conform to what the degrees require,
should he be dropped from the rolls and his money refunded?
Decision: The rule is that if after election but before initiation an
applicant is discovered to be ineligible by reason of physical disqualifications, the Master should not proceed with the initiation but may direct
withdrawal of the application and refund the fees (C.M.C. 531e).

Dear Brother Tigh:
On my return from an extended trip, I have received many communications and clippings relative to publicity given your statements
regarding action taken by the Supreme Council of the Grotto countenancing gambling. I enclose herewith copy of a clipping taken from the
Oakland Tribune of June 20, 1957.
This publicity has done incalculable damage and has caused confusion among the Craft in this jurisdiction. Our law is speci.6c to the
effect that no lodge or individual Mason shall directly or indirectly give
the aid or countenance of Masonry to any raffle, lottery or other gambling enterprise forbidden by law, nor shall any Mason participate in
the conduct or promotion of any such raffle, lottery or ~ther gambling
enterprise conducted in the name of or directly or indirectly for the
pecuniary benefit of any lodge or of any organization a prerequisite of
membership W'herein is that the person be a Master Mason. ( Masonic
Code, sec. 685. )
Every Mason is subject to the laws of Masonry whether he is acting
as a member of some other organization or not. He cannot as a member
of the Grotto do what he cannot do as a Mason.
If you do not desire to have disciplinary action taken against your
organization in this state. it would be well for you to take immediate and
affirmative steps to counteract this unfavorable publicity which you
have visited on the Craft in this state, and to advise me just what steps
you are taking to rectify the damage which has been done.
An early reply is requested.

Sincerely and .fraternally,
Enclosure
L. HAROLD ANDERSON

FREE AND AccEPTED MASONS
OP CALIFORNIA
May 28, 1957
To All Lodges and Masons in the furisdiction:
It appearing to me. after investigation and ·h earing. that the following
facts are true:
1. The Royal Order of Caritas is a fraternal organization recently
iJlCorporated in the State of California, and Masonic affiliation or related
Masonic affiliation is a requirement for membership therein:
2. Said Royal Order of Caritas was promoted, formed and organized
by a dissident group who are or were members of the Order of
Amaranth:
3. A legal proceeding was heretofore commenced by the Order of
Amaranth against said dissident group or some of them Who are or were
members of said Order of Amaranth and who are the promoters and
organizers of the Royal Order of Caritas: as a result of said legal proceeding a judgment was entered in favor of said Order of Amaranth
permanently enjoining said dissident group f~om doing ~e acts and
things complained of in said proceeding, and said judgment 1s now final:
i . One of the prime purposes of said Order of Caritas is to take over
the control and sponsorship of a purported charitable organization
known as the Amaranth Foundation. Inc., a self-perpetu ating corporation;
5. Much bitterness, discord and strife exist among and between
Masons by reason of the foregoing facts, and said schemes are misleading and questionable, and the good name of Masonry and the peace and
harmony which should exist among Masons is thereby seriously jeopardized, and a continuance thereof would be injurious to the Grand
Lodge of California and the Craft generally:
Now, Therefore. I, L. Harold Anderson, Grand Master of Masons
in California, after careful and long consideratio n and in pursuance of
my powers and responsibility for supervision of the Craft (C.M.C. 13"4,
etc. ) , do hereby proclaim and decree that no Mason subject to the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California shall be, become, or remain
a member of said Royal Order of Caritas nor said Amaranth Foundation. Inc., or their successors by change of name, nor shall any sudh
Mason, directly or indirectly, aid or assist said Royal Order of Caritas
nor said Amaranth Foundation , Inc .. or their successors by change of
name, in any manner whatsoever.
A known violation of this Edict shall be deemed un-Masonic conduct, and any Mason found guilty of such violation shall be subject to
the penalty of reprimand, suspension or expulsion.
This Edict shall be read in Lodge next following its receipt.
Attest:
Fraternally yours,
LLOYD E. WILSON

that said group, or some of them, •have secured and attempted to secure
members for said group by use of threats of economic reprisal, boycotts
and other injury and by actual economic reprisal, boycotts, coercion, and
slander of persons who have not chosen to join them or agree with diem
and by the harassment of such latter persons and their families 1have
inflicted serious injury and caused distress to such persons in their
businesses and in their peace of mind; and
It having been established to the satisfaction of the Grand Master
that such acts and practices have been widespread and lb.ave been
encouraged and participated in by many members of the aforesaid group,
both individually and in concert with others, and that said acts and practices are wholly questionable in nature, unethical and unmasonic, and
have resulted in much injury. distress, bitterness, and masonic unrest,
and have brought discredit upon Masonry:
Now Therefore, I, Grand Master of Masons in California, pursuant
to section 134 of the California ·Masonic Code among others, do hereby
order and enjoin that no Mason in this jurisdiction S'hall become a member of. or continue to be a member of, the group attempting to form said
El Zaraa Temple of the Shrine, or any other named new temple of the
Shrine in the San Jose area, or of the so-called Temple Steering Committe for said El Zaraa Temple, unless and until this order s'hall be
modified, revoked or rescinded by the Grand Master or by the Grand
Lodge of California.
And I 'further direct that this order shall be read at the next stated
meeting of each lodge located in die Counties of Santa Clara, Santa
Cruz, San Mateo, Monterey and San Benito.

December 5, 1956

To All Masons and Particularly to the Potentates, Chief Rabbans and
Members of the Several Shrine Temples within the Grand Jurisdiction
of the Grand Lodge of California:
There have been many complaints of commercial, unethical and misleading operations by the Shrine ( A.A.O.N.M.S.) in operating circuses
for which tickets were sold to the public.
Specifically, the Committee on Commercialism has verified and found
these violations: ( 1) The circuses are commercial ventures in which the
Shrine engages a commercial organization to operate the circuses which
diereby use the good name of the Shrine and of Masonry for commercial
purposes; ( 2) Tickets are sold to the public on the basis of the good
name and reputation of the Shrine and of Masonry and with an inference that the proceeds go to charity: ( 3) High pressure "boiler room"
solicitation is condoned and often suggested by the advance agents of
circuses: ( 4) Ticket sales to the public far exceed the actual seating
capacity: and ( 5) The proceeds do not go to charity but, after deducting

117

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

circus costs. profit, and commissions to pitch men, go to the local Shrine
Temples to be used for whatever pul'lpose they elect.
Suc!h conduct violates basic Masonic law and tends to bring discredit
upon Masonry. It is conduct unbecoming to Masons. Since it involves an
organization requiring its members to be Masons, it involves Masonry.
Moreover, Masonry in general is being harmed in that the general public
is involved. Unless action is taken to stop these practices, there may
result a destruction in that influence which Masons ;have in this country.
We must so conduct ourselves at all times as to keep our obligations and
carry out our responsibilities as Masons operating in a free, democratic
country. (See Ross Digest 126.1, 127: Resolution of Jurisprudence Committee, 1956: 321.)
Unethical Projects.
Ross Digest Sec. 126.1
No Lodge or body, or organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership, or member thereof shall,
directly or indirectly. engage in any business, project, venture,
.promotion, scheme or plan which is unethical, fraudulent, misleading or illegal. Any violation of this section shall be deemed
unmasonic conduct. ( 1955.)
Commercial Ventures.
Ross Digest Sec. 127
A Lodge shall not sponsor, or by resolution or otherwise sanction, or permit the use of the name of the Lodge in connection
with, or for the purpose of furthering any collateral financial
undertaking, or commercial venture, whether for profit or not,
which shall not have- been approved by the Grand Master, nor
shall any member of any Lodge be permitted to do so except in
his individual capacity. and without the use of the name oif the
Lodge.
No Lodge or member of a Lodge, 'Shall solicit, sponsor, insert,
place or print advertising of any kind in or for any medium or
publication, which purports to be Masonic in name or character,
or which is published by or .for any body, order or organization
requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership.
(1954.)
Resolution of Jurisprudence Committee.
In the light of the Report of the Committee on Commercialism, your Committee on Jurisprudence begs leave to present the
following resolution:
Resolved: ~hat the Committee on Commercialism is directed
to make serious and exten'Sive investigation of all business and/or
entertainment schemes of organizations making membership in
the Masonic Order a prerequisite to their membership: and that

if any such organization continues any enterprise found by the
Committee to reflect upon Masonry in general, or violating the
laws of this Grand Lodge, that the Grand Master is directed to
take all necessary action to force any such organization to cease
and desist any such enterprises.
Resolved, further, that the Grand Master direct trials for unmasonic conduct of any Mason who engages in any such enter·
prises.
Unanimously adopted. ( 1956.)
In addition to the California Masonic law above quoted, Imperial
Shrine law, Section 232, provides as follows:
Sec. 232. Use of the word Noble, etc., as advertising, prohibited. The use of the word "Noble," "Shriner," or any variation
thereof. or any term, sign or symbol of the Order, for commercial
or other business enterprises is prohibited. Any Noble violating
this Section may be suspended or expelled from the Order.
Should the Temple of which the offender is a member neglect to
take action, the Imperial Potentate may suspend such offender
until the next regular session of the Imperial Council, at which
session the suspension may be made permanent. Any Temple
neglecting to take action in such a case is subject to having its
charter arrested by the Imperial Potentate. Provided, however,
that this section shall not apply to those Who are regularly engaged in standard Shrine supplies. uniform'S, regalia and emblems.
Accordingly. and good cause appearing therefor, it is my order and
edict, effective immediately, that no Mason in California or under the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California shall directly or indirectly
engage. take part, or participate in sponsoring, holding, conducting, or
operating any circus or like commercial venture or event which is spon·
sored, conducted, or operated, directly or indirectly. by any organization
of prerequisite Masonic membership or temple, club, committee, or agent
thereof, and for which public support is requested or for which tickets,
programs, or other items are sold to the public. A violation of this order
and edict will be considered a violation of basic Masonic law and, therefore, unmasonic conduct and will subject the offending Mason or Masons
to expulsion from the !fraternity.
It is suggested that this order be read in its entirety at the next regu·
lar meeting of the Temples within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of California.
Fraternally and sincerely yours.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE
GRAND LoDGE
FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS
OF CALIFORNIA

September 9, 1957
Mr. H. E. McCutcheon, President
Transportation Crippled Children's Club
5935 North Agnes Avenue
Temple City, California
Dear Brother McCutcheon:
It appearing to me that:
( 1) The Transportation Crippled Children's Club remains essentially a Masonic prerequisite group;
( 2) The primary purpose of said Club is to obtain and receive
donations, from Masons and non-Masons, for the Los Angeles Unit Shriners Hospital for Crippled Children, and for
that purpose said Club has identified itself with A.I.D.;
( 3) The Shriners Hospital for Crippled Children is wholly
owned and operated by an organization to which only Masons can belong;
( 4 ) The said 'hospital is generally regarded by the public, including Masons and non-Masons, as a Masonic charity
whereas in truth and in .fact said hospital is not a Masonic
charity;
( 5) The solicitation of donations for such purposes tends to and
does lead the donors, or many of them, to believe that their
donations are for the benefit of a Masonic charity; and
( 6) The Institution of Masonry does not seek or solicit charitable
aid, but, to the contrary, takes care of its own;
( 7) The continuation of the activities of said Club tends to mislead and could bring Masonry into disrepute.
Now, therefore, I, L. Harold Anderson, Grand Master of Masons
in California, after careful and long consideration, and in pursuance of
my powers and responsibility for the supervision and care of the Craft
(C.M.C.) 134, etc.), do hereby order the said Transportation Club
to cease and desist from its charity activities; and I further order that
receipt of and compliance with this order be acknowledged on or before
September 15, 1957.
Fraternally yours,

L. HAROLD ANDERSON
Grand Master

November 1, 1956
Jurisdiction:
This
in
!Adges
To All
Request has been made of the Grand Master for a ruling on the
question:
May a Lodge or Temple Association invest its funds in state
or federal building and loan associations1
The answer fs "no." See Decision No. 5, Grand Master Clausen,
1955: 46.
There was presented at the 1955 Annual Communication a resolution to amend our Masonic Law so that a Lodge or Temple Association
may invest its funds in insured building and loan or savings and loan
certificates or shares. This was not approved by a 5/6 vote, but it did
receive a majority vote and so was held over to the 1956 Annual Communication as unfinished business. R.D. 351.
At the 1956 Annual Communication the proposed Amendment was
presented but did not receive a 2/3 vote and so was defeated. R.D. 351.
Consequently, it is my direction that by January 10, 1957, the Lodges
and Temple Associations and any trustees or agents acting for them
adhere to the Masonic Law which now exists in this respect, and dispose
of any investments in building and loan or savings and loan certifkates
or shares, or deposits with such institutions. I have set the date at
January 10, 1957, so that any accrued interest which might ,faJl due
before that time may be received. In this connection, attention is invited
to the provisions of the various building and loan or savings and loan
concerns which may provide that interest ceases on notice or request
for the withdrawal of funds, and it is therefore suggested that the timing
of such notice or request for refunds, in compliance with this directive,
be given so as to obtain the maximum interest consistent with the date
I have fixed for observance of our Law.

November 15, 1956

To the Inspectors. Masters. Wardens and Brethren of the Jurisdiction:
Request has been made of the Grand Master for a ruling on the
questions:
. .
May a Lodge 'hold social or similar meetings in a building
where liquor is sold over a bar? Or may a Mason belong t? .an
organization requiring Masonic membership as a prerequisite,
which holds such meetings in a building where liquor is sol.d o~er
8 bar? (I am assuming that neither the Lodge nor the organization
itself sells and dispenses liquor or holds a liquor license.)
The answer to each is "yes."
Decision No. 4 of Grand Master Stewart, 1956, held that an o~g~n­
ization composed of Master Masons may not hold meetings in a building
where liquor is sold over a bar. This decision was based on R.D. 596
and 668 to the effect that it would not be proper for a Masonic Lodge,
as such, to hold meetings for lodges' uses and .purposes in a building
in which liquor is sold over a bar.
/
It is my view, however, that the decision of Grand Master Stew~rt
does not apply to meetings of lodges or of such organizations for social.
luncheon, dinner or similar purposes, held for example in a hote~ or club
where there is a bar. There is, of course, a matter of good taste involved
which also should govern.
Nothing herein shall be construed to alter the Masonic policy and
laws to the effect that a Mason should not belong to such an organization
if it is licensed to sell liquor or sells and dispenses liquor, or confers
degrees in a building where liquor is sold over a bar.
This shall be read in lodge at the stated meeting next following its
receipt.
Fraternally yours,
L. HAROLD ANDERSON

Attest:
LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary

Grand Ma.stet

November 21, 1956
To the Masters and Secretaries of the Lodges of this Jurisdiction:
Request has been made of the Grand Master for a ruling on the
question:
May a Master Mason make voluntary contributions to a
Lodge Blood Bank Fund? The lodge, in tum, would purchase
blood through the Salvation Army or other organizations to
replenish the Masonic Blood Bank in the area.
The answer is "yes."
It has been estimated that approximately 30% of the members of
the lodge cannot actually donate blood because of age and approximately another 15 % cannot donate for other reasons. Therefore,
approximately 45% of the members of the lodge cannot participate,
either to help themselves if they need blood, or to help other members
of the lodge, or to help other Masons.
There are many in the remaining 55% who find it inconvenient to
go to a blood bank center, or who cannot take the time from their daily
vocation to do so, or who may even have an aversion actually to giving
blood. Many of these members. as well as those wiho cannot give blood,
might prefer voluntarily to contribute to a blood bank fund whieh would
have the effect of maintaining a Masonic Blood Bank at the proper level,
thereby assisting not only their own members but other worthy .Masons
who may require blood.
Fraternally yours,
L. HAROID ANDERSON

Grand Master

LLOYD E. WILSON

The California Freemason is your publication. It is a source of
Masonic information and inspiration, and it is an important arm of our
Masonic education. A special effort must be made to get the California
Freemason into the hands of every member--especially those members
·
who are unable to attend their Lodges regularly.
The cost of publishing the California Freemason is met by the annual
subscription charge of $1.00, in addition to an appropriation by the
Grand Lodge. I ex.pect the cooperation of the Masters and Officers of
every Lodge to help increase the circulation of our quarterly by doing
some of these things:
1. The Lodge <is authorized to subscribe for each of its members, the
expendifore coming from the refreshment fund.
a. If the Lodge budget will not permit this action, the Lodge should
authorize a year's subscription for each Entered Apprentice at the time
of his initiation.
2. Appoint one or more members to solicit subscriptions for the California Freemason among your members and sojourners in your area.
Request a supply of subscription receipt books from the California Freemason office, 394 Paci6c Avenue, San Francisco 11, California.
3. Order sample copies mailed to members who cannot be seen .p ersonally. Order these from the California Freemason by sending the
names and addresses. The Lodge will be billed 25c for each sample copy
sent after eliminating present subscribers.
i. Announcement of subscription offers should be included in your
Lodge bulletin.
5. Interesting, timely articles from current issues should be read to
members at stated meetings or monthly dinners. The articles found in
each issue are meant to stimulate thought and discussion. See that they
are .pointed out as recommended reading to your membership.

PROCLAMATION OF THE GRAND MASTER
L HAROLD ANDERSON
38TH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

The week of April 29 through May 4, 1957 has been designated as
the 38th Annual Public Schools Week in California.
This event is of first importance among projects of California Freemasonry in the interest of public welfare. I echo the hope and restate the
aspiration c>f every Grand Master since 1919-that this year's program
will be one of new and expanding accomplishment. In the area of Public
Welfare, Masonry has asserted a tremendous influence by its support of
the Free Public School System. Public Schools Week, while first a Lodge
affair, has now been firmly established as an affair of the whole public
community: however. t1here must be no lessening of interest or support.
I therefore proclaim and direct:
That every Lodge in the Jurisdiction of California observe Public
Schools Week April 29 to May 4, 1957, inclusive.
That no meetings be held during that week except stated meeting if
they fall therein and meetings .for Public 'Schools Week observance.
That the suggestions offered by the Public Schools Committee be
followed whenever possible.
That a renewed and continued interest in the welfare of our public
schools, and their needs and problems, be considered throughout the
year.
That interest be stimulated as much as possible in the Grand Lodge
Scholarships for Graduate Study and Public Education and qualiJled
people be encouraged to retain their interest in the Public School System.
That this Proclamation be read at each stated meeting prior to April
24, 1957.
Attest:
LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary
January 15, 1957

"As every man receiveth the gift, even so
minister the same one to another, as good
stewards of the manifold Grace of God."
( 1 Peter: 5, 10)
To Aid and Assist.
The word "charity" has not been ~sed in the Revised Standard Version of the Ancient Manuscripts. Ancient translators found use for the
word only in the New Testament-an d it is not to be found anywhere in
the books of the Old Testament.
As originally applied, the word "charity" defined acts of human kindness. benevolence, compassion and good will. It reflected a tenderness o'f
heart and a generosity of spirit that was born of love . . . God's Love,
which is the Law, the Beauty, and the Harmony of the Universe. In
keeping with this Universal Harmony, the revised translation now reads
" ••• faith, hope and love abide, these three, but the greatest of these is
love."
Our Masonic Homes are the highest and noblest expression of brotherly love and affection. They stand as monuments of security to relieve
the distresses of dur elder brethren, to protect their widows, and to
support and educate the orphan.
"To aid and assist" is an inviolable landmark of the Craft, not with
"charity" but ·with a tenderness of heart and generosity of spirit that is
born of love. Ever remember h t the blessings we enjoy are only entrusted to our stewardship, and that we folflll our earthly purpose only by
sharing them in the spirit of benevolence. compassion and kindness.
As long as life endures, our Masonic Homes need your love. It
becomes us as Masons, therefore, that each of us according to his blessings. minister the same. one to another, as good stewards of the Grace
of God.
This Proclamation is to be read at the stated meeting held during the
month of May.
Dated: March 25, 1957.
L. HAROLD ANDERSON

L. HAROLD ANDERSON

Grand Master

To the Masters, Wardens, Secretaries and Members
of the Lodges of this Jurisdiction:
Brethren:
We have been invited to cooperate with "Californians for Public
Schools" in a matter of statewide public school importance.
I ask your helip because the general and specific provisions of Masonic law, sections 330, 331 and 33la, C.M.C., so authorize.
In view of a recent court decision, ste.ps will be taken about May 1
to start obtaining signatures on an initiative petition to amend our State
Constitution to prevent property tax exemptions for private sohools
under collegiate grade that compete with our public schools.
It is my desire that all aid be given this worthy and constructive
endeavor within the permissible limits of our law, including discussion in
lodges, committees for collection of finances and use for this purpose of
the membership roster.
Financial contributions should be sent to P.G.M. Leon 0. Wihitsell,
1027 S. Country Club Boulevard, Stockton, California, or P.G.M. Louis
C. Drapeau, Suite 1112, Citizens National Bank Building, Los Angeles
13, California.
P.G.M. John R. Moore, 453 South Spring Street, Los Angeles 13,
California, has been designated as my personal representative to direct
this campaign in the lodges for funds and signatures. In the immediate
future you will receive detailed instructions from him and I earnestly
solicit your enthusiastic cooperation.
It is directed that this communication be read at the stated meetings
in May, June, July and such other meetings as may seem appropriate.
Reference may be made to this subject in the lodge's monthly communication to the members of the lodge.

To the Lodges of this Jurisdiction:
The Grand Lodge of California maintains Masonic Clubhouses at
the Un·iversity of California at Berkeley and the University of California
at Los Angeles.
Membership in these Clubhouses is open to students who come from
Masonic families or have some other closely related tie with the Masonic
Fraternity.
The Grand Lodge of California operates and maintains these facilities. The only expenses to the students are nominal dues, which may be
used to defray the cost of special social events.
Tihe facilities of the Clubhouses are quite complete. They include a
library, study room, typewriters, adding machines, pool and ping pong
tables, dance floors. stages for amateur theatrical productions, television
and radio rooms, and kitchen and dining facilities.
The wholesome atmosphere surrounding the Clubhouses is much to
be desired by students on the campuses, particularly those away from
home.
I sincerely hope that every Mason will be made aware of the availability of these facilities. I request that the lodges have this communication read at the meeting following its receipt and that the brethren be
askd to inform their friends who have children who plan to attend either

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT-D ECOTO HOME
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
Brethren: It is my •privilege and pleasure to present to you my second
annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for the year
ending June 30, 1957.
Conditions during the past year have continued to be most satisfactory, which is a pleasure to report, and several improvements for the
betterment of the Home ·h ave been made during this period. The morale
of the residents is quite high, and they have been most cooperative and
helpful this past year.
At the beginning of the fiscal year we had a total of 338 in the Home,
consisting of 133 men and 205 women. During the year 40 women,
average age 78.49 years, and 40 men. average age 78.40 years, were
admitted. There were 29 women, average age 83.65 years and 28 men,
average age 83.57 years, who passed away. One man and four women
were withdrawn from the Home during this past year. The total population as of July 1, 1957, was 356, consisting of 144 men and 212
women, including 15 married couples.

On April 1, 1957, Miss Bess L. Payne, who had been our Hospital
Supervisor since 1951, resigned to take up lighter duties. She ;h ad always
been proficient in her duties and loyalty to the Home.
Mrs. Rosalind Almond succeeded Miss Payne as Hospital Supervisor and is very competent in her work. She is well liked by all the
residents and by the visiting doctors. With the Supervisor's competent
staff, the residents, both in the Hospital and out, are being given excellent care in a kindly and efficient manner.
There are 75 patients in the hospital. of whom 68 are considered
permanent. In addition, there are 28 men and 35 women in the main
building who require supervision and receive care.
Our medical staff is being furnished by the Palo Alto Clinic. The
doctors visit five days each week seeing the patients in the ·hospital,
those who are ambulatory in the Clinic, and visiting others in their
rooms when necessary. Patients needing further attention are sent to
Palo Alto for further examinations or treatment. During the past year

On April 3, 1957, Brother Lowell L. Cain, a member of Benicia
~dge No. 5, assumed the responsible duties of Assistant to the Supermtendent. He has taken charge C'f the outside and maintenance personnel. He is extremely interested in the Home and its residents, and shows
them every kindness and consideration. He has been a great help to me
in spite of his short time at the Home.
Ou~ Matron, M~s. Sara Paris, with her capable staff, has performed
her duties most efficiently during th~ past year.
Our Office Manager, Brother Edward C. Hildebrand, retired after
14 ye~rs of service. He was succeeded by Brother Fred Boyle, who has
been m the office since June 1, 1952, and has performed his duties with
proficiency.
Chef William Emmal, Purchasing Agent Paul Reichert, and our
Home Chaplain, Reverend Martin L. Tonner, have been very cooPerative during the year and have performed their duties in a highly
satisfactory manner.
During the ~ast year we have had the pleasure of welcoming a total
of 42 lodges to either confer a degree in the Temple or present a program
in the Auditorium. We are grateful to these Brethren for their interest
in the Home and its residents. It has been necessary for them to travel
many miles to present these programs, as we have had visitations from
lodges all over the northern part of the state and from as far south as
San Diego.
This year we have had the pleasure of having 48 movies furnished
(gratis) by Columbia, RKO, Twentieth Century, United Artists and
Warner Bros. Film Distributing Co. of San Francisco.
On August 18, 1956, we had the pleasure of welcoming the East Bay
Past Matrons Association of the Order of Eastern Star for their annual
visit. The many Chapters presented jams, jellies, fruit and other delicacies, as well as many items of clothing, games, books and yarn.
Following a delicious luncheon, a reception was held in honor of
Worthy Grand Matron Mabel Tellefson and her Grand Chapter
Officers.
I wish to extend to the many members of the Fraternity and various
groups our thanks for their generosity and their donations, which have
brought much happiness and enjoyment over the past year.
Th~re we~e 4,~41 registered ~isi~o~s to the Home, representing 378
lodges m California, 18 other jurisdictions and 2 foreign countries.
It was a privilege and pleasure to welcome the Board of Trustees on
Dec. 15, 1956, to the Home for their quarterly meeting. A reception was

held in their honor and after their very interesting remarks, the residents
presented a sketch from the TV program "What's My Line?" for their
enjoyment.
During the past fiscal year, the following improvements were made:
The kitchen, dining room, auditorium, men's dormitory, temple and
many of the rooms and halls were redecorated. The flooring in the men's
dormitory was refinished with asphalt tile. The bed springs throughout
the Home were rebuilt and new mattresses purchased to replace the
worn ones.
Since our last report, we disposed of all the cattle and pigs. Because
of strict regulations by the State and the difficulty in getting the proper
personnel, this seemed the best policy. In addition, we could not raise all
our requirements, therefore it is as economical to purchase all our meats
rather than only 80% of our needs.

To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge of California:
It is with sincere satisfaction that the Masonic Homes Endowm ent
Board submits herewith the Twenty- fifth or Silver Anniver sary Annual
Report covering the period from July 1, 1956 to June 30, 1957, indusive .
IN THE BEGINNIN G

Masons may well be proud of their record in ":Caring For Their
Own.'' This is surely true of the Grand Lodge of California. It is difficult
for us in this modern age to realize the difficulties, the hardships, and the
problems that were faced by our Masonic brethren during the formative
days of California. 'Jet the records will show that they were equal to
their task.
Above aU, they planted the seed whereby a Masonic Homes
Endowm ent Board was created by Constitu tion and Ordinanc es, Artide
V, in 1932. The Board as constituted consisted of fifteen members, and
was charged with the responsibility of enlightening the brethren regarding the needs and work of our Homes, and to present a proper plan
whereby contributions could be made for their support. In short, the
purpose of the Board was stated, "To study, devise, and carry out plans
for the securing of adequate endowment for the Masonic Homes of
Californ ia."
From the beginning the Board took their work seriously. It was no
easy task for them to meet the challenge. Slow progress was made, but
a Orm foundation was formed and by 1937 the million dollar goal had
been reached. In spite of depressions, War, many new chaUenging programs, the work of the Board has continued in a masterful fashion purely
on an educational basis.

Quo VADIS

Milestones have been ]aid, and the course charted during the past
quarter of a century. We are proud that we have passed the seven
million dollar mark, but much remains to be done. During the pa~t
quarter-c entury many unforseen eventual~ties have intervened, but lll
spite of these our progress has been continuaUy upward and forward.
It is inconceivable that we will waver from our proven success~ul rout~.
The extent of our cooperation and the magnitud e of the enthusiasm will
be the only factors that will determine "quo vadis."
THE MASON IC HOMES ENDOW MENT BOARD
ERNEST G. BASHOR, Chairman
BYRON COLEMA N, Vice-Chairman

THE KALEIDO SCOPE

It has often been said that there are two things that are certain,
namely, "death and taxes." To this one can rightly add, "CHAN GE."
It has been manifested in all phases related to the growth, operation,
and development of our two Homes.
In the early years fifty-thousand doUars or Jess was ample to care
for the needs. Now our two Homes are operated on a budget of over
$650,000. Since only the income from the Endowm ent Fund is used,
one can readily realize the necessity of a considerable amount .of money
before a satisfact ory goal can be reached. Namely, one, the income of
which will care for our two Homes.
GRATITU DE

Every memb~ of the Board is grateful for his privilege of serving
on such a chaUenging Masonic program. Yet we are well aware that the
success has been due to the fu]] cooperation of so many phases of
Masonic life.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL

Advanced for Relief •........................... $56,545.74
Funerals conducted ..................................••.•..925 ,
Total calls made ........................................30,638

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
~he Board of Control submits herewith its annual report covering
the activities, statistical information, and other important data for the
18 boards of relief and six employment bureaus maintained within
our jurisdiction.

We are happy to report that the work being carried on by our
Executive Secretaries and Employment Managers is progressing in
a satisfactory manner. In regard to em•ployment, it is interesting to
note that the number registered for employment has again decreased,
indicating that a larger number of our craft and their immediate
families are gainfully employed.
We wish to report to this Grand Lodge 'that we have had numerous
requests throughout the jurisdiction to change the name of our
Masonic Boards of Relief. The most numerous request is to change
this name to "Masonic Service Board" or "Masonic Service Bureau."
The Board of Control has taken the position in the past and now wishes
to reiterate their position in the matter, which is that we do not feel
inclined to recommend such a change to this Grand Lodge and further
that we are, through the medium of this report and through personal
contact in our meetings throughout the State so advising the members
of our Boards of Relief. We are also advising those interested in
making suC'h a change that, if they wish to pursue this matter, it should
be brought to the Boor of Grand Lodge through resolution duly presented to the Grand Secretary at least 90 days 1prior to the annual
communication.
·
The Board of Control wishes to take this opportunity to thank
the Most Worshipful L. Harold Anderson, Grand Master, for attending our meetings and taking an active part and interest in our
work. We also wish to thank the Grand Master's corps of officers
for their help and particularly the Grand Secretary, Lloyd E. Wilson:
the Assistant Grand Secretary, Henry D. Oliphant, and their staff.
BoARDS OF RELIEF

Each of our eighteen Boards of Relief are required to keep records
of their financial transactions and also statistical information relative
to their work. These records are audited annually by competent accountants, and reports are forwarded to the Board of Control.
These reports have been carefully studied by your Board and found
to be in good order. The following are a few of the statistical high ..
lig'hts covering die Masonic year ending June 30, 1957.

161

Approximately one-haU of our Boards of Relief maintain blood banks
for the benefit of our Masonic brethren and their families. The following
indicate the extent of this activity.
Units of Blood donated ..............................2,762
Units of Blood withdrawn ..........................2,343
Actual cost saved our brethren ................ $60,042
EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

Employment Bureaus are maintained in six of our Boards of
Relief, and a study of the statistical audits revealed the following:
Registered for Employment ........................ 5,247
Jobs secured ..................................................2,025
Positions offered by employers ....................5,582
No charges of any kind are made to either the employer or the employee for these services. If the 2,025 jobs secured had been acquired
through commercial employment fee agencies, the cost to our Brethren
and their families for securing these jobs would have been $191,114.
APPROPRIATIONS

It 'has been the custom of Grand Lodge to assist the employment
bureaus financially when necessary by means of an appropriation.
The Board of Control has approved and recommended the following
appropriations:
East Bay ···-·····-~·-·················-~·············$ 2,500.00
Long Beach .......................................... 2,260.00
Los Angeles .......................................... 5,500.00

San Francisco ...................................... 2,500.00
Total ....................--···-··--···--····$15,683.00
The above application for appropriations together with the recommendation of the Board of Control has been ·flied with the Chairman of
the Finance Committee as required by the Ordinances, Section 265 of
the California Masonic Code.

REIMBURSEMENTS

'fihe Board of Control wishes to commend our Board of Relief Secretaries .for the excellent manner in which they are discharging their duties.
Respectfully submitted,
Guy A. TOLLE, Chairman
REGINALD M. MILLS, Secretary
EDWARD A. JOHNSON
RICHARD CROWE
IRVING MAGNES

We are glad to report that only two of our eighteen Boards of Relief
'have made requests for reimbursements. These requests have been carefully reviewed by your Board and presented to the Finance Committee
with our recommendations for approval. They are as follows:
Case #I-Sacramento Board of Relief
This case involves a brother who was a member of an Eastern lodge.
He passed away in the Sacramento area in October of 1956. The Secretary of our Sacramento Board of Relief contacted the brother's Lodge
for authorization to conduct a Masonic funeral. The Lodge advised that
the burial should be turned over to the County as their Lodge had no
funds for such expenses. The Secretary of our Sacramento Board of
Relief advised the Lodge that the California Grand Lodge made certain
that every Mason in good standing within its jurisdiction was given
decent burial. The deceased brother was given a Masonic funeral: however the Lodge refused to contribute anything more than $I 0.00 for a
floral piece.
The cost of the burial was $221.60: however our Sacramento Secretary was later promised $198.00 from another source, which left an unpaid balance of $23.60.
Case #2-Glendale Board of Relief
The Secretary of our Glendale Board of Relief advanced small sums
of money on two di.fferent occasions in July and August of 1956 to a
Brother who was a member in good standing of an Eastern Lodge. The
brother was desperate for funds and claimed that he had recently suffered a :h eart attack. Our Glendale Secretary sent a collect telegram to
the brother's lodge, stating the situation and requesting permission of
them to advance the brother $100.00. The lodge refused · to accept the
telegram.
Our Glendale Board of Relief Secretary then dispatched letters to
both the Master of the brother's lodge and the Grand Secretary of the
State where the lodge is located, requesting reimbursement of $58.82
which had then been advanced to the brother. The above all took place
nearly one year ago, and to date our Board of Relief Secretary has had
no reply; although he again wrote a letter to the Grand Secretary of the
State on May 9, 1957.
The Board of Control recommends that Glendale Board of Relief be
reimbursed in the amount of $58.82.
Total Requested for Reimbursements:
Case No. 1.................................................... $23.60
Case No. 2..................................................... 58.82
Total .........................................:............~$82.42

REPORT OF THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS COMMITTEE
You have demonstrated a sharp and positive interest in Public
Education and Public Schools during the past year, greater than in
any former year.
For 38 years California public schools have enjoyed the benefits
of cooperation, support, inspiration, helpfulness and interpretation
through the efforts and expressions of Masonic Lodges, Masonic organizations, Masonic bodies and members.
Do you know. what the persistent efforts of Masons in California
have actually been largely responsible for bringing about in our program
of Public Education? While we seek no credit as public acclaim for
our efforts, nor do we accept honor alone for ourselves, yet we do
fl.nd great inspiration to advance our plans and efforts in that we
definitely, justifiably, claim responsibility as we share in the advancement of our cause.
Vocational education, special education for the retarded and
handicapped, school child transportation, advancing standards of
teacher training, Adult Education, Education for Moral and Spiritual
values, Safety and Driver Education, and especially the development

PUBLIC EDUCATION IN CALIFORNIA TODAY

A report to our members of the accomplishment in such an important
area of responsibility as Public Education requires specific statement.
We must present statements in our report which will give understanding
of:
1. Public Education in California today.
2. Masonry and Public Education today.
3. Specific report of accomplishments.
4. From Here On.
In California today, we find Public Education more accepted in
proportion than Public Education is accepted in other states. This
means that the Public School program of Education, the Public Schoo]
facilities, the Public School teacher and teaching, the Public School
standards for learning are all not on]y accepted but are demanded and
to a high degree, well met in California. In addition, California parents,
taxpayers, students, not only demand the best, express wil1ingness to
pay for the best, but they require an advancing and improving program
of Public Education.
The demand for tota] years of Public School opportunity per child
exceeds that in other states. The demand for breadth of Public Schoo]
curriculum offerings in California schools is greater than in other states
and it is constantly extending. The requirements by way of 'public school
services from kindergartens and transportation to co1lege ]eve] public
education and enriched Adult Education is equalled only by the demands
for recreation services. child care, feeding, health services, and social
community services.
You as Masons need to know that you are requiring certain speci8cs
of our sc:hoo]s. What is it that Masons emphasize when they express
their wishes concerning Public Schools? Here are a few of your recorded
desires. You want good teaching, a high standard of ]earning in fundamentals and skill subjects. You demand good discipline, you ask for
t!he best in school spirit, citizenship and service. You want a high calibre
of moral and spiritual tone in school life. You are asking that schools
give more persona] attention to the individual child and its needs. You
want relief for half-day sessions and crowded classrooms. You hope
for comp]ete]y adequately trained teachers. You are anxious that we

For Masons of every age, of all degrees of advancement in their
Masonic study, for each level of interest there is possible to be found a
.field of inquiry, study, and service which will strengthen the public
school, its staff and influence. There is a vivid, active, duty-full opportunity for every Mason to think right and act right about our Public
Schools. No Mason in our jurisdiction should allow to prevail in the
Public Schools overcrowded school room conditions; unsafe, unsanitary,
unclean facilities; inadequate staff and substandard work by instructors
or students; we must not tolerate poor citizenship and discipline in a
school; we favor no curriculum which short-changes youth in matters
of practical, cultural, physical, and academic values. No Mason will
allow public education to be maligned, defamed or unfairly criticized
without first doing his utmost, alone and through his Fraternity, to
make Public Schools worthy of constructive support. In relationship to
these demands which every Mason places upon himself, he knows there
is a manner and a way in which he can rally help and give assistance to
bring about remedy.
In addition to the remedy for that which should be corrected, there
are advancing frontiers which ,Masons and the organized interest and
strength of the Fraternity in all of its bodies must advance and promote.
This positive program requires continuous study, alert leadership, cooperative effort and regular report to the Lodge or particular Masonic
body interested. Here is a Masonic Decalog of commitments for us as
each Mason looks forward.
1. Our faith in Public Education is unswerving. Public Education
is fundamental to the safety and continuance of Democracy as a way of
life.
2. The child, the well being of children and youth, and the ways to
successful manhood and womanhood as planned and developed in our
Public Schools System are first calls upon the loyalty of good citizens,
the public funds, and the cooperative helpfulness of all Masons in
California.
3. Teaching is the medium by which Public Education accomplishes
its results. Teaching is the foundation of learning. The well trained,
personally dedicated, politically unfettered, properly paid, secure teacher
is the teacher whom we as Masons hope to have our Public Schools
provide for every child in Public Schools.
4. A wholesome atmosphere. good equipment, adequate text books
and materials of instruction combined with safe, clean, comfortable
buildings are necessary to create the environment in which Masons
believe good Public Education takes place.
5. Community knowledge of Public Schools, understanding of the
methods, practices and standards of learning required are deserving of
expression by all who can interpret them and Masons may well expend

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

167

rnuch effort to make occasions where these interpretations and understandings may prevail.
6. Friendship for Public Schools is as important as faith in these
schools. No institution or structure is perfect, so we may decide the
better way of helping Public Schools if we struggle to support and
improve, to strengthen and make more perfect the Public School than
if we become negative, .finding fault, and discouraging thereby those who
should have our help. who should help us, and with whom we may join
hands in quietly and hopefully improving the Public Schools.
7. We as Masons strive not to run the Public Schools, to select,
criticize or complain of personnel. practices or conditions. We follow.
in our efforts, the lessons of our Fraternity which are those of faith,
hope. charity and diligent hard work. We stand ready as loyal supporters of Public Education ready to put our words into action.
8. Masons represent men of great faith and, as such, Masons see
in the Public Schools no place for a particular creed, no discrimination
because of race. creed, color or sex, no audience where other than the
ideals of Americanism can be found. Masons flaunt no authority.
display no power. deal in no threat. Only as we support what is right,
deal kindly. and are God fearing. do we hope to help our Public Schools.
9. Masonry recognizes the struggles of the course of the History of
our Country. Masons admire the leaders who have stood and do stand
for our country. We want the teachings of History of our Country. our
State, and of Public Education as a foundation for all that is American
to be strongly emphasized.
1O. Indefatig,f!ble effort in constant expression by Masons in
Masonic Lodges at every possible meeting will bring well informed
understanding to the support, strength and advancement of Public
Education in California. Except in Public Schools themselves there is
no unified, dedicated. pledged faith in Public Schools comparable with
that found in near 700 Masonic Lodges, in the hearts of nearly 240,000
members of the California Lodges who after 38 years reaffirm their
dedicated loyalty to Public Schools .first. better than ever, and everlastingly strong.
SPECIFIC REPORT oP AccoMPLISHMENTS

We say that you report a good year. You indicate fine committee
work accomplished by your Lodge Committee brethren. you tell of
enthusiastic interest in Public Schools Week observances. Let us make
report of specific things done, special ways of keeping alive a Lodgecentered loyalty to Public Schools. May we look at the workings of
Masonic Public School activity?
Who can estimate the value of stimulating interest on the part of
1.750,000 parents, citizens and children to visit and study and share in
programs in their public schools during Public Schools Week? Can you

judge the values to be found in the 4,000 columns of newspaper and
school publication issues which had as their theme "Public Schools'' and
"Public Education"?
In our state, thanks to extended cooperation, there were an estimated
200 television programs, 350 radio broadcasts and spot statements
featuring Public Schools. The number of service club, church, organizational meetings and parent groups was beyond count. The greatest
feature was the school programs in the school attended by these
1, 750,000 guests.
The theme of "The History and Reasons for Public Education in
America," was emphasized in high schools and public junior and senior
colleges throughout the state. Cooperation extended by all phases of
Government and .pronouncements issued by His Excellency, the Governor of California, the State Legislature, by Mayors, Governing Boards
and members of the Judiciary, and many others in public office was
tremendous this year. The interest of Business and Industry was significant, their expressions of helpfulness were outstanding.

1. Making Masonic and Lodge interest in behalf of Public Education a vivid, constant and year-round activity is a "must."
2. Preparing and disseminating Public Educatio? "~ews-no~~" to
the Lodge, to the entire Fraternity and to the community is an activity of
much worth.
3. Winning the children to a knowledge that Masonry strives for
good education for all children in Public School~ and that Masons a~e
among the finest friends children and the Public School can have, is
always a popular activity.
4. Maintaining an active contact with the public school administrators, the P.T.A .• Public School Teachers and personnel so that our
availability to help when hdp is needed, so that our Masonic interpr~­
tation of Public Education and that of Public Education leadership will
be in harmony is a very important frontier.
5. How to see the Public Education program as a whole, locally,
state-wide, and nationally is an area calling for study and interpretation.
6. The development of a Masonic Speakers Bureau primarily on
a local basis, so that at any time a good, well informed, interested
and interesting speaker is available to present inspiringly and instructively the Public School story is exceptionally valuable.
7. The preparation of a bibliography of visual materials, literature,
booklets, pamphlets, .Alms and such, for genera.I use emphasi~ing Publ~c
Education is a most pertinent living front m understanding Public
Schools in Ametica.
8. The development of cooperative and collaborative relationships
with Public School professional organizations of teachers, administrators
and all personnel of Public Education is mutually helpful and in the
end reflects benefits for th~ children.
9. The need for vision and understanding of youth, the leadership
of youth groups, the types of adult sponsorship which are desira~le
through individual or c.ommittee or group interest are all essential
and may well engage the mind of every Mason. S~ch needs are wo~hy
of discussion, consideration and report by Public School Committee
members in Lodges.
1O. Projecting Public Education in the local Public School district
is a responsibility grave and important. No one better than Masons
should be well informed as to future growth, future needs, future
trends and future financial, personnel, and plant and building requirements. To know of these and to have ideas to express and interest to
reveal is certainly among the greatest of duties our membership can
manifest in behalf of the future of Public Education, yes the future
of our country.

From community after community came reports that posters, hand
bills, special announcements in many original styles, "just covered the
place." Literally millions of bulletins were prepared by schools and
Lodges. The very intimate Lodge room meetings where crowds came in
for a particular program and atmosphere which can only exist in such a
session were a growing feature of the 1957 observance. The use of
motion picture films was especially prominent and the various films
suited to this type of Public Schools interpretation was large.
Social events where community. school and Lodge gatherings joined
having children present and featured. with dinners, buffets, snacks and
refreshments proved appealing, always happy and entertaining. Picnics
were popular. Athletic events sponsored for the occasion were numerous.
Many contests. awards, student activities were sponsored. Exhibits and
displays of the work of children were ever popular. Essay contests on
subjects such as "Why the Public Schools" and "Why I like my
School" were conducted. Awards for orations, speeches at gatherings,
scholarship, citizenship, leadership and community service were stimulated. Poster contests, radio, television, newswriting and editorial work
were awarded prizes. certificates and scholarships. Original slogans,
banners, emblems, insignia and badges suitable to occasions were encouraged in areas throughout the state.

CONCLUSION

REPORT OF COMMITIEE ON SEGREGATION

The dominant, developmental characteristics of Public Education
in California are growth, expansion, extension, and improvability.
The determined purposes of Masons are to see that Public Education advances its developmental characteristics in a manner typical
of the historical backgrounds of American Public Education, especially
in our state. Your zeal in support of the Grand Lodge policy and
program to protect, advance, and enrich Public Education in its .philosophy, methods, texts, and materials of instruction, facilities and
equipment within schools, and its :finance and unfettered position in
matters of politics or un-American interferences is the greatest operative
function of Masonry in California.
Every individual Mason in California bears a tie with Public
Education in Public Schools. All who know us as Masons not only
recognize us as servants of Public Education, but they see in the
living of our Masonry an example of manhood which demonstrates
the power of enlightenment. Nothing other than the intelligent Godfearing individual Mason in his daily living is as important to this
Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons in California as is the
work we yet must do for Public Schools.
Ye men of faith in youth, make operative that faith by your works
. in behalf of the Public Schools which when right are the citadels of
strong manhood and womanhood for a more magnificent United States
.
of America.
Respectfully presented,
VIERLING KERSEY, Chairman
Public Schools Committee

book for distribution to prospective members. A copy of the handbook
accompanies this report.
The Presidents of the student club have prepared reports for us,
covering the activities during their terms of office. The reports indicate quite a varied program of activities, suitable to the purposes of
the club, and that they are in a good 8nancial position.
During the year the use of the Clubhouse facilities was extended
to the following organizations, The East Bay Masters & Wardens
Association, University Square Club, Jobs Daughters and Rainbow
Girls Guardian Councils. Henry Morse Stephens Lodge and a combined
group of District Officers Associations. Their meetings have served
to publicize the Clubhouse and create interest and assistance to the
membership.
In this connection we express our particular appreciation to the
Most Worshipful L. Harold Anderson. Grand Master, for his recent
letter to the lodges, requesting them to publicize and become aware of
the Clubhouse facilities and privileges.
Generally speaking the Clubhouse property is in excellent condition,
although a recent survey indicates that in the near future certain repairs and alterations will be necessary to maintain the building on its
proper level and surroundings.
Some concern has been indicated regarding expansion plans of the
University that might affect the location of the Clubhouse. Authoritative
information indicates that any expansion plans will exclude the Clubhouse propertieis. This of course will place the Clubhouse in an excellent
position for a permanent location in the center of the University activities. For example the University YWCA is just across the street,
the University Placement Bureau is next door.
Only one major replacement item has been required during the
year. Banquet tables have been purchased to replace the old wooden
tables that have been in use since the club was started in 1924. The
replacement was felt to be a very necessary and attractive addition to
the equipment.
Due to the resignations of Bros. R. P. Wisecarver and Ray Langbrey, and on recommendation of the Grand Master, Bros. W. E. York,
PM of Y erba Buena Lodge and Gordon Black, PM of Riverside Lodge
were accepted and elected members of the Board at our last annual
meeting. Bro. Black's daughter Jean is a former club member and officer
of the student club.
Our proposed budget, submitted to the 8nance committee earlier,
is a basic operating budget and includes only minimum operating costs
for the coming year. Our estimates are con8rmed by the annual auditors
examination of accounts and expenditures during the past year. Copies
of the auditors examination are a part of this report.

other countries and states are members of the club including Porto
Rico, Costa Rica, Pennsylvania, Iran, and Australia. Our Executive
Director, Mrs. Esther Mainwaring has been very instrumental in the
direction and reception of the membership and guests.
