To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Board of Directors takes pleasure in submitting its report for
the fiscal year ending June 30, 1957.
It is not our intent to burden this report with repetitious information
regarding the yearly operation of the Club House. Reference to last
year's report will give a good explanation of our operations.
We will elaborate here on some of the major items of expense
either actually sustained or yet to be incurred.
In last year's report an item of $2,000.00 was included as the
probable expense for a moving picture, describing the club and its
yearly operations. It has been felt that if more publicity were given
among the lodges. by means of a movie, we could stimulate membership
in our club. There have been several meetings between the student
council and some representatives from a major movie studio to work out
a script: when the final script has been chosen it is to be submitted to our
Board for approval and the picture will be taken. It is anticipated
that this will be done shortly. We have found that many Southern
California Masons are not familiar with the dub or its activities and
it is hoped that a movie showing these activities to be presented to the
Southern California lodges will help to get the desired publicity. Our
membership is on the increase, but, as mentioned in last year's report,
we could still serve twice the membership at very little additional
cost to Grand Lodge.
One other major item that was undertaken was the changing of
the lighting and seating arrangement of the study. This change was
the first in twenty-eight years and from the improved lighting observed
and the refinishing of the tables, the change was certainly for the
better.
During the year we regretfully accepted the resignation from
our Board, of Brother Tyler Parker ( 599). He asked to be relieved
because of pressure of other activities. He has been replaced on our
Board by Brother S. Roy Howell ( 662). Brother Howell is a Past
Master of Henry Knox and as a successful business man brings to our
Board years of sound business experience.
The Board has adopted a budget for the coming year which is submitted as follows:

Grand Lodge was c.alled on at 10:00 A.M., the Grand Master presiding. The Grand Chaplain delivered the invocation. The minutes of

REPOR T OF THE TRUSTEES, CALIF ORNIA
MASON IC MEMO RIAL TEMPLE CORPO RATIO N
The Trustees of the Californ ia Masonic Memorial Temple Corpora tion present their third annual report for the Masonic fiscal year
ended June 30, 1957.
The Board of Trustees met following the close of the 1956 annual
communication of Grand Lodge, as is required by the By-laws, for
the purpose of organiza tion. The election of Brother Leo E. Anderso n,
Deputy Grand Master, Brother Phil N. Myers, Senior Grand Warden ,
and Brother Joe L. SheJJ, Junior Grand Warden , was formally reported
to the Board, and on motion duly made, seconded and carried, they
·
were elected members of the Board.
A WoRD OF APPRECIATION
This year has been ofBciaJJy designat ed "the year of the Temple"
by the Grand Master. Most Worship ful L. Harold Anderso n has
been most cooperative during this year. His enthusiasm for this great
"Memor ial" to our war dead has been of genuine assistance to many
of our lodge campaign chairmen and officers. His regular attendan ce
at the weekJy meeting of our Building Committee is most apprecia ted.
We direct to your attention and recommend as a must for your
reading, his message in the "Autumn 1957" issue of the Californ ia
Freemason.
VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTIONS
T·he confidence evidenced at the close of the 1955 annual communication where several bret'hern during the closing moments of
Grand Lodge called attention of all those present to the importan t job
ahead as respects construction and finance of the California Masonic
Memorial Temple. The efforts of those brethren were no idle gesture.
The impetus gained from those expressions continues and have carried through this entire year. Again, we on the Committee and the
Board of Trustees express our thanks and appreciation for the continued evidence of confidence and loyal support.
During this year and for comparative purposes only (using 12
months) an addition al 110 lodges reached Merit Roll status and contributions for the year aggregat ed $288,870.84.
Recapitulation of production to date from voluntar y contributions
is as foJJows:

Of the 313 lodges having reached Merit Roll status as of Septe~­
ber 13, 1957, 109 have taken advantage of the refreshment fund
procedure. Of these lodges. 58 have either partially or totally reimbursed their refreshment fund through their continued activity in
behalf of the California Masonic Memorial effort.
To and including July 31, 1957, 114,761 individuals have contributed to the Temple fund. Of this number 22,841 became contributors
during the twelve months under review.
FINANCING

To date, September 10, 1957, we have drawn on the banks under
our loan agreement, a total of $888,000. All bills for the month of
August, payable in September, have been paid.

NoN-LoANABL E ITEMS

In our negotiations with the banks, it was determined that certain
items could not be purchased out of borrowed money. These items
include furniture, carpets, etc., items not strictly a part of the structual
part of the building. In order to meet our obligations in that regard
arrangements have been made, with bank approval. to set aside in a
reserve fund cash received from per capita $1.00 and the $9.00 contribution. It is out of these funds progress payments have been made
on items falling in this category. Ultimately any unused balance will
be applied against payment of the loan or used for construction payments in lieu of additional borrowing.

THE OPEN Boox

Your Board of Trustees has given much careful thought to the
production of "The Open Book." Obviously, all the details have not
been developed. As we study the problem we are increasingly impressed however with its importance, with its size and the cost involved.
Every Mason in California, members of a California or Hawaiian
lodge, has been given ample opportunity to have his name recorded.
We sincerely hope that_ ~II those "with good intentions" will take
positive action. In order to have "The Open Book" :in place at the
dedication in September, 1958, consideration is now being given to
the necessary steps to be taken in order to accomplish that objective.
We will need the assistance of every lodge, particularly the secretary, in checking final detail on "lists of contributors" spelling, etc.
We urge your continued cooperation.
We express our thanks again for the time our secretarys have so
generously given and go forward with conftdence that they will be ever
present with a •helping hand when the call comes.

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
FOR THE RECORD

Your Building Committee and Board of Trustees regret that
circumstances beyond our control required us to issue the Templegram
dated August 26, 1957, as follows:

GOOD JUDGMENT SAYS: "NO"
Worshipful Master.
Please make sure that your members coming to Grand Lodge
get this information.

*
*
*
It is natural that we have had many Masters and others ask the

question, "Will we be permitted to 'tour' the Memorial Temple while
at Grand Lodge?" We think it would serve many good purposes if
it were feasible, but there are too many excellent reasons why it is
not an advisable thing to do.
In the first place, Monday through Friday would have to be ruled
out completely due to work operations in all parts of the Temple, and
we must not in any way interfere with construction, or be a party to
work interruption.
On Saturday and Sunday, there are equally good reasons why
tours by individuals or groups are not permitted now. and should not
be permitted during grand lodge. Some of the reasons are:
1. Any construction job is always potentially dangerous to
the casual visitor.
2. Inspection from time to time by our own Building Committee is permitted only by written consent of the Contractor, and at our own liability.
3. Such consent "en masse" should not be sought or granted.
4. The hazard of nails, loose boards, and objects not permanently fixed is ever present.
5. Elevators are not running. Stairways and stairs are in
the rough, unfinished, and there are no guard rails.
6. Scaffolding is still up outside, in the Memorial Foyer, and
in the Auditorium.
But-why go on? We are sure you will agree with us: "Take a
good look from the outside, but don't try to get by the guard on the
inside."
We had :h oped that conditions might permit conducted tours-which accounts for the late date of this flnal decision.
Thanks for agreeing with us that "GOOD JUDGMENT SAYS
'NO'!''

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. 8 A. M. of California:
The ln~estment Committee concludes its seventh year of activity,
and herewith renders its report for the eleven months ending June 30
1957. For .the record, inasmuch as a large number of members present
are attending Grand Lodge .for the first time, each year's report gives a
certain amount of historical background and basic information. Such
information should be helpful to those who wish to avail themselves
of it.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by Grand
Lodge at its 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges the
identical Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge .. F. & A. M. of CaUfornia was formed for the purpose of administering the investable funds
of Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, and the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent Lodges. Grand Lodge makes the services of its
investment advisor available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are now
m~ng use of this s.ervice, as evidenced by the fact that 192 Lodges
with $4,321,482 of investments are now consulting with our investment advisor.
The Investment Committe is composed of the Grand Treasurer,
the Assistant Grand Treasurer, the Chairman of the Finance Committee, the President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees or a
Trustee of that Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the
Masonic Homes Endowment Board or a member of that Board designated by him. The President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees
has designated Brother Past Master Ralph H. Head and the Chairman
of the Endowment Board has designated Brother Past Master J<>hn W.
Davey, as members of the Committee.
By Ordinance, under Section 86 (now 246) with respect to invest·
(now 403) respecting
mvestments by Constituent Lodges, the following provisions were
promulgated:
~ent of Grand Lodge ~unds, and Section 152.1

GROUP I. At least 40% of the funds available for investment
must be in:
A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obllgations of the United States.

Obligations of the State of California and its political
subdivisions.
D ) Such other securities as are legal investments for California
savings banks.

C)

GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securi·
ties Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall
not include railroad equipment trust issues ( 1955).
B ) Preferred stocks, which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and
Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange,
except that full listing and registration of preferred stock
shall not be required whenever the common stock of the
corporation issuing such preferred stock is folly listed and
registered on such an exchange, provided that such pre,ferred stock is traded on such an exchange ( 1956).
Up to 40% may be invested in:
GROUP III.
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that
this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance stocks.
B ) Shares of Investment Trusts.
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and HI. the
Ordinances read as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of .purchase will result i~ the total market value
of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent (or
forty per cent) of the total market value of all the cash, bank accounts
and securities held,"-the controlllng point being that there cannot be
more than 20% or 40% invested in Groups II and III, respectively. at
the time of purchase.
Since its formation the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. Between quarterly meetings, the business of the
Committee is handled by correspondence or telephone.
As stated, we have just completed seven years of operation. The
following is a summary of the consolidated market values of securities
owned, plus investable cash, together with a record of dollar income on
these investments, beginning with November 30, 1950, and for each
succeeding fiscal year, through June 30, 1957, including the percentage
income on the market value of each year.

The following charity football games were certified by their sponsors
to meet these requirements, and permission was accordingly granted
by the Grand Master.
1. East-West Game--San Francisco, California.
2. North-South Game--Los Angeles, California.
3. Aloha Game--Honolulu.
4. Lumber Bowl Game--Redding. California.
5. Potato Bowl Game--Bakers•field, California.
6. Northwestern California All Star Game--Eureka, Calif.
Al Ba:hr Temple in San Diego conducted a football game in San
Diego under a contract with a state tax supported institution which
requires a division of the .net proceeds with such institution. As other
arrangements could not be made the Grand Master withheld his consent and the game proposed for 1957 was not held. Your Committee
has been informed by the Potentate that other plans are under consideration and that they will be able to comply with the rules promulgated
by the Grand Master in time to hold their game in 1958. In view of
the past conduct of this Temple, this attitude in indeed refreshing.

SHRINE

One of these organizations was the Ancient Arabic Order of
the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, commonly referred to as the Shrine.
In his usual positive and direct manner the Grand Master called a
meeting of the Potentates and Ohief Rabaans of California Shrine
Temples, for November 10, 1956, in Los Angeles. The Grand Master
and Deputy Grand Master, as well as all the members of your committee were in attendance at that meeting. Your committee has a complete memorandum of the meeting in its files but it is too long to attach
to this report, nor would it serve any ·purpose to do so. This meeting
formed the basis for the Edict issued by the Grand Master under date
of December 5, 1956, banning circuses and like commercial ventures
for which public support is requested and for which tickets, programs
and other items are sold to the public. We recommend your close
attention to. and approval of. the Grand Master's Edict.
The cooperation of the Shrine has been excellent. Several Shrine
Temples have raised their dues and others are contemplating doing
so. Members whose dues have been raised have thanked the Grand
Master and this committee, pointing out that the increase in dues was
modest in comparison to the former tribute levied in the sale of circus
tickets and particularly are they grateful that 1high pressure methods
are no longer used. They are also proud that they now support themselves and are no longer levying tribute from the ·public.
A further outcome of this meeting was the strict limitations placed
upon Shrine charity football games. These games, beginning with the
East-West game in San Francisco, have spread to Los Angeles and
San Diego in the South; to Redding and Eureka in the North and to the
lovely Hawaiian Islands in the West. The original purpose, to build
the endowment fund of the Shrine Hospitals for Cdppled Children
had not been carried out in some of the newer games. Splitting of qame
proceeds, diversion of a part of the game receipts to local Shrine Clubs,
and other practices had subverted the original purpose. The Grand
Master charged the various Shrine Temples and Clubs to operate under
rules ·providing that;

AMARANTH FOUNDATION. INC. AND THE ROYAL ORDER OP CARITAS

In . this Committee's report of 1955, reference was made to the
Amaranth Foundation, Inc.: its telephonic solicitation of funds and the
employment of one or more motorcycle runners to bring in the "take,"
50% of which went to a 1promoter. Our late Brother Gaylord Quinn,
Inspector, was compelled to take action through the Hayward City
Police Department to stop this practice in that area.
Solicitations of donations through the sale of so-called Christmas
seals has continued. For this reason and because dissension and legal
injunction proceedings had become the pattern within the order of the
Amaranth itself, the Grand Master instructed this Committee to get
the .facts and submit them to him. For that purpose a meeting of the
Committee was held in San Francisco on ·February 9th and 10th. 1957,
to enable Dr. John D. Humber, a Member of Wake Forest Lodge No.
282 of North Carolina, to appear with the books and records of the

200

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Amaranth Foundation, Inc. Our Grand Master was present during a
part of this meeting.
Dr. Humber's testimony under questioning showed the following:
The Order of Amaranth has maintained a home for girls for over
thirty years in the City of Santa Monica. Some fifteen years ago the
Amaranth Foundation, Inc., was formed by the Order of Amaranth
for the specific purpose of receiving gifts for this home by donations
from individuals and courts of the Order of Amaranth and by bequests.
The Board of Trustees o'f the Foundation was self.-perpetuating except
for the Royal Matron and Royal Patron of the Order of Amaranth.
Dr. Humber has been President of the Foundation since its organization
and in control thereof. A tract of land was acquired in Northern California purportedly to establish a "Boys Town of California" and the
original intent of the foundation was ignored. As a result of disputes
the ex-officio trustees resigned, thus severing any responsible link with
the Order of Amaranth and leaving the Foundation free to utilize the
name of "Amaranth" with no control of its activities.
Donations continued to be solicited from individuals and courts of
the Order of Amaranth; t'he Christmas Seal campaign was continued
and the name of Masonry used in solicitation.
The office of the Foundation is the home of Dr. Humber. All
solicitations and requests for donations emanate from him and all funds
donated are sent to his •home. No record is kept of the number of seals
printed or the number of seals sent out and we were shown no receipt
books. Dr. Humble could not explain entries in the books about
which he was questioned, nor could 1he reconcile the books with the
financial statements-and it might be added-neither could the Committee. From the testimony of Dr. Humber and from the records of the
Foundation and from the financial statements it was and is apparent
to your Committee and to your Grand Master, that the so-called charity
aspect of the Foundation, if it exists at all, is truly an injustice to the
donors and should not be permitted to continue. The following example
of a financial report rendered by the Foundation will, we think, be
sufficient to justify the position of your Committee.
The 1955-56 financial statement of the Foundation revealed a total
of $3,797.52 collected; $357.30 disbursed to charity, largely to a single
individual. name not given; $1,353.58 added to surplus and $2,086.64
expended in operating the Foundation. In collecting approximately
$1,200.00 in the Christmas Seal campaign, $900.00 was expended, a
ratio of $3.00 spent for each $1.00 netted to the Foundation. Financial
statements for each year since 1945 disclose a similar pattern.
Thus the plan is again established. A group having no Masonic
~urpose having obtained the use of the name of a prerequisite organization uses the name of Masonry for ends which are peculiarly its own.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

201

In the latter part of 1956 or early in 1957, Dr. Humber and others,
some of whom are likewise members of the Board of Trustees of the
Foundation, being o'f the opinion that the corporate charter of the
Order of Amaranth had lapsed, incOJ:porated a new Order of Amaranth
in California and claimed jurisdiction over the individual members and
courts of the Order of Amarant'h. Strife and dissension ensued.
Masons were pitted against Masons. A lawsuit was instituted by the
old group seeking an injunction against the new group. After a court
proceeding judgment was entered against the new group and it is now
final. Dr. Humber and his associates then proceeded to form the
"Royal Order of Caritas" for the avowed purpose, as testified to by
him, of replacing the Order of Amaranth in California and to further
his own ambitions, particularly with reference to the Boys Town project
as promoted by the Foundation.
The entanglement of the Royal Order of Caritas movement with
the Foundation: the internecine warfare existing between such organizations and the Order of Amaranth: the strife and dissension, all
resulting in violent disturbance to the peace and •harmony of the Craft
were reported in full to the Grand Master. After careful and long consideration and pursuant to his power and responsibility for the supervision and welfare of the Craft the Grand Master did, on May 28th.
1957, issue an Edict providing that no Mason subject to the jurisdktion
of California "shall be, become, or remain a member of said Royal
Order of Caritas nor said Amaranth Foundation, Inc., or their successors
by change of name, nor shall any such Mason, directly or indirectly,
aid or assist said Royal Order of Caritas nor said Amaranth Foundation,
Inc., or their su~cessors by change of name, in any manner whatsoever."
His Edict is evidence, if any was needed, of his great love and
care for, and courageous service to, the Craft. He has left for his
sm:cessors, not only a beacon of light of faith in the supremacy of this
Grand Lodge, but a straight path of "right and truth without inclining
to the one hand or the other" but in all his doings having the welfare,
peace and harmony of the Craft in view.
It is with deep regret and much concern that we must report to
you that some of our Brethren have forgotten their Masonic obligation
to abide by and conform to all laws, rules and regulations of this Grand
Lodge. Regret, because it has been necessary for the Grand Master
to cause charges to be filed against certain Brethren; Concern, because
Masonic Brethren place more emphasis on the interest in collateral
groups which are in no sense Masonic. It is inconceivable to your Committee that any of their Masonic Brethren would place such groups above
the welfare, peace and harmony of the Craft. Strange as it may seem
to you and to us, we have evidence that some of our Brethren are planning, scheming and conspiring to circumvent the Edict of our Grand
Master, issued for the sole purpose of that welfare, peace and harmony,

202

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

which should be a paramount goal of every member of the Craft. Such
conduct points up the continuing necessity for this Grand Lodge to be
ever vigilant H the Brotherhood of Freemasonr y, which we all love,
is to remain unsullied.
Let it here be said that neither the Grand Master nor this Committee
holds any brid for the Order of Amaranth nor was the investigation
made by this Committee nor the Edict issued by the Grand Master with
any thought of assisting that organization in the slighest degree.

TRANSPORTA TION CRIPPLED CHILDREN'S CLUB

.

Tihe Transportat ion Crippled Children's Club was originally formed
among employees of the Southern Pacific and Santa Fe Railways to
collect funds from fellow employees, both Masons and non-Masons , for
the benefit of the Los Angeles Unit of the Shriner's Chippled Children's
Hospital. It then branched out to include other transportati on, utility
and industrial companies. It thereafter obtained designation as the
beneficiary of A.I.D. fonds for the same purpose. Originally requiring
Masonic Membership only it was required by the Grand Master to
amend its by-laws to permit non-Mason s to become members. Though
this was done Jn the hope that its status as a Masonic group would be
eliminated, your Committee has been advised of the admission of only
one non-Mason, he being a Catholic. The group remains for all practical
purposes a Masonic prerequisite group.
The distribution of fonds donated was made by the Club during the
year of 1956 as follows:
Shriners' Crippled Children's Hospital ···-····---$2,000.00
Los Angeles Orphanage ...................................... 300.00
Children's Lukemia Ward-Cit y of Hope .... 300.00
Hillside House, Santa Barbara ........................ 300.00
Santa Teresita Hospital ...................................... I 00.00
One of these is a Catholic charity and of course only one is conducted by Masons. The reason for the contribution to the Catholic
c<harity, according to one officer, was the A.I.D. was Catholic dominated
and hence the Club felt that it would be wise to make a token donation
'
at least, in order that the Club could maintain good relations.

A full report was made to the Grand Master
felt might be warranted. From the activities of this Club it appeared to
the Grand Master, among other things, that the solicitation of funds
by the Club tended to and does lead the donors, or many of them, to
believe that their donations benefit Masonry and is therefore misleading,
and also that such activities could react unfavorably upon the Craft.
He therefore ordered the Club to cease its charity activities.
SANTA FE MASONIC CLUB-SAN BERNARDINO

The Santa Fe Masonic Club of San Bernardino, composed entirely
of Masons, has for a number of years taken the children of the Covina

MYSTIC ORDER OP VEILED PROPHETS OP THE ENCHANTED REALM

During the month of June, 1957, a report was released by the United
Press, and there appeared in newspapers an article under the headlines
of "Masons Drop Their Ban on Gambling.'' 'I'he first portion of the
article reads as follows:
"A nationwide group composed of members of the Masonic Order
yesterday repealed a law which prohibited gambling in its individual
units.
"The action was taken in Buffalo, N.Y. at the Supreme Council
meeting of the Mystic Order of Veiled Prophets of the Enchanted
Realm - - - .
"With the repeal, members of the order in the United States,
Canada, Cuba and the Canal Zone will be permitted to conduct raffles,
bingoes, drawings and other games of chance 'for worthwhile, charitable
and humanitaria n projects.' "
This organization is more commonly known as the '"Grotto.''
Needless to say, the Grand Master took swift action which he has
reported in his message and need not be repeated here. No such action,
however, can combat the adverse publicity which the Craft has been
subjected to. We believe the time has come to call a halt on those prerequisite organization s who grow fat on the false claim of Masonic
Affiliation and in doing so violate our fundamenta l laws and principles
and in which the individual members therof violate their obligations
taken before the Altar at which we all kneeled. Those organization s
believe that what they do is no concern of the Grand Lodge. We sincerely suggest that their actions and conduct are the concern of this
Grand Lodge. A Master Mason can bring reproach upon the Fraternity
in ways other than being convicted of a felony or some similar offense.
In many instances, of which the present case is a most perfect example,
the good name of Masonry is more lastingly harmed, and causes our
friends to wonder and our enemies to rejoice. We therefore ask these
questions. Should a Master Master, belonging only to a Blue Lodge,
be subjected to greater burdens and responsibilities than a Master Mason

205

· PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

who belongs to a prerequisite organization? Does our law permit a
Master Mason to do in a prerequisite organization that which he
cannot do in his Blue Lodge? Is Masonic law to apply in the one
case and not in the other? The answer is obvious if the good name of
Masonry is to be protected and made secure from collateral attack.
We therefore recommend that appropriate leg·islation be adopted that
will henceforth leave no room for doubt and put all prerequisite organizations on notice.

adopt legislation which would clearly and unequivocally set forth that
Masons, belonging to other organization s which require as a prerequisite
to membership, either directly or indirectly, Masonic membership or
affiliation. be subject to Masonic law, in the same manner and to the
same extent as a Blue Lodge Mason.
Brethren: Masonry recognizes that there must be Wisdom to contrive, Strength to support and Beauty to adorn every great and important
undertaking . We submit that the challenge of a great and important
undertaking today is the guiding of the ideals, principles, hopes and
destiny o>f our beloved Institution into the harbor of fulfillment of
tomorrow. This has been a year of momentous decision and action.
The Supremacy of Symbolic Freemasonr y has been challenged. Masonry
needed the leadership of man possessing Wisdom, Strength, Courage
and Fidelity, and her need was answered in the person and character
of the Most Worshipful L. Harold Anderson, Grand Master of Masons
in California. To know him, to serve this Grand Lodge under his leadership, to have been the recipient of his trust, loyalty and support has
been a rare and satisfying experience. In our hearts he has laid up a
crown of rejoicing that will continue when time shall be no more.
Respectfully submitted,
RALPH K. PIERSON

· Silverado Lodge U.D .. located at Na.pa in the County of Napa.
was instituted July 3, 1957. We believe this Lodge to have a very fine

general. In view of all the circumstances, your Committee feels that the
interests of Silverado Lodge U.D .. and of Masonry in general. would
be best served by continuing this Lodge under dispensation for the
ensuing year so that the officers and members can acquire experience
and closer familiarity with Blue Lodge administration and philosophies.
We, therefore, recommend that Silverado Lodge U.D. be continued
under dispensation for the ensuing Masonic year.

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON CORRESP ONDENC E
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your committee has received and reviewed the proceedings of most
of the grand jurisdictions of the world. Each quarter in the California
Freemason we print short summaries of a number of these reviews,
selecting those matters which we believe are of the greatest interest
to our California readers :
This is the fourth year during which your committee has been assigned the task of publishing quarterly the California Freemason, your
Grand Lodge's official publication. During this year our magazine has
had a total of 228 pages. As in former years we have had many excellent
articles available to us which were £rst printed in other Masonic
publications. We have abridged most of these to fit the space we had
available. More and more original articles have been submitted and
printed. We have kept our readers well informed as to Grand Lodge
officers and their activities. A greater use has been made of photograph s
and illustrations.
We report a gradual increase in circulation. H it was not for the
experience of other grand jurisdictions, the ratio of subscribers to
the total membership would be disappointing. About 15% of our
membership now subscribe. This is about the experience of New York
and other Grand Lodges when subscription s were required. New York
now sends its magazine to all of its 300,000 members at a cost of 60c
for each brother.
Our cost analysis for the past fiscal year reveals that cost of
preparing and mailing the four issues is $.5432 per subscription. The
balance of the dollar collected and the appropriatio n of Grand Lodge
is expended in soliciting new subscribers, keeping a record of and
sending out notices for renewals and in processing subscriptions received.
There are many reasons why it would strengthen Grand Lodge
and Freemasonr y in California if the California Freemason could be
sent to all of our 234,000 members. T·his could be accomplished for
from 50c to 60c a member. ·
This is our financial report for the year ending June 30, 1957:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on By-Laws have had under consideration 172
amendments and resolutions affecting by-laws and meeting places of
lodges.
We note that 30 lodges increased their fees. and that one lodge
decreased its fees. Twenty-five lodges increased !'heir annual dues to
$15: 5 lodges increased their dues to $16; 16 lodges increased their dues
to $18; 2 lodges increased their dues to $20: and one lodge increased
its dues to $25. This indicates clearly that there is a necessity for the
increasing of dues in many lodges because of increased cost of operation.
It is not to be expected that a lodge can properly function if its dues are
so low that it has difficulty in meeting current expenses, and we recommend that each lodge study and analyze its financial condition with a
view to determining whether or not an increase in dues is advisable.
Thirty-five lodges adopted amendments changing date, time or place
of meeting and eight amendments provided for time of meeting when
the stated meeting falls on a legal holiday. Nineteen lodges adopted
the Uniform Code df By-Laws. One lodge. the famous Volcano No.
56, changed the date of its annual election of officers from December to
November because of the danger of snowy weather limiting the attendance at the December meeting.
We desire to express our appreciation of the splendid work done by
Brother William Nankervis and his Committee in the preparation and
compilation of the new annotated California Masonic Code. This
volume, with its orderly arrangement of the Masonic Law governing the
Craft in the Jurisdiction of California, and its complete and comprehensive index, has greatly aided the work of our Committee and we are
certain that it will enable all committee members and lodge officers to
perform their duties more efficiently.
All of the following amendments and resolutions have been approved
by the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master as to form and Masonic
Law requirements. Our Committee has carefully examined and approved
them. and recommend their approval by Grand Lodge.

To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Masoni c History begs leave to submit the following report:
William M. Howard fl.rst appeare d on the California Masonic scene
as a visitor in San Jose Lodge No. 10 on the evening of September 25,
1852 when he presided as Master pro tem in the absence of the Master,
H. P. Dorsey. No farther mention of him appears until August 8, 1853
when ihe again served as Master pro tem. Then on December 21, 1853
he was elected Master of the lodge by acclamation. This is rather
significant in view of the fact that he did not become a member of this
lodge until April 15, 1854--o ver four months later. Howard was still
Master o'f San Jose Lodge when he was elected Grand Master of Californ:ia in 1854, an office he •held three consecutive terms. In 1863 he
withdre w from San Jose Lodge and is listed as the first Master of

Members of the Committee are participating in the seminar program
to be presented to Grand Lodge under the direction of the Research
Committee, and have also lectured in some of the spring seminars.
Permit the Committee to suggest that t'he several lodges appoint

mittee realizes that, perchance, this is one of the projects to which Grand
Lodge cannot contribute funds, but being an old Masonic building in
the heart of the great San Joaquin Valley, members of the fraternity
who belong to lodges in the vicinity may with propriety take more than
a passing -interest in its preservation.
There are a number of unusually interesting Masonic Lodge buildings in this jurisdiction, of which the old Visalia Temple is but an
example. Others are: the Old Temple at Los Angeles, and Columbia,
and the first Masonic Temple in California at Benicia. A partial list of
others would be: Volcano, Mountain Shade, Harmony, Texas, Fort
Jones, Hornitos and Mendocino. It is entirely conceivable that the
fraternity would benefit culturally, spiritually, and impressionably in
the establishment of a chain of 1historic Masonic shrines throughout
California, much as the Roman Catholic ChurC'h has benefited by the
establishment and restoration of the chain of Missions which helped
colonize California. With all of our other financial obligations, of
necessity, private funds would have to be obtained to finance such an
objective. Your Committee believes the idea possesses considerable
merit from a number of standpoints and recommends that this Grand
Lodge approves the idea in principle of a "Chain of Historic Masonic
Shrines," in California.
Our History Committee submits the following resolution and moves
its adoption:
That the sum of $500.00 be appropriated and set aside for the use
of the History Committee for the ensuing Masonic year.

We are pleased to report the completion of the indexing of the
books which Grand Lodge owns in its library. The library consists of
about 800 volumes now indexed according to the Library of Congress
system. In addition, but not indexed, there are about 5000 volumes of
all the ·proceedings of American Grand Jurisdictions and most of those
of Canada-a remarkable collection for reference and research purposes.
Our indexed collection contains many valuable, rare and unusual items,
some of which are of museum quality and should be displayed behind
glass only. It is our •h ope this Grand Lodge will provide suitable facilities
to care for this collection.
It has been called to our attention that cemeteries of lodges now
extinct have long since been woefully neglected and have become the
breeding ground of unseemly weeds and rubbish which ill-becomes
the resting place of those who wore the square and compass and
practiced the speculative art. Active working lodges ipresently situated
in close proximity to these extinct lodges could take as a yearly project
the cleaning up and beautifying of these Masonic burial places. Work
of this kind would redound to the lasting credit of Masonry and remind
the profane that members of the fraternity are not unmindful of those
who in the years past held high the banner of Masonry. For the most
part these neglected cemeteries are on the Mother Lode, but not
exclusively so. Nowhere in our dtual, or history, are we released from
our obligations to one another by the incident of death. Rather, there is
adequate proof to support the contention that our obligations continue
as before. Is our sense of obligation so S'hallow and our memory so
short, that we can uncharitably permit departed brethren to lie in graves
covered by rubbish?
T he Tulare County Historical Society is endeavoring to preserve
the old Masonic building in Visalia as an historical monument. For its
historical and cultural value this old building is worthy of preservation,
and the efforts to save it are fully justified. It was originally a joint
project o'f the Masons and Odd Fellows. The upper ·s tory was used for
lodge rooms. In 1941 the Odd Fellows sold their interest to the Masons.
'rhe latter used iit until the new temple was built. Your History Com1

FREEDOM'S HOLY LIGHT
RALPH H. HEAD, Grand Orator

Most Worshipful Sir and my Brethren in Freemasonry:
We are living in the greatest age in the history of the world, a time
of great hope and adventure. If men can successfully retain their freedom
and their inalienable rights they may yet advance beyond the horizon to
a new age, an age in which poverty and famine begin to disappear and
new and better standards of living emerge for all people, an age when
water converted from the sea will make desert lands productive and
when minerals and chemicals will be produced in abundance beyond
man's present imagination.
It seems opportune to look toward this brilliant horizon at the conclusion of a year in California Masonry marked with progress, planning,
and growth. It is an especially appropriate time because our Grand
Master, Most Worshipful L. Harold Anderson, represents both in his
thinking and in his profession the prophets of the new era of peace and
scientific achievement.
Before men can attain this goal they must first adopt and accept
without uncertainty or doubt and without equivocation certain principles
of integrity, morality. righteousness, and honor. Before men can realize
the dream they must learn the importance of liberty and the worship of
God and that the two are inseparable.
People who worship God realize the unique importance of the individual. They resist the tendency of government to violate the rights of
the individual. For if men do not practice the virtues of honesty, generosity, charity, and brotherly love they cannot be free. Unless men have
an unfaltering belief in God and an inextinguishable love for freedom
the bright day of abundance and peace may never be within their reach.
It becomes apparent then that there is existing and has existed for
centuries, perhaps far back into the dim past of unrecorded history, a
great moral force dedicated to freedom, faith, and morality. This great
force, this great teaching, is Freemasonry. It is not set forth in textbooks, published as a creed, imposed as a dogma. It is organized within
the structure of the Craft, in its rituals, in its symbols, and in its lectures.
'Jlhis is the secret of Freemasonry. This is the secret of its growth.
Somewhere in the dark past of antiquity building with stone had its
beginning. A primitive man may have placed one stone on another at
the entrance of his cave. He may have hidden a possession under a carefully laid pile of stone. But whatever he built, and ·w hatever man has
built thereafter, the motivating force has been the quest for security, for

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

217

protection against the weather, for freedom from fear of the unknown.
It does not appear as a mere coincidence that the art or even the act of
building has from almost the beginning of civilization been closely and
understandably associated with the search for freedom.
Somewhere in the early dawn of history there came into being groups
of men who became skilled in the art and science oif building with st~ne.
Even by the beginning of the age of recorded history there w~re. anci~t
ruins of such magnitude that only men of considerable skill m engineering and geometry could have erected the original building~. These
builders-these masons~mployed wood, and stone, and chemicals and
fire. Their work was often tricky and dangerous. Only an expert, a
trained and qualified man, could be entrusted to produce finally !11at
which was useful and beautiful and which would stand the test of time.
How were these men educated thousands of years age when there
were no printed text books or trade schools or seminars or the publications of scientific papers? All evidence points to the f~ct tha~ knowledge
was accumulated by men who organized themselves mto gmlds or clubs
according to their craft or profession. The building craft was. called
masonry. To enter such a craft a youth had to start as an apprentice ~nd
then prove himself willing to be trained and educated over a long period
of time by the master workman.
Freemasons, men who worked with and carved freestone, instead
of being bondsmen, were free to move where their work demanded.
These Freemasons and not the craft in general founded and fathered
that which ultimately developed into the fraternity of which we are a
part. As they moved to the site of a new community they first arranged
homes for their families. Then they erected buildings called lodges.
These lodges had a master and assistants whom we would call ward~ns.
The work they did was dangerous and complex. If an arch or a pillar
was not perfectly constructed it might collapse. T~e mason~ themselves
often worked on the tops of walls or high scaffolding. Their tools.w~re
many and difficult to use. For these and many other reasons the bmldmg
craft insisted that their members should keep their skills and arts and
processes strictly to themselves. These were "trade secrets" and Freemasonry became known as a secret organization.
Around the fourteenth century the Freemasons began to make their
lodges permanent. A permanent body had to have a charter in order to
meet so a scribe drew up a document which became the lodge rules and
regulations. Gradually it came about that if a group of F~eemasons could
get a copy of that document or version they could, on its strength, organize a new lodge.
.
During these early times Freemasons probably admitted into their
lodges an occasional non-working member, what we would call today
an honorary member. As the number of lodges increased more and more
non-operative members were admitted. T hese were called Accepted

Masons. They held meetings behind guarded doors, used pass words
and grips, emblems and symbols for purposes of identukation just as the
older craft lodges did in order to preserve the secrecy of the art and
science of building.

who had come to America did so because they were dissatisfted with the
social, economic, political and religious institutions of Europe. Only
those brave enough to break with the past and face the danger of
frontier life were able to survive. Those who did were alert and versatile.
The new frontier had a constant leveling influence on the lives of the
colonists. This stimulated a practical application of brotherhood emphasized by the Masonic fraternity. At last the individual had become
important.
Masonic philosophy in America reached a stage sufficient for leader.ship at the very time and place when the opportunity for such leadership
arose. Freemasonry was the only organized philosophic institution common to all the colonies. It drew the leading citizens of the towns and
villages into bonds of unity and brotherhood. This made mutual trust,
confidence and cooperation possible in working toward the common
cause of independence.
From 1733 with the formation of St. John's Lodge at Boston until
1775 Masonry grew rapidly in America and historians point out the
great influence exerted by Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanac
Arst published in 1732 when he was elected Junior Grand Warden of
the Provincial Grand Lodge df Pennsylvania.
The Almanac was a collection of popular wisdom so cleverly phrased
that it had a strong appeal to the public. Its recommendations of thrift
and industry and the value of the practice of virtue was an ex•hibition to
the general public of the philosophy taught by Freemasonry. The
Almanac was published during a period of great activity in Masonic
lodges which sowed the seeds of Masonic philosophy in all parts of the
Atlantic seaboarcl. By 1775 there were more than 100 stationary lodges
and 50 military lodges.
It would be difficult to determine specifically what influence Masonry
played in the Revolution and in the ultimate formation of the Republic.
It is not difficult, however, to show that Masons were deeply involved
and that they furnished leaders all out of ·proportion to their number in
the population. Masons constituted less than two percent of the population yet provided for one third to one half of the leadership. It seems
impossible to conceive of American victory without such men as James
Otis, a Massachusetts Mason, who declared that taxation without representation was tyranny. or Samuel Adams, the leader of the Sons of
Liberty. or General Joseph Warren, Grand Master of Massachusetts,
who dispatched Paul Revere on his historic ride, and then died a patriot's
death at Bunker Hill. or Ethan Allen. the Vermont Mason, who led his
Green Mountain boys in the successful attack against Ticonderoga, or
Haym Salomon, born of a Jewish family in Poland, who spent his
personal fortune and died in bankruptcy for the holy cause of freedom.

Such were the Masonic lodges at the beginning of the eighteenth
century. Then one day in June in the year 1717 the lodges of London,
England, met for the purpose of forming a Grand Lodge which proved
to be the Mother Grand Lodge of the world. Out of this came the Grand
Lodge system of Freemasonry.
This is Masonry of the past recited according to the best authorities
not because its fascinating story is unfamiliar to the members of this
Grand Lodge, but only in an attempt to demonstrate how Freemasonry,
first operative and then speculative, is completely and inseparably interwoven into the affairs of mankind from time immemorial. If we who
stand at the threshhold of a new and better world are to pass through
its entrance then we must make certain that this great moral force will
continue to exert its equalizing benevolent influence in the years ahead
just as strongly as it did in the pre-historic period. as it did in the Dark
Ages. during the Renaissance and the Reformation, and during the
birth of freedom in America.
When men in their quest for freedom turned to the New World
they also turned to Freemasonry as a philosophic weapon against
despotism in all its forms. The Dark Ages had been times of violence
when oppression was the usual cqndition of society. Unless a man were
of the nobility or of the hierarchy of the church he could do nothing
without the consent of his feudal lord and master. Under such conditions
there was no hope for the weak. But the craftsmen found it possible
through their guild system to retain their freedom of movement. At this
point Freemasonry became the guardian of the rights of the individual.
a role it has continued to play from the Age of Darkness to the Age of
the Atom.
·
When men came to the New World they were faced with problems
which their past experience had not equipped them to handle quickly
and easily. No longer was it a question of man striving against man. It
was man striving against nature. They were possessed with complete
freedom to try to wrest from nature those things they desired. Old
concepts and institutions which were not adapted to this pursuit were
cast aside and the jungle law of the survival of the fittest was again
supreme. Work became ·the passion of the individual. Circumstances of
birth did not determine leadership but individual abilities and attainments.
The new land of America provided a tremendous challenge to the
European, a challenge both intellectual and physical. Most of the people

While it may never have been proved conclusively that Masonic
philosophy provided the motivating force in the fight for American Independence , there is no doubt that the early American Masons were
almost unanimous in their pursuit for freedom. Without the sympathy
and moral support of such distinguishe d English Masons as Edmund
Burke and William Pitt the Revolution might have failed. Masons in
France helped to establish the grounds upon which France could intervene on behalf of the American Revolutionists. The philosophy of
liberty, equality, and fraternity taught by Freemasonr y appealed to
soldiers of freedom on both sides of the Atlantic.

With the end of the Revolutiona ry War there appeared for the first
time in its history the opportunity for Masonry to play an important role
in the creation of a new economic and social order. The knowledge
Masonry had accumulated over thousands of years had taught that the
individual seldom gained ·his liberty as a gift of government. Experience
had proved that only through limiting the powers of the government had
liberty for the individual been assured. Masons had found that freedom
of thought is effective only when the individual has learned to think
intelligently. Freedom to form opinions has value only when the individual has learned to determine right from wrong and the true from the
false. He has freedom to def end his liberties only when he understands
the principles of law which guarantee those liberties.
One hundred and seventy years ago today plus one week there
occured in Philadelphia the most important event in political and social
history of the world. Think of that first Constitution Day when George
Washing ton and representati ves from the thirteen independen t American states signed the great charter written in convention attended
by 8fty-8ve delegates of whom thirty-three were Masons. Of these two
were Past Grand Masters, two were Grand Masters, and two were to
become Grand Masters.
These Masons were the most influential leaders in the Masonic fraternity in America. Since Masonry was the only institution at that time
governed by a federal system, it appears conclusive that the principles set
forth in the Constitution were not drawn from any source other than
those developed throug·h the centuries by the Masonic fraternity. The
similarity the government of the United States bears to the government
of Masonry both in theory and structure cannot be credited to mere
coincidence. These precepts provided .for a liberal democratic order in
whiC'h mankind is led through education to a more equitable and just
society, a sovereignty which is the sovereignty of the people, a limited
government, local self-government, supremacy of the national government in matters affecting all of the people, and separation of powers into
the executive, legislative and judicial.
They formed a Constitution giving the government only 20 powers,
and no more, because all history had taught them that government, when
it becomes big, becomes tyrannical: it takes away man's freedom, and
the writers of the Constitution wanted no part of it. They'd been through
that. They wanted a limited government.
After writing this document they met again, and they were still
unhappy. They made ten amendments to it: they called this the Bill of
Rights. There are some 'Who believe that these were rights that government gave to the people, but they were no such thing. They were ten
prohibitions against the government.

Had the influence of Freemasonr y only found expression and action
during America's quest for independenc e then the contention that
Masons in all ages have been the most forward advocates of freedom
may not be well founded. But the relation between Masons and a willingness to fight for the liberty of the people has been well established.
Benito Juarez as a Mason and President of Mexico gave his country the
most liberal government it had ever had. Giuseppe Garibaldi, Grand
Master of Palermo, had an unquenchab le thirst for freedom which satisfied itself in France and Uraguay and then resulted in the unification of
Italy. Simon Bolivar was a South American patriot, a general, a statesman, and the '"George Washingto n" of South America. Within him
the flres of liberty burned strong for he was a Mason.
Presidents and princes, emperors and kings, have been members of
the Craft. If Freemasonr y celebrates these famous men who have been
Masons, it is not out of conceit or even with pardonable pride, but to
demonstrate to its initiates by precept and example the universality of
Masonry and to show that the true Mason has often been the true
soldier of freedom.
A Masonic poet, Douglas Malloch, successfully joined together
Masons of all ages in his thrilling words:
"Fine men have walked this way before,
Whatever Lodge your Lodge may be,
Whoever stands before the door,
The sacred arch of Masonry,
Stands where the wise, the great, the good
In their own time and place have stood.
You are not Brother just with these
Your friends and neighbors; you are kin
With Masons down the centuries:
This room that you now enter in
Has felt the tread of many feet
For here all Masonry you meet.'

They said, "Look, Mr. Government. I have given you twenty powers. Now bear in mind that you can't take away my freedom of religion
or press, or speech: you can't prevent my carrying arms in my own
defense; you can't stop me from educating my children; you can't stop
me from petitioning my government: you can't stop me from writing or
speaking. And most important of all, just in case I've forgotten something you can't do, don't assume that power belongs to you. That belongs to us."

A wise and frugal government does not levy complicated and confiscatory taxes on payrolls. thus taking from labor's mouth the bread it
has earned.
A wise and frugal government can restrain men singly or in groups
from injuring one another without telling them what to sow and when
and how to reap it.
A wise and frugal government would punish crime; but it would
otherwise leave men free to govern themselves according to the Ten
Commandments of God, rather than undertake to force universal compliance with tens of thousands of commands of government.

The Constitution was based upon the theory of inalienable Godgiven personal liberty that had been categorically proclaimed in the
Declaration of Independence. Personal rights were made enforceable
by the individual person himself and this was at once the distinguishing
feature of the American constitutional system: never before had the
indi_vidual citizen b.een legally authorized to enforce his God-given rights
agamst all the ma1esty and power of his government.
Because man freed himself from domination by government, man has
built in f'-merica the greatest civilization ever known to mankind, beyond
all mans dreams. This was not because of our national resources, not
because of wealth or any different intelligence of ,people. Man freed
himself, and his energies, his thoughts, and his inspiration to work out
his own salvation in life, to do as he pleases, just as long as he respects
the rights of other men to do as they please.
1

The principles necessary for freedom and the good life came into
the world thousands of years ago. They were written in the Ten Commandments that Moses brought down from Mount Sinai. They were
perpetuated as Jesus Christ elevated the ancient law and glorified it in
the Sermon on the Mount. They were guaranteed by the Magna Carta
at Runnymede. They were preserved through the Dark Ages, the Middle Ages, and the Reformation by groups of men called Freemasons.
And when the New World opened up new perspectives and horizons to
men who loved freedom is it any wonder that in America there developed a. go~~nment whose ~urpose was to preserve the God-given rights
o~ the individual, to keep him free so that he might conscientiously fulfill
his personal responsibilities to God and to his fellowman?
Today we must ask ourselves this question: do we still wish to be
free and therefore govern ourselves, or do we wish to be made secure
by whatever governmental regulations and regimentation are necessary
to produce security?
It was Thomas Jefferson who said: "A wise and frugal government is
one which shall restrain men from injuring one another, which shall leave
them otherwise free to regulate their own pursuits of industry and improvement and shall not take from the mouth of labor the bread it has
earned." This is the principle of liberty and self-government.

A wise and frugal government would not engage in 19,000 different
businesses or own 21 percent of the land in America.
A wise and frugal government does not, except in times of great
emergency and national peril, pay for its debts out of money which remains in the pockets of its citizens after they have paid their taxes.
Somewhere along the way I have been given a ten-word cycle of
civilization. Bondage is the first word; bondage, the place where civilization wakes up. Faith-in-God is the next word; then out of faith comes
courage, and with courage men acquire their liberty. Then with liberty
eventually comes abundance, the top of the arc. After abundance comes
selflshness, and after selfishness comes complacency. From complacency
comes apathy, and from apathy, dependency. and after dependency.
back, if you please, to bondage again.
Where are w~ on that cycle now? We have long since passed the
point where religious faith gave us the courage to acquire our liberty
and the greatest abundance the world has ever known. Where are we
now-at selfishness? complacency? apathy? or dependency?
Our Founding Fathers realized that men were free only as long as
they would willingly assume the burden of governing themselves.
At the birth of our country the Masonic fraternity furnished morally
strong self-disciplined and self-sacrificing men. They knew that freedom
demands personal sacrifice and continuous self-restraint. They knew that
when government undertakes to provide economic security for its citizens
it must take freedom and self-government in exchange. The time may be
near at hand when Masons may again be called upon to lead a courageous campaign to save the right to self-government they inherited
from their forebearers. It was necessary for the Masons of 1775 to use
the weapons of violence: the musket, the cannon, and the sword. Today
our weapons are more plentiful and more effective: freedom to speak
through initiative and referendum, the power of the ballot box, the
strength of a free public school. and the knowledge that faith in God.

having once produced a free government for free men, can help pre.serve it.

ignorance and doubt only to be brushed aside. But one by one these
snowflakes of the mind communicate themselves to other men, the
crystals of intelligence begin to check the devastations of the enemies of
light, until at last the great terrifying bulk of oppression and ~ranny
and despotism is brought to a halt and become a hollow thing, a

Tihe preservation of the Constitution of the United States of America
is just as much the business of the Mason of 1957 as it was the Mason
~f 1787. If it were not for the Constitution of the United States neither
private business, nor private property, nor private employment, nor
private rights, nor personal privacy would exist in this country. Without
the Constitution we would all be involuntary servants of the government.

If the United States is ever destroyed it will not be because . of
someone else's bombs, but because of our own indifference. The spirit
of freedom is not dead in this country. It has been ridiculed by the socialists and the communists to the point that it sometimes goes into hiding.
It has been unsold to some of our workers in our .factories and fields, but
since there is a spark left let us breathe new life into it while there is
still yet time.
Few are willing to heed the warning today, because the gravy train
is running in three sections and the .factory whistles are making too much
noise. They figure God will save America without giving Him any reason
why. But there are green years, new frontiers for America's pioneers.
We can, if we will, protect this wonderful land where any man willing
to stand on his toes can reach the stars.
The collective force exerted by men of goodwill is fantastic in its
power. I well remember years ago when I rode as a passenger on a
train across the plains of the middle West. It was winter and slowly
snow began to fall. The flakes fell into the hot smoke and exhaust of
the engine and were consumed. They 'fell on the hot cover of the boiler
and were licked up in an instant. They .fell under t'he wheels and were
destroyed as the train rushed on. What chance of life has a snowflake
again·s t sixty tons of steam driven power? Countless millions were
hurled aside and destroyed, unwept, and unsung. But swiftly and
softly the tiny flakes continued to fall and where a million were consumed a million more leaped to take their place. And soon, in spite of
its mighty strength, the great locomotive began to slacken, more and
more slowly it moved until with a last expiring burst of power, it stood
still, panting and helpless in the whirling white.
As is the power of the snowflake so is the power of collective human
thought and action. Light and often alone they strike the engine of

Our fathers bestowed upon us our liberty at a high price. If we do
not defend and protect it and pass it on to posterity, then our distant
descendants must, through toil and slavery in centuries to come, retrace
the bloody steps which will lead to another era of liberty, freedom, and
peace when men will once again be given the opportunity to accomplish
the destiny which God in his infinite wisdom planned for them.
· Right here and now, in these our times, the question is being decided.
May God give us courage to face the task. May He arouse in us the
power of our convictions and help us to acquit ourselves like men.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully
submits its report for the 1956-1957 Masonic year.
During the year the Committee has approved eleven applications to
incorporate new Masonic temple associations under the non.iproflt laws
of the State of California: nineteen new temple sites have been acquired;
and thirteen new Masonic temple buildin·g projects have been sanctioned.
Scores of other applications to exipend funds pursuant to Section 199 of
the Ordinances ( C.M.C.) have been processed. A resume o·f the details
of the activities of the Committee are made a part of this report and
will be printed in the official proceedings of this Grand Lodge. Your
attention to this portion of t'he proceedings is respectfully recommended.
Because this is my last appearance before the Grand Lodge in my
capacity as Chairman of the Committee on Lodge Financing, I beg your
indulgence for a few moments while I point with pride to the accomplishments of the past eight years of the Committee's existence and

226

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

perhaps to view with alarm some of the disturbing facts surrounding
the financial condition of our Masonic temple .properties.
On the bright side the Committee takes justifiable pride in the small
part it has been privileged to 1play in the greatest Masonic temple
building program in the history of this or any other jurisdiction. In
the eight years that I have served as Chairman of the Committee more
than a hundred new Masonic temples 1have been completed free and
clear of outside indebtedness and more than a score of others are in
various ·phases of construction. Of course, as you know, these temples
were to all intents and purposes built by the members of the respective
Lodges with their own hands, a record of accomplishment in operative
Masonry unparalleled in contemporary ·history. It might be interesting
to you to know that the replacement value of these new temples approximates that of all the Masonic temples built in California over the
previous one hundred years. In spite of the great record of building
during the past decade, Masonry is still lagging far behind the phenome.. nal growth of this great jurisdiction of ours. The brethren must continue
to work and sacrifice to provide new Lodge homes to accommodate the
thousands of good and true men who, we trust, will continue to enter
the portals of Masonry. To this end the Committee on Lodge
Financing will continue to encourage, to assist, to enthuse the brethren,
and will ,pray along with them in their efforts to accomplish the fruits
of their dreams.
W 1hile this unprecedented building activity has been taking place,
your Committee on Lodge Financing has been greatly concerned as to
whether or not the business affairs of the new temple properties were
being properly administered. The Committee has a very definite responsibility in this phase of the program because approval of the
building plans has, in every instance, been predicated on the showing in
the applications that the new Lodge homes would be going concerns
after they were completed and occupied. The committee was convinced
that the same faith, courage, ingenuity and determination displayed by
the brethren in the building of the temples would be required in the
future operation of them.
So, in order to give the Committee on Lodge Financing an opportunity to review the business administration of all the Masonic temple
properties in California, this Grand Lodge in 1954 adopted legislation
which was then known as Section 78.1, Ross' Digest, and now known
as Section 200, California Masonic Code. This new law required all
Lodges owning and operating real property and all temple associations
owning and operating real property and controlled by a Lodge or
Lodges to submit financial statements to this Committee. During 1955
much time and effort were · expended in the developing of necessary
forms and establishing a list of Masonic temples, such a roster not

existing prior to that time. Therefore, for all practical purposes, this is
the first year the Committee has had an opportunity to study. the
financial condition of the Masonic temple properties in this jurisdiction.
It was indeed startling and disconcerting to your Committee, when
these reports started to come in to find such a universal. unrealistic
approach to the business management of our temple properties. Most
discouraging of all, perhaps, was the apparent fact that the business
affairs of many of the new temples were falling into the same inefficient
pattern that has been employed in the older properties.
These financial statements submitted pursuant to the new ordinance
disclosed many violations of Masonic law. There were instances where
building sites were acquired, commercial buildings erected, and large
sums of money expended for alterations made in previous years without
first obtaining written approval from the Committee on Lodge Financing
in accordance with Masonic statutes. Most of these irregularities, however, ·have been cleared on the record. Some applications were presented
to this Committee for contemplated building activities which, because
of prior violations, had to be referred to the Grand Master for his
decision before Committee approval could be granted. In all such
instances, with the Grand Master's sanction and the cooperation of the
applicants, the problems were resolved to the satisfaction of all concerned.

1

In one application requesting approval of the expenditure of temple
association funds this Committee's jurisdiction was seriously challenged.
However, the Committee's action was sustained by the Deputy Grand
Master and the Jqdge Advocate. By virtue of a recommendation by the
Grand Master, together with additional evidence submitted, your Committee subsequently approved the request.
Now, my brethren, your time and your patience are being imposed
upon, but the problem of temple property management is of such great
importance that I trust you will bear with me a few more minutes.
In the opinion of your Committee we have reached the crossroads
of temple property success or failure in this great jurisdiction of ours.
Either we do something constructive now to get our financial house in
order or we travel down the road of indifference, :inefficiency and default,
to arrive at last to the point of no return, with a possible loss of many
temple properties and a consequent reflection on our beloved fraternity.
Perhaps a few statistics derived from a breakdown of the .financial
statements above referred to will serve to paint a picture of the serious
problem confronting all of us.
Although two requests were made through the Grand Secretary's
office to all of the organizations involved to submit financial statements
sixty out of the three hundred and forty-one temple properties failed
to respond and are thus in violation of Section 200 of the Ordinances.

228

These organizations will again be notified in due time. Of the 281
reporting, 170 or 62% showed a net operating loss amounting to
$244,182.86 for the year 1956. These statements also indicate that
organizations other than Blue Lodges cost the temple properties a
total of $431.278.54 in subsidies through reduced rentals or no rentals
at all. The difference between the net loss of $244,182.86 and the loss
by subsidy is made up by exorbitant rents charged the Lodges, the sole
owners of the properties in most cases. Thus, the Lodges are required to
pay for the deficit .financing, either through high rents or the transfer of
Lodge funds to the temple association, placing a serious financial burden
on Lodge treasuries. Twenty of our Lodges operating temple properties
charge no rentals at all to the prerequisite organizations, whicli is
contrary to the language of 409K of the California Masonic Code. Five
of these Lodges have less than $1,000.00 each in liquid assets in their
treasuries. We have evidence where some affiliated organizations have
apparently become self-conscious and have made small contributions at
the end of the year to keep the Blue Lodges solvent.
This situation, my brethren, I submit, is a sad commentary on the
business administration of the temple properties during these times of
unprecedented prosperity. Most assuredly, H Masonic temple properties
cannot pay their own way now, there can be no optimism for the future.
Another matter giving the Committee much concern is the fact that
only a handful of our temple properties are setting aside cash reserves
for depreciation and maintenance. Many properties are, consequently,
being neglected and are in a bad state of repair. Many are requesting
permission to borrow money to make repairs and the Committee has
had to deny some of these applications until rental schedules have been
adjusted. Of course, you and I agree that Masonic tem1ples should be
the best maintained properties in the communities, but we find some of
the brethren more willing to place a mortgage on the temple properties
or otherwise allow them to deteriorate, rather than to review the possibilities of increasing income from the Lodge facilities.
Is there a solution to this problem? Of course, there isl But my
brethren the problem is in your hands and the solution is entirely up to
you. T he Committee on Lodge Financing was established to protect
the interests of the Lodges in all their financing problems. This it has
tried hard to do. It was formed to assure Grand Lodge, and you are
the Grand Lodge, that Masonic building enterprises are self-supporting ,
properly financed and to assure that adequate funds are on hand to
properly maintain and support them when completed. To perform these
functions properly is all that can be asked from a Grand Lodge
Committee. It is time consuming and requires great sacrifices on the
part of its members. It should not be called upon to delve into all of
the details of temple property management. It cannot.
1

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

229

Your Committee has been admonished that it has no authority to
set up budgets or adjust rentals in our Masonic temple properties or
to even suggest what rentals ought to be charged to other organizations.
We agree that specific law is not now on the statute books granting
such authority. We believe, however, that the intent is there. Neither
is there any specific law which grants a Lodge or its controlled temple
association the right to give free or nominal rents to prerequisite
organizations. On the contrary.
Time after time, in its contacts with temple associations, the Committee has found itself the only advocate for the Blue Lodges. The
Committee has been told that every Lodge and temple association has
local ·problems and Masonic family personalities with which we are
not familiar and, therefore, cannot intercede for the Blue Lodge. We
!have been told in almost every instance where the question has arisen
that the affiliated organizations are 1having financial difficulties and
cannot pay the costs of using the Lodge 'facilities. That it is the Masonic
family duty of the Lodge to care for a sick and ailing member of the
family.
I personally belong to several affiliated groups and I cherish the
associations that go with such fraternal membership. It would be quite
easy for me to have my Masonic interests divided, but my first and most
important duty is to my Lodge, and I am sure that you feel your interests
are the same. I firmly believe that no affiliated organization lb.as any
right to be a burden on the Lodge or its temple association, no matter
how deep our sympathies lie.
There may be a responsibility on the part of Masons as individuals to
care for an ailing' member of the Masonic family or it may be that you,
throug'h the Grand Lodge, would like to assume that responsibility. But
surely, it is not justice or equity .for the Blue Lodges of this State to be
called upon to subsidize these organizations in the amount of $500,000.00
a year which, in effect, decreases the total market value of their temple
properties $5,000,000.QO.
The Committee is informed that recommendations .for corrective
legislation designed to effect a solution of this very important and very
serious problem will be offered to this Grand Lodge by the Grand
Master. We trust you will give serious consideration to these proposals
and we know you will, as always. act in the best interests of Masonry.
In summarizing the year's activities the Committee has processed
more applications than in any previous year, another record in the
progress of Masonic temple building programs in this jurisdiction whiC'h
started with the close of World War II. In every instance where consent
was granted to start construction of new temples, the stipulation was
made that no collateral financing be employed and that no liabilities,
either for labor or material, be incurred without first obtaining written
consent from the Committee on Lodge Financing.

Today, there are two dynamic forces in the world working constantly to change our Constitution and t'he way of life it has promoted
and evolved. These forces are Roman Catholicism and Communism.
Both are antagonistic to the principles of self-government expressed
by our founding fathers in the Constitution and in the Declaration of
Independence. Both these forces are dangerous because they seek to
work their will by devious, insidious, and hypocritical methods. They
embrace the round-about way, the long pull. Both of these forces work
under the p hilosophy that time is in their favor. And they are right!
They make their best progress when men become tired and weary,
their attention diverted, and the sentinels sleep at their posts. Of course
the Communists renounce the use of force in changing our form of
government. Why not, Wthen it can be done peacefully, within the
framework and structure of unconstitutional processes. The Roman
Catholics have not yet made any direct attempt to impose their
church as a State religion but when they have indoctrinated and converted enough of our people to compose a majority, what is to prevent
erasing our constitutional guarantees of religious liberty by amendment? Or, without any amendments, and with those guarantees still
safely embedded in the Constitution, they have already partly joined
their church to our State.
