REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON CONSTITUTION MONTH OBSERVANCE
Most Worshipful, Grand Wardens, and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
Your Committee on Constitution Month Observance begs leave
to report as follows:
William Gladstone, Prime Minister of England, said that the Constitution of the United States is "the greatest piece of work ever struck
off .at a given time by the brain and purpose of man."
Although fashioned 170 years ago under vastly different conditions than those we live under today, designed to govern 3,000,000
people, of which 750,000 were slaves, it has proved to be a living document. It has withstood the corrosive effects of adversity, war, selfishness, expansion, and of prosperity. People from all the countries of
the world, representing all degrees of knowledge, have come here and
under its benign influence have combined their talents to form the
greatest, the most prosperous, the most advanced, the most powerful.
the most productive nation on the face of the earth and in the history
of civilization. The keystone of our Constitution is Freedom: moral,
physical, intellectual and spiritual Freedom in whidh the dignity of
man is first, uppermost, and which glorifies HIM, rather than the State.
'J'lhe magnificence of this document is amazing but what is more amazing is that there are those among us who would cltange it out of all
recognition, whose frustrations lead them to believe that there is more
comfort in some other ideology, in some other philosophy of government promising so much but conferring so little.
Many times have the members of this Grand Lodge heard extolled
the virtues of our Constitution and of our form of democracy. We
know all the words and phrases. It is not the purpose of this report

have already dipped into the public treasury for funds to finance their

on their part has only just begun. In addition to some class-room materials and public transportation of ipupils, there is little doubt tihe day

We Free Masons have accepted the responsibility of protecting
and safe-guarding our Constitution, the work of our brethren which
was consummated in Independence Hall, Philadelphia, on September
17, 1787. While we weep at the memory of their suffering and hardships
in the flght to establish this nation, we, at the same time. rejoice in
the success which resulted in our way of life. Accordingly, your committee this year adopted as the theme of our Constitution Observance,
"A Patriotic Festival." expressed in last year's report to this Grand
Lodge. As a joyful event, it should be celebrated, and in t'he very nature
of the celebrations we would be reminding our people of the blessings
and of the privileges whieh our Constitution confers. The Grand
Master confirmed our recommendation that the theme be, "A Patriotic
Festival." It suggested seriousness of purpose, ingenuity and fun, at
the same time affording the Lodges an opportunity to display our wares
in the public marketplace. To give better direction to this effort, your
committee prepared the booklet, "A GUIDE TO YOUR CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE CELEBRATION," which was sent out
to every Lodge, Inspector, and others, in May. This "Guide" is a first
effort, and as suoh is far from perfect. We hope that we have laid a
foundation upon which future committees can erect a satisfying superstructure. By co:incidence, due to the time of this Communication, our
work is not yet finished and we are presently in the midst of the
Observance period.
For years, the observances have been handicapped in closely following the summer vacation period. In fact, the ·p eriod of observance started
while many people were still away on vacation. This has created some
problems and, in our opinion, has been a deterring factor in rousing
enough enthusiasm to obtain maximum success. Accordingly, we
prevailed upon the Grand Master to set the period of observance to
commence on the birthday of the Constitution, September 17th, and
to run for about thirty days, until the 15th of October.
In an endeavor to improve the Observance program, your committee
adopted the idea of the Lodges promoting public speaking contests on
the subject, "What Our Federal Constitution Means to Me." These
contests would be fostered through co-operation with the Public Schools
Committee within each Lodge, with prizes to be awarded by the Lodges
to successful contestants. With the support of Brother Vierling Kersey,

the suggestion. It was suggested that it be confined ?nly to the H~gh

forward and made a part of our Constitution Observance pro~ram. We
visualize that it can accomplish much in the direction we wish to go:
that it is capable of expansion to the point where it can become. statewide in scope; that it could even be a vehicle for the granting of
scholarship aid to needy and worthy students.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The field covered by the Research Committee is a vast one, for it is
the field of Masonic education. The terms "research" and "education"
are used synonymously in this Jurisdiction.
Great credit should be given Most Worshipful L. Harold Anderson,
Grand Master, for his active and sincere interest in research projects.
The Grand Secretary and Assistant Grand Secretary have also been
of inestimable help to the Committee during the Masonic year just
closed.
The basic unit in our scheme of operation has been and still is the
individual constituent Lodge. Each Lodge. with few exceptions. has had
a committee on research. The names of the chairmen of these committees
comprise a mailing list kept in the office of the Grand Secretary. and
over this mailing list each release from t:'he committee has readied each
Lodge. At last year's Communication we reported the great demand
for printed materials which coufd be used by Lodge committees in their
educational work. Grand Lodge provided fonds for printing and we
have thus been able to place four separate booklets in · the hands of
local chairmen. Each booklet. called "Research Notes" contains a
number of articles prepared by California Masons, not previously
published and thus giving the Lodge committee exclusive material for
its use. A very common manner in which Lodges have profited from this
plan is to call on t'he chairman of the committee for a five or ten minute
report at a stated meeting. May I sugegst to Masters and Wardens
who have not been making use of this help that your Lodge committee
has material in its hands and may appropriately be invited to take part
at each stated meeting.
1

The next larger unit with which we deal is the district meeting or
sometimes a meeting of a combination of districts. The key man here
is the Inspector who usually suggests the scheduling of the meeting by
the Officers Association or the Masters and Wardens Association. The
programs supplied by the two Research Lodges are popular at these
meetings where a larger audience is assembled and let me say that the
work of both Research Lodges has been invaluable in supplying
previously used programs and developing new ones.
The next higher unit is the regional seminar serving an entire region
and cutting across district lines and sometimes division lines. Locations
are selected some distance from the metropolitan areas of San Francisco
and Los Angeles which can be serviced easily by the Research Lodge
iocated there. Nine regional seminars have been held this year and
three more are scheduled. each in a different city ranging from El
Centro to Santa Rosa. They were organized by the Grand Lodge

Committee on a do-it~yourself basis with local talent presenting material
supplied by the Committee. Tihe Committee .devised a standardize d

were encouraged to meet local needs. The Research Lodges were

on each seminar is attached to this report marked "Schedule A" and will

The Research Lodges were encouraged to take responsibility for
their respective metropolitan areas. Northern California Research Lodge
devised a unique evening program which was presented at Concord,
Oakland and San Francisco. Southern California Research Lodge used
one seminar for the northwest Los Angeles area and a large number
of district meetings. It should be remembered that the Research Lodges
are cpnstituent chartered Lodges, not an arm of or supported by Grand
Lodge and not under the direct control of this Committee. We have
respected their integrity but have never failed to receive their full and
friendly cooperation when requested. Northern California Research
Lodge reports 26 appearances, a total audience of 3000 and 7000 miles
traveled by participants, all at their own expense. The corresponding
figures for Southern California Research Lodge are 67 appearances, a
total audience of 6600 and 10,500 miles traveled by participants .
The last subject we report on is the Research Seminar to be held
this evening at 25 Van Ness Avenue. This is a continuation of, and,
we hope an improvement on, the seminar held last year when 800
attended. The grand division of the seminar will be between those
seeking practical help in the efficient and successful operation of a Lodge
and those interested in subjects of general interest to Masons. By this
time, we are sure that all now present have made reservations at ·the
registration counter and the advance reservations indicate at least as
many will attend this year as last.
We want to emphasize these points which will assist in the smooth
running of the seminar tonight:
1. ·All Master Masons are welcome.
2. The entire Teiiiple will be tiled so Masonic identification must be
presented at the door. Your Grand Lodge credentials are sufficient for
this purpose.
3. Classes start on time. Please allow a ·few minutes to locate your
classroom and Snd a seat.
4. Be sure to bring your seminar program with you. It gives the
number of the hall, the Boor and the time scheduled for your classes.

May we express the gratitude of the Committee to the present and
past Grand Officers and the numerous members of the two Research
Lodges who are serving as the faculty. The time, effort and travel they
are contributing presages a most profitable and instructive session
tonight.
The members of the Research Committee are divided three from
the north and three from the south. Their assistance has been especially
valuable in reviewing papers to be used for research purposes and in
planning the Grand Lodge seminar. The chairman thanks ea~h of them
for a noteworthy contribution to the march of education.
The recommendations of the Committee are
· ( 1 ) That the present research program be continued:
( 2 ) That the budgetary allowance of $2000.00 be repeated for the
coming year.

SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON TRIAL PROCEDURES
This special committee on trial procedures was appointed as a
result of a recommendation by Most Worshipful Edgar V. Stewart in
his message as Grand Master at the annual communication of the
Grand Lodge in September, 1956.
"Having had first hand experience this year with Masonic trials
and noting some of the results, I am convinced that at least some improvements could be made in our trial procedure and possibly, it
might be entirely revamped and simpli'Bed. For this purpose, I recommend that the incoming Grand Master appoint a special committee of
brethren experienced in this field to report their findings and recommendations to Grand Lodge next year."
It will be noted that the Grand Master did not suggest any specific
amendments. His apparent purpose was to leave to the committee the
task of reviewing the present system and then to make findings and
recommendations on either ( 1 ) improvements in details in our present
procedure or ( 2) an entirely new and simplified method or ( 3) a
combination of the two.
The first decision of the committee necessarily dealt with what
line of research and investigation was to be followed. The committee
is composed of two past chairmen of the Grievance Committee of Grand
Lodge and an inspector who has acted as Trial Master on several
occasions. It was familiar with the present method of conducting
Masonic trials in California and therefore decided that the first task
to be undertaken was a study of the trial procedures in other Masonic
jurisdictions.
In this they were immeasurably assisted by Most Worshipful Lloyd
E. Wilson, Grand Secretary, who in 1956 conducted a similar study
for the Conference of Masonic Grand Lodge Secretaries. He placed
the results of this survey in the hands of this . committee, and also
furnished to it the laws of several Masonic jurisdictions relating to
trials of charges against members.
It became immediately apparent that there is a complete lack of
uniformity throughout the United States and Canada in the handling
of this important phase of Masonic jurisprudence. The committee was
unable to identify any common tradition or ritual which would assist
it in this field as it does in other problems confronting the fraternity.
A review of the trial procedure in other jurisdictions should be of
assistance to this Grand Lodge in determining its future course of
conduct.
In every jurisdiction examined, Masonic trials are instituted by
the filing of written charges by a Master Mason in good standing, but
from this rpoint on a wide divergence exists.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

259

In some states no form is prescribed for these charges. In others
a form for charges is provided for in the law, but the form varies from
state to state. In some jurisdictions the charges are presented to the
Master, in others to the Lodge, and in the State of New York they are
presented to the Grand Master. When they are presented to the
Master, in many jurisdictions he passes upon their sufficiency before
ordering a trial. Where the Master does not have this power, and in all
cases where charges must be presented directly to the Lodge, the
Lodge itself by a majority vote decides whether they shall be received
and a trial had. In the State of New York the Grand Master has the
sole power to decide whether the charges will be entertained.
The conduct of the trial itself varies to such an extent that only
a general summary of the various methods used is possible in this
report.
In twenty-six Grand Lodges in the United States and Canada,
trials are conducted by commissions or committees. In only five Grand
Lodges are these commissions elected by the Lodge. In eight they are
appointed by the Master, in ten by the Grand Master and in six by
a combination of methods.
Where the trial is conducted by a commission, in some jurisdictions
it decides upon the verdict and punishment, and in others it reports
to the Lodge upon the facts either with or without recommendations,
and the Lodge then decides the case and fixes the punishment. It is
particularly interesting that where a trial commission is provided for,
it is frequently with the stipulation that none of its members shall
belong to the Lodge of which the accused is a member.
In nine Unite-d States Grand Lodges and one Canadian Grand
Lodge, the trial is conducted by the individual Lodge, with the Master
presiding. At the conclusion of the trial, the Lodge decides upon the
verdict and punishment, either by a majority, two thirds or three fourths
vote, depending upon the jurisdiction.
In two Grand Lodges all trials are conducted by a referee appointed
by the Grand Master. In one the referee acts only as a Trial Master.
In the other he recommends the verdict and sentence.
In nine United States Grand Lodges and two Canadian Grand
Lodges, alternative or optional methods are used, where the trial is had
either by a commission appointed by the Grand Master or by the Lodge
itself. The option to use one or the other method is exercised by the
Grand Master, the Master, the Lodge, the accuser or the accused, depending upon the jurisdiction, and in some cases by more than one of
this group. This alternative method of trial procedure had great appeal
to this committee, and will be referred to again in this report.
The methods of three states merit particular attention.
In New York, as already noted, charges are Bled directly with
the Grand Master. If he believes them to be meritorious, he refers

261

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

them to a special officer of Grand Lodge, the Proctor•. who prepares
formal charges and secures and presents ·the necess11ry evidence to a
commission appointed by the Grand Master and consisting of three to
five Past Masters of Lodges other than the Lodge of which the accused
is a member.
In Georgia, the state is divided into twelve districts, in each of
which twelve commissioners are elected to conduct all Masonic trials.
In Illinois the optional method of trial is used. If either the Lodge
by a majority vote. or the accuser or accused requests a commission,
the charges are referred to the Grand Master. If he decides it is a
proper case, he appoints a commission to hear the evidence. decide
upon the verdict and ·fix the penalty.
In all jurisdictions. reprimand , suspension or expulsion are imposed
as penalties. Some provide for suspensio n for a definite term, others
for an indefinite term. and still others for both. In one state, a fine may
be imposed. In several the costs of the trial are assessed against the
accused. the accuser or the Lodge. or apportion ed among them.
As a result of its studies of the various systems of Masonic trials,
including that of California, your committee has formed a definite
opinion as to the reason for the faults in the California system. Our
opinion is that these faults, and the many complaints made concerning
them. can be traced to the basic fallacy of attempting to formulate a
procedure which will accomplish substantia l justice and at the same
time can be administered by Masons with no experience in conducting
trials.
This does not imply that a procedure should be adopted which can
be used only by lawyers, for this is by no means necessary. In many
phases of civil life, trials are conducted by non-lawye rs. But where
such trials are properly handled. it is due to the fact that those conducting them have had previous experience, as with trade commissions,
civil service trial boards, and similar permanen t and semi-perm anent
groups.
In our own jurisdiction. the individual Lodge usually has a different
Master each year. In many cases the Master has had little experience
in presiding over meetings. and none in conductin g trials. In our endeavor to frame a trial procedure which would be readily comprehensible
to such a Master and at the same time be in accord with those general
rules of jurisprudence which have proved their worth over a period of
many centuries. it should be a source of wonder that we have succeeded
as well as we have in accomplishing substantia l justice.

Grand Master or elected by the Grand Lodge. and with no power of
trial by the individual Lodges. However, individual members of your
committee have discussed such a plan with officers and Past Masters of
the constituen t Lodges, and have found that many were of the opinion
that this would deprive the individual Lodges of their inherent right
to the · original trial of all charges. That this right is not inherent is
evident from our review of other jurisdictions. and is also establishe d
by previous decisions of this Grand Lodge. In Section 1026 of the Ross
Digest we find the following language:
"Formerly all charges for Masonic offenses were tried only in the
General Assembly of Masons, but upon the organizati on of Grand
Lodges the power develved upon them. For convenience this Grand
Lo'dge has delegated to its subordina tes power to try offenses; and. in
the exercise of this power, the subordina tes and the commissioners
they select act, not from any inherent power, but for and on . behalf
of the Grand Lodge. which retains complete control and supervision over
all the proceedings. This delegation of power to the subordina tes is
not exclusive, for the Grand Lodge cannot divest itself of this. one of
its fundamental rights. but retains the power to try and punish offenders
by the action of its own body."
While your committee believes that Grand Lodge commissions would
be desirable, it considers its function to be that of research and report,
rather than of advocacy of any particular system. It desires the opinion
of this Grand Lodge on general policy to be expressed before it prepares specific legislation to accomplish any of the suggested changes.
It is possible that an alternative system may be desired, providing
for either a Lodge trial and a trial by a permanen t or semi-perm anent
commission. If such an alternative system is adopted, the use of a
Grand Lodge commission over a period of years may convince the
individual Lodges that it is the most efficient in securing a proper
administra tion of justice.
We have therefore prepared two sets of propositions for the consideration of the Grand Lodge, the first being amendmen ts to the
present trial procedure by Lodges. and the second being an optional
method of trial by a semi-perm anent commission.

As a result of its studies, your committee has arrived at a unanimous conclusion that the ideal method of conductin g a Masonic trial
is by a permanen t or semi-perm anent commission appointed by the

I.
AMENDME NTS TO PRESENT TRIAL PROCEDUR E BY LoDGES

1. Upon receipt of charges by the Master, he shall first determine
whether a Masonic offense is . charged. If he shall so determine, he
shall then appoint a committee to investigat e the evidence. Such committee shall make a full and complete investigation, which shall include
interviews with the accuser and with the accused, if possible. and shall
report in writing to the Master, setting forth the evidence obtained and
the names and addresses of the witnesses.

262

263

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

The weakness of our present procedure in this respect is that the
Lodge is put to the trouble and expense of a trial whenever charges
in proper form are presented to the Master, even though such charges
cannot possibly be substantiated.
It is possible also that this committee of investigation might be given
the duty, if it found the charges to be of a minor nature, to endeavor
to bring about a reconciliation between the accused and the accuser.
Difficulties in Lodges sometimes arise by reason of misunderstanding,
and it would be accomplishing a truly Masonic purpose if such a committee could restore peace and harmony through its efforts.
2. Upon receipt of the report of the committee, the Master shall
determine whether probable cause exists for the trial of the charges.
If so, he shall direct a qualified Master Mason to prepare formal charges
based upon the report of the committee and to prosecute the same before
the trial commission.
Casting the burden upon the Junior Warden to prepare charges
and prosecute the same is in most cases unfair to that officer and to the
Lodge. He has usually had no experience of a similar nature, and there
have been trials in the past where a miscarriage of justice has resulted
from an inexperienced Junior Warden preparing charges and prosecuting the same against an accused represented by an experienced trial
lawyer.
3. Upon the filing of such formal charges, the Master shall cause
a copy of the same to be served upon the accused with a summons
directing him to answer within a definite time. The failure of the
accused to answer shall be an admission of the facts charged, and any
facts admitted by him in this manner or in his answer shall require no
further proof.
Under our present system, the entire case must be prepared without
knowledge of the plea of the accused. This is a departure from all
other rules of civil and criminal procedure of which the committee has
knowledge.
The fact that there is no provision in our ordinances for a plea of
guilty by the accused has been a matter of concern for sometime, and
your committee has prepared specific legislation on this particular matter.
4. When the answer of the accused has been fl.led, or the time to
answer has expired, a copy of the charges and the answer shall be sent
to the Grand Master, who shall appoint a Trial Master to conduct the
trial of the charges. A trial commission shall then be elected and the date
of trial set as under. our present rules.
Some years ago the Grand Lodge enacted legislation authorizing the
Grand Master to appoint a qualified Past Master to act as Trial Master.
It has been the experience of the Grievance Committee that where a
Trial Master other than the Master has presided over a trial, the conduct
of the trial and the trial record have been more satisfactory than where

the Master has presided. Unfortunately, the legislation authorizing Trial
Masters gives the Grand Master the option of appointing either a Past
Master or the Master himself, and our Grand Masters in the past have
in practically every case appointed the Master to preside, unless he
requested the appointment of another. Your committee believes that the
law concerning Trial Masters should be amended to provide that the
Master of the Lodge should not be Trial Master.
5. The trial shall be divided into two parts, the first dealing with the
facts leading to a determination of the specifications charged and whether a Masonic offense has been committed, and the second with evidence
to be considered in fixing the penalty.
In an ordinary criminal court there are three distinct steps: arraignment and plea: trial: and prob~tion and sentence. In a Masonic trial,
these are all joined in one hearing in a manner that makes it difficult for
even a lawyer to allocate to each its proper part.
6. The trial shall be conducted in accordance with the rules of evidence contained in the California Code of Civil Procedure, including the
right to question the accused upon all matters connected with the
charges.
There would ·seem to be no sufficient reason why a Masonic trial
should be conducted in the same manner as a criminal prosecution. No
fine or imprisonment is involved, the only penalties being reprimand, suspension or expulsion. The rules against self incrimination on matters
which might lead to an indictment in the criminal courts would of course
be available to the accused.
7. Forms for charges, summons, notice of trial, subpoenas and the
like, shall be prepared and printed by the Grand Lodge for use by the
constituent Lodges when needed.
Similar forms are available in most of our civil courts and are a great
convenience and time saver to those who practice law. They should be
equally valuable to laymen in individual Lodge trials.
Your Special Committee on Trial Procedure desires to report and
recommend as follows:
Our trial procedures do not provide for the entry by an accused of
either a plea of guilty or of not guilty. Neither do they provide for any
procedure other than by trial before an elected trial commission, in the
event that the accused makes no answer to the charge of unMasonic
conduct.
Your Committee is of the opinion that the process of election of trial
commissioners may well be eliminated in those instances when the
accused either admits his guilt of the offense charged, or does not wish
to contest the truth of the charge. We believe that in such instances it
would be entirely proper to rely upon the Master of the Lodge to make
a complete and fair investigation and report, in writing, and to fix the

penalty. subject, of course, to a review by the Grand Lodge of his action.
We therefore propose the following resolution and move its adoption:
RESOLVED: That Sections 692.1, 692.2, 692.3 and 692.4 as hereinafter specified be adopted and become embodied in the California
Masonic Code: and that Section 693 be amended as hereinafter specified.
Sec. 692.1 PROCEDURE ON RECEIPT OF CHARGES: Upon
the presentation of such charges, the Master shall carefully examine the
charge and specifications. and, if they are evidently frivolous. or if the
act or acts with which the accused is charged is or are clearly such as do
not constitute a Masonic offense. he may refuse to entertain them. But.
should it appear otherwise, and it is known to him that the accuser is a
Master Mason in good standing, he shall cause true copies of such
charge and specifications to be made, shall cause one of such copies to
be forwarded to the Grand Secretary. and cause to be served upon the
accused one of said true copies. together with a notice to the accused in
the form hereinafter provided: said service of said true copy of the charge
and specifications and of said notice to be made in the same manner provided for the service of summons by Section 707 of this Code.

shall not have flied in writing, with the Secretary of the Lodge, 'his plea
of not guilty, the Master of said Lodge shall make complete investigation
and shall determine whether the charge and speciBcations are true,
causing the facts relating thereto to be reduced to writing, in triplicate:
and he shall make a finding as to the guilt or innocence of the accused,
shall fix the penalty therefor, and shall cause two ( 2) copies of said
complete written record to be forwarded to the Grand Secretary and
shall cause one copy thereof to be filed in the archives of the Lodge. At
the next meeting of the Lodge he shall announce his findings and the
penalty imposed by him.
Sec. 693 IF the accused shall. within said time limited in said notice
specified in Section 692.2 hereof. file his written plea of not guilty of the
charge, the Master shall call a special meeting of his Lodge as soon as
practicable.
Such special meeting may be held on the same date as, and in conjunction with, a stated meeting. Thereafter, proceedings shall be had and
taken as provided for in Section 694, to and including Section 743 of this

H.
OPTIONAL METHOD OP TRIAL BY SEMI-PERMANENT COMMISSIONS

The foregoing suggestions are designed to remove as many of the
present difficulties in trial procedure as possible without any basic change
in principle. The next portion of the recommendations covers the appointment of trial commissioners by the Grand Master instead of their
election by the individual Lodge. They are set forth in general form in
order that they may be considered as a whole. If acceptable in principle,
there should be no difficulty in changing details to meet individual
objections.
1. For Masonic trial purposes the state shall be divided into geographical divisions in a manner which shall take into account the number
of Lodges and Master Masons and the convenience of travel in each
division.
2. The Grand Master shall each year appoint in each division twelve
Master Masons, preferably Past Masters, who shall act as trial commissioners in that division. T he first member appointed to the commission
shall be its chairman and shall appoint three members to act on each
charge referred to the commission.
3. The Grand Master shall each year appoint in each division one
or more Proctors, whose duty shall be to prepare formal charges on all
cases referred to such commission. and to prosecute the same.
4. When charges are presented to the Master of any Lodge, he shall
proceed as set forth in the foregoing amendments to the present trial
1

266

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

procedures in Lodges to the point where he determines that probable
cause exists. If he decides that probable cause exists, then at the option
of the Master, the Grand Master, the accused or the accuser, the charges
shall be referred to the Proctor and Grand Lodge Trial Commission in
the division in which the Lodge is situated, and the procedure thereafter
shall be as set forth for individual Lpd,ges, except that it shall be conducted by the Proctor and Grand Lodge Trial Commission instead of
the Master and the Lodge Commission.

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON DE MOLAY

CONCLUSION

It will be noted that no specific legislation has been prepared for submission to the Grand Lodge, the committee being of the opinion that the
Grand Lodge should first express its policy upon any changes in trial
procedures before such legislation is prepared.
For the purpose of determining the policy of the Grand Lodge, the
following Resolutions are submitted.
1. RESOLVED, That it is the policy of the Grand Lodge that the
recommendations of the Committee on Trial Procedure on amendments
to the present trial procedures by Lodges be adopted, and that a' committee be appointed to prepare legislation accordingly for presentation
at the next apnual communication.
2. RESOLVED, That it is the policy of the Grand Lodge that the
recommendations of the Committee on Trial Procedure on an optional
method of trial by a semi-permanent commission be adopted and that a
committee be appointed to prepare legislation accordingly for presentation at the next annual communication.
Respectfully submitted,
Special Committee on Trial Procedures

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Committee on DeMolay is pleased to submit the following report
for your approval. The projects of various Masonic groups in behalf
of DeMolay and the basic DeMolay activities in the state have been
carefully outlined to you in the reports of previous Committees on
DeMolay and, therefore, will not be repeated in this report. Suffice it
to say, the projects and activities have been continued and improved
upon. The Order of DeMolay continues to grow constructively and a
great deal of credit should be given to its leadership.
The policy of this Grand Lodge permitting constituent lodges to
sponsor chapters of the Order of DeMolay has had a most salutary
effect on the relationship between the body of the Masonry and the
Order of DeMolay in this state. In Southern California, alone, Letters
Temporary have been issued for nine new chapters as a direct result
of this policy. Many constituent lodges have taken over the sponsorship
of DeMolay Chapters from Masonic Clubs and the immediate improvement has been most gratifying.
Every "ism" in the world's history has ae'hieved its objectives by
incukating its philosophies in the minds of the young people under its
influence. We are all painfully aware of the attendant results. The
teachings of the Order of DeMolay, which include the support of the
public schools, as evidenced by this excerpt from their ritual, "Devoted
championship of the Public Schools is a cardinal teaching of the Order
of DeMolay," and the inculcation of the precepts of Filial Love, a belief
in God, Courtesy, Comradeship, Fidelity, Cleanness and Patriotism,
are consistently parallel to the teachings of Masonry.
Experts in the field of population trends have predicted that, not
only will the population in the State of California grow at an amazing
rate in relation to the growth throughout the United States, but that the
immediate growth in the 14 to 21 year age bracket will be completely
out of proportion to the general trend. It stands to reason, therefore,
that we must devote a great deal of our attention to this segment of
our population.
This Grand Lodge 1has expressed a concern for juvenile welfare and
this concern is well founded. It becomes very apparent then that this
concern can best be served by the encouragement of the DeMolay
movement in every way possible. The present policy of this Grand Lodge
relating to the DeMolay movement has done a great deal to inspire
activity in this direction.
In view of the foregoing, your committee recommends that the
following steps be taken. It is our firm conviction that each is in the
best interests of Masonry.

One. That the committee be continued and that a minimum of nine
members be appointed thereon. The intensified interest in the Order of
DeMolay has multiplied the problems requiring the personal attention
of the members of the committee. The committee is also receiving many
more invitations to address different Masonic groups. A good geographical distribution of its membership would enable the committee to
more effectively discharge its responsibilities.
Two. That the sum of $750 be appropriated to cover its necessary
expenses.
T1hree. That the permission given this year's committee to publish an
informational brochure be continued to next year's committee. Because
of the increased activity of the committee and other circumstances
beyond its control, this project was not completed during the Masonic
year just finished.
Four. That the Grand Master issue a statement to the constituent
lodges clearly defining the policy of the Grand Lodge regarding the
Order of DeMolay. Confosion has been created in a few localities by
dissident minority interpretations of the policy.
This committee wishes to express its appreciation to this Grand
Lodge for the opportunity of serving it during this past year. We are
convinced that by laboring in behalf of the young manhood of today we
are giving a distinct service to the Masonry of tomorrow.

"My attention was first directed to this subject on a visit to Fiddletown, about six miles easterly of Plymouth. Here I found a Masonic
cemetery neglected and in disuse and everything but a credit to our
Fraternity. I then inquired of Ralph Pierson, chairman of our Committee
on Commercialism, if he had at any time explored the subject. He told
me that an investigation had found a number of them but was not in a
position to ascertain the state of maintenance or if they were being
operated in accordance witlh Masonic regulations."
This assignment seemed simple enough. All we would have to do
would be to list the Masonic cemeteries within the State and then get
a report as to their condition. Brother Hargrave, a member of the
Committee on Commercialism, sent us their list of Masonic cemeteries
and a questionaire used by that Committee. A letter was addressed ·to
the Cemetery Board of the Department of Professional and Vocational
Standards, State of California. They regretted to inform us that they
do not maintain a list of cemeteries in the State. Only since 1939 have
they maintained records and then only on those having ten acres or more.
They did enclose a list of four Masonic cemeteries under their jurisdiction, namely, Vallejo, Modesto, San Francisco and Gilroy. Communication with the State Library. the Morticians Association and our
own Boards of Relief did nothing to increase our list of Masonic
cemeteries.
A letter and questionaire was sent to all of our inspectors. This
proved to be an inspiration. By return mail the questionaires started
coming in to the committee. From our first mailing, replies were received
from all but thirty of our inspectorial districts. A second mailing reduced
this number t~ thirteen and as of the date of the preparation of this
report only 6 districts are yet to be heard from.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Master wrote as follows to the members of the Special
Committee on Masonic Cemeteries: "In my travels, I have seen Masonic
cemeteries which, because of ghost towns, neglect or disuse, have become
all but forgotten. Within our borders are some twenty five cemeteries
dedicated as the fl.nal resting place of our departed brethren. Many of
them do not reflect any credit to the Craft. A committee will be appointed
to give full consideration to this Masonic responsibility. Suggestions
which will help formulate a policy for the care and preservation of the
cemeteries will be most welcome.

We wish to pause and thank the inspectors of this jurisdiction.
Without their wholehearted support, this report could not have been
made. We are indebted to them for their assistance and for assuming
an additional task in their already busy lives. Many of the inspectors
added personal notes to their answers. and others, feeling that the
answers to the questionaire did not fully explain the situation, wrote
long letters full of detail and important information. Almost all assured
us of their continued willingness to cooperate.
Our first question was: "Is there a Masonic cemetery in your area?"
We thought the answer would be "yes" or "no.'' Such, however, is not
the case. There are many types of answer between yes and no. After
considered study, we 'have decided that Masonic cemeteries should be
classified into several different groups.
At this point, we will not consider those districts which have replied
that no Masonic cemetery exists in their area. As near as we can
determine, those who have answered "no" to our inquiry are correct in

4. KEYSTONE LoDGE No.161-MI LTON.
Keystone Lodge owns betw~n three and four acres. which they
operate as a Masonic cemetery. They report t·h at its appearance is good.

5. MosA1c LoDGE No. 218-LIVERMORE.
The Livermore Masonic Cemetery is owned and operated by Mosaic
Lodge. It was organized in 1882. The original parcel of flve acres was
laid out in plots 20x20 feet, each plot containing ten graves. A second
piece purchased adjoins the first and is 2.82 acres. Tihis has not yet
been developed. Of the original plot about 90% has been sold. Only
one grave has been sold in the second plot. There is no perpetual care
and the present condition is poor. It is supported by the sale of graves
and the use of Lodge funds, when necessary. It has been the custom
of the Lodge to clean up the cemetery once a year to make it presentable
for Memorial Day. The Lodge secretary informs us that, while the
cemetery is known as the Masonic Cemetery, it is in reality a public
cemetery. No section 1has been set aside for Masons and plots are sold
to the public. He states that several years ago, the Odd Fellows, the
Catholic Church (who also operate cemeteries) and Mosaic Lodge
worked toward having a cemetery district placed on the ballot. The
plan started with enthusiasm but bogged down. Now, he believes, that
high taxes would prevent voter approval. His final statement is: "It is
entirely possible that if the cemetery were put into a presentable year
'round condition, we would sell enough graves to completely finance its
care until we run out of graves. Another alternative might be to develop
the undeveloped 2.82 acres under a perpetual care plan."

10. RosE's BAR 1.oDGE No. 89-SMARTSVILLE.
The inspector of this district reports that there are no Masonic

reports that in 1870, Rose's Bar Lodge and others founded the cemetery
which is now owned and operated by Rose's Bar Lodge. Graves are
sold to the public and the sale of the lots provides for the care of the
graves. It is of interest to note that a sixteen foot square lot sells for
$14.50. One headstone bears the inscription "Born in 1795." Because
of the confusion and to be sure of our facts, a member of this committee
visited the cemetery. He reports that he found the grounds in "fairly
good condition, considering the lack of interest of Rose's Bar Lodge,
other than Brother Asa Pippin." He further reports that once or twice
a year, Brother Pippin takes some of his farm equipment into the cemetery and removes dry grass and shrubs from the paths and graves.
From time to time, he has requested assistance from the Lodge members
but seldom has any one responded. Brot:her Pippin's sons have assisted
him in the clean up; all of this without any assistance, financial or otherwise, from the Lodge. Water is piped to these two and one hal~ acres
and if Brother Pippin could have some helip from the Lodge, this
cemetery could be put in shape without too much trouble.

13. STANISLAUS LooGE No. 206--MODESTO.
This cemetery was organized in 1872. There are ten acres of which
about three-quarters of the graves have been sold. The cemetery was
incorporated on September 16, 1917 as a Masonic Cemetery Association. All lots and graves sold prior to incorporation were maintained
by individual owners or by .payment of an annual upkeep fee. Under the
incorporation, there are no financial ties with Stanislaus Lodge, although
. all members of the Lodge are members of the Cemetery Association by
virtue of said membership. The Board of Directors must be elected
from the Lodge membership at the annual meeting of the Association.
After incorporation, the owners were given the privilege of placing their
graves under perpetual care by depositing $25 ·p er grave in the Masonic
Cemetery Irriducible Fund. The interest from these invested funds is
placed in the gerteral fund to be used for the care of the graves. The
principal remains intact and cannot be expended. Practically all of the
graves in the older portion are not self-supporting. Brother Loren D.
Hudson; president of the association, informs us, that whereas the
Cemetery Act of 1953 requires that fi.fty cents per square foot be paid
into the endowment fond, they have been placing 50% of the sale
price of the graves in the fund. He also says that they are proud of the
fact that they are considered one of tthe best cared for and most
efficiently managed cemeteries in California. In 1956 a 180 crypt
mausoleum was built. They have provided the Cemetery Committee
with a printed copy of their by-laws, a brochure of their mausoleum,
colored negatives of the cemetery, and a form letter which accompanies
all certificates for endowment maintenance. Space in the cemetery is

there are about th.e same number which are cared for by private arrangement between lot owners and private gardners. The GAR and Mexkan
War plots are cared for by the City of Sacramento. All of the remaining

kept free of weeds by mowing four or five times a year by the staff of
the Cemetery. Tlhis is done so as not to detract from the general appearance of the grounds. According to their 1955 annual report, the income
for that year was $30,669.32 and the assets were $269,891.36, plus a
trust fund of $275,000 with no liabilities. The earnings from the trust
fund should be ample to cover the cost of upkeep and supervision.
There are about 800 pre-need graves sold: the cemetery is completely
sold out. Trustees of the Association are elected annually. Graves are
sold to the general public. In addition to the above, there is a small
section, about 25 x 50 feet, which is actually in the City Cemetery
immediately adjacent to the north west section of the Association
property. which according to the few records available, was purchased
by the Masons of the community about 1850 or 1851, by popular subscription. This was for the interment of sojourning Masons. This
section is also kept free of weeds by the Association. Very little is known
of this plot and most of the graves are unmarked. Except for the few

23. ST. MARK's LoocE No. 85-FmDLETOWN.
The Grand Master mentioned the neglect of this cemetery shortly
after he was elected to office. The Committee, with excellent assistance
from Inspector J. Wesley Sibole, has had some difficulty in unearthing
the records necessary to establish ownership. At our request, the inspector had a quick searC'h of the title made. From this we learn that
on February 8, 1871, a deed to Lots 26 and 27 of Block 11 Fiddletown
was delivered to St. Mark's Lodge No. 85. This deed was never recorded

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

281

in the Amador County records. However, the County Recorder informs
us that the title is good as it was a Judge's Certificate. The property
is located in the north west corner of the Community Cemetery, not
separately fenced, and contains .63 of an acre.
The charter of St. Mark's Lodge No. 85 was revoked in 1894. No
mention of the cemetery was made by the Grand Secretary in his report
of October 9, 1894. However, Masonic Law says that the assets of any
Lodge having its Charter revoked, becomes the property of Grand
Lodge. If suC'h a record did exist in the files of Grand Lodge, then we
are informed by our Grand Secretary, they were destroyed in the fire
of 1906.
It is the opinion of this Committee that a complete search of the
title should be made, that the title should be cleared and transferred to
Grand Lodge and that Grand Lodge should be authorized to immediately
restore this long forgotten burial ground of old St. Mark's Lodge.

15. HUMBOLDT LoDGE No. 79--EuREKA.
On January 25, 1957, the secretary of Humboldt Lodge No. 79
wrote to the Committee on Commercialism and said, "One of our local
cemeteries, known as Myrtle Grove, was incorporated in 1863 and in
1866 Humboldt Lodge purchased orie acre of the ten acre plot for
Masonic burialS'. In 1876 another one acre was purchased ... Of the
last acre purchased, about one half remains vacant. About forty years
ago, the original cemetery association went out of existance and since
that time the cemetery became old and worn with much decay and
vandalism occurring. In 1949, a new Myrtle Grove Cemetery Association was organized with the idea of placing the old cemetery in a
modem condition." The letter concludes, "In order to clear title, to the
old cemetery, we had all fraternal organizations deed their interest to
the new cemetery, including Humboldt Lodge. We will have to go to
court to clear title on those unknown and those whom we were unable
to locate. After we have completely gone over the cemetery, the City
of Eureka has agreed to take it over as an historical park and maintain
it in the future." He also said, "We undertook the raising of funds to
bring the cemetery up to date with lawn and sprinkler system and a
new fence around all of it. We contacted as many of the lot owners as
was possible. asking them to contribute $50 per grave. We were
fortunate in having one person promise that when we had $25,000 in
the bank, it would be matched. This •has been accomplished and we have
about $55,000 to do the work." All of this had to be done to avoid having

the old cemetery condemned as it is now situated in the center of the
growing city. In a letter to the Grand Secretary Humboldt Lodge said,

No new plots are being sold. Burials are permitted only when a

BAKERSFIELD UNION CEMETERY-BAKERSFIELD.

In 1900, three or four lodges in Kem County purchased fourteen
blocks in the Bakersfield Union Cemetery, as a burial place for local
and sojourning Masons. These blocks were in the old section of the
cemetery where there is no perpetual care. A small charge was made

the years passed, the monthly charge kept increasing to the point where
it was difficult to collect the maintenance charges from the Lodges.
Finally after several years passed and the maintenance had not been
paid, four blocks of our section were turned back in settlement of the
money due Union Cemetery." The remaining ten blocks are now full,
with a total of 162 Masonic burials. The six Bakersfield Lodges covered
these ten blocks with six inches of pea-gravel. Each lodge is now
charged with the care of these plots two months each year. The Union
Cemetery Association also has a Masonic section in their perpetual care

This group in itself could make an entire report and endless years of

293

CONCLUSIONS:

Your Special Committee on Masonic Cemeteries makes the following
recommendations for your consideration:
First: The limit of time and available information on Masonic Cemeteries makes this report one which skims the surface of the problems involved. To complete the task and to see that it is carried through in complete detail. we recommend that the work of the committee be continued.
Second: Although the committee has listed some twenty-three ( 23)
cemeteries now owned and operated exclusively by our lodges, we feel
in our own minds that continued searC'h will unearth others.
T1hird: 'J'lhe Committee having studied many of our cemeteries with
perpetual care suspects that at least in two or three cases, lodges have
sold graves and represented that they have perpetual care. As time
passed poor investments reduced the income for the care to a point where
the monies would no longer pay for the upkeep. and the remaining funds
reverted to the general funds of the lodge. These cases should be examined to determine the facts. This would permit the Committee to
make a specific recommendation to Grand Lodge.
Fourth: Our report shows seventeen ( 17) Cemeteries formerly
owned by California Masonic Lodges and now maintained by public
funds. This group we feel should have a specific study. Were they trans£erred to avoid responsibility? Should tax money be spent to cover Masonic obligations? W •here do our responsibilities end? When we see our
interest waning should we encourage our political subdivisions to assume
the burdens whidi we originally undertook? These questions s'hould be
considered for the benefit of California Masonry so that a fair, equitable
and workable solution can be :presented to Grand Lodge for its consideration.
Fifth: The report covers nine (9) cemeteries all owned jointly by a
Masonic lodge and some lodge of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows. Should this practice be encouraged or should an effort be made to
secure complete control of the property? It is the studied opinion of the
Committee that this practice of joint ownership could lead to a shifting
of responsibility to the detriment of the cemetery.
Sixth: Regarding Masonic plots in private cemeteries, we believe
that Grand Lodge should adopt definite rules covering the use of the
name "Masonic" in these plots. You should be reminded, however, that
all thirty-five such plots are in excellent condition. As a group. they put
our own efforts to shame. Why is it that private cemeteries can operate
at a profit, whereas so many of our own are neglected and without
funds?
Seventh: Two 'hundred thirty-seven (237) lodges report that they
do not own a Masonic cemetery. We wish that we could be sure that
that is an accurate count: however. our experience in finding Masonic

294

295

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

cemeteries in unusual places, neglected and forgotten, makes us question
this.
Eighth: Twenty-nine ( 29) lodges have not replied to our questionnaire. A continued effort should be made to secure the necessary information for the records of Grand Lodge.
Ninth: To the Committee a Masonic emblem on a tombstone is just
as important in reminding us of our obligations to the dead as an entire
Masonic cemetery.
Tenth: Some cases will require a search of title to determine ownership. We recommend that a small budget be set up to cover the expense
of such search.
Eleventh: We recommend a complete search to the title of old St.
Mark's Lodge No. 85; that its title be transferred to Grand Lodge and
that Grand Lodge take immediate steps to restore the cemetery to a
condition of credit to the craft.
Twelfth: That a study of the cemetery at Columbia be undertaken to
determine our responsibility if any.
Thirteenth: That the cemetery at Decoto be developed to its fullest
possibility so that it will stand out as an example for Masons the world
over.
Fourteenth: Have each lodge set up a committee to review old past
records and determine its status relative to this important function.
Have each lodge set up a maintenance committee to care for the cemetery regardless if it is a whole cemetery, part or just a plot.
Make it the duty of each Master to have a report read each year at a
Stated Meeeting following installation.
We conclude this report with a quotation from Ross's Digest:
"There are duties which we owe our dead that are equally sacred
with those due the living. The performance of those duties should be encouraged. It will tend to gild the gloom which will settle around us in the
hour of death to know that when we are laid to rest our brethren will at
least annually visit and surround the spot, deposit their garlands of
flowers and think of us at our best. Of all the acts of a lifetime none are
freer from selfis'h motives.
"The fleeting pleasures of life, the demands of business, and all the
cares incident to this mortal sphere are for the time forgotten, and man's
best nature, the latent jewel of his composition, is thus brought forth like
the sparkling diamond from the skilled workman. Washing ton Irving
has beautifully and truthfully said that 'sorrow for the dead is the only
sorrow from which we refuse to be divorced. Every other wound we seek
to heal--every other affliction to forget: but this wound we consider a
duty to keep open-this affliction we cherish and brood over in solitude.'
Such sorrow is sacred When we have woven our chaplets of flowers and
have tenderly deposited them upon the graves of our dead, we return to

our homes and our duties with lighter hearts. A day thus spent will never
be regretted. Our offerings. intrinsically, are trifles; yet they mean much.
I say much, for the spiritual relief and sweet peace they bring are inestimable. The mind is directed for the time into new and better channels of
thought, whence arise higher and holier aspirations.
"I would rejoice to know that this observance had grown into an annual custom with every lodge in this jurisdiction, so that upon the occasion most convenient to eaC'h, when nature is radiant with verdure and
the blossoms of springtime, the Lodge might convene in Special meeting,
put on the habiliments of mourning as is usual on foneral occasions, and
repair in procession to the cemeteries, bearing flowers to deck the graves
of departed brethren."
This ruling was given to Grand Lodge by Past Grand Master Hiram
N, Rucker in 1888.

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON
JUVENILE WELFARE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
This is a newcomer to the family of Grand Lodge Committees, having come into bei,pg after the dose of the last annual communication.
As a special committee, it was charged by the Grand Master with
the significant task of exploring ways and means and suggesting possible
methods by which California Masonry might assume a more active role
in furthering the cause of juvenile welfare.
Before entering upon a discussion o.f the subject matter of the report,
we wish to exrpress to the Grand Master our personal appreciation that
the opportunity was given us to take part in this exploration, and further
to write into the record the thanks and commendation of the Craft for
his foresight and leadership in initiating what may in time become another important chapter in Freemasonry's history of community service.
The consideration of this subject by Grand Lodge is both appropriate
and timely. The development of a proper program could lead to lasting
benefits to the young people of our state.
Although well over 90 percent of the juvenile population pass
through the experience of growing up without coming in conflict with the
law, so that the good far outweighs the bad, reports of law enforcement
and related agencies and newspaper accounts of juvenile crimes have
served to headline juvenile delinquency among the youth of the country
as a problem of alarming proportions, not only from the standpoint of

296

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

numbers involved but because of an apparent trend toward more serious
kinds of lawless behavior.
The public attention drawn to this state of affairs has sparked a
widespread interest and concern, from the highest levels of officialdom
to the "man on the street."
In search of ways to stem the tide and apply more effective remedial
measures, statistics and case histories are being studied, surveys are
being conducted, procedures in the handling of juvenile offenders are
being re-examined, and techniques in diagnosis and treatment are subjects of experiment and review. At the same time, educators, religious
leaders. social welfare and civic groups, service organizations and youth
themselves are seeking to develop programs and activities which might
serve a preventive purpose.
Meanwhile. the staf.fs and facilities of the agencies responsible for
dealing with the delinquent are being taxed to and beyond their capacity.
From many quarters the importance of interpreting to our communities the problems of youth and their needs in these high pressure, complex times is being stressed. In the words of one noted psychiatrist.
"unless the public does understand better and we do something more
constructive about it, we will continue to lose ground".
While no extensive discourse on causes and cures would be appropriate in this report. a few observatiions may be helpful in giving us a
sense of direction.
We would like to be able to identi'fy the ingredients of delinquency
with the precision that a chemist analyzes a compound. and to reduce the
solution to a universal formula. Experience shows this is not possible.
Complex factors in varying number and combination are involved. so
that rarely are two cases found on close study to be alike in all respects.
although they may have many common elements.
In the field of corrections. we are in a period of transition from the
strictly punitive approach to the use of treatment as a means of rebuilding the young offender into a law-abiding. well-adjusted member of
society. In this process. diagnosis has become increasingly important in
order that treatment may be adapted to individual need.
As skill and experience in both diagnosis and treatment increase.
flndings may be expected which will prove reliable guides to preventive
as well as corrective measures, and provide a sound base on which to
build community action.
Many of the youth-serving programs in our communities are designed to meet the needs of the "underprivileged" and to bring him up
even with ·his peers. In general. his status as "underprivileged" is determined by applying an economic yardstick. By this test, the underprivileged is the one who is poorly or inadequately fed, clothed and

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

297

housed and without the means or opportunity to do and have the things
that other youngsters do and have.
These circumstances of deprivation make up a fertile soil in which
delinquency may flourish. and services to alleviate such conditions are
eminently worthwhile. But the evidence is mounting that while economic disadvantage and the like are contributing factors, the bacteria of
delinquency germinates most readily in an unhealthy emotional setting.
So it would seem that we must enlarge our concept of underprivilege
to include another kind of deprivation-the kind that results from failure
to meet the youngster's emotional needs--a concept which recognizes
emotional malnutrition as fraught with consequences usually more serious than a meager diet.
The home. because it is the first community in which a c:hild lives and
becames aware of relationships witth other people. has. and must be
charged with. a primary responsibility for healthy emotional growth.
Too often it fails and the broader community with its varied services
must try to make amends. Invariably. it has been found easier to remedy
an empty stomach than an empty heart.
Among the basic needs of importance to C'hildren and grownups alike
are the need of belonging. a need for achievement and a need for recognition. These we should take particularly into account as we plan a juvenile welfare program.
We turn now to the question. "What may Masons do for juvenile
welfare?" In attempting to answer it, we must consider the action that
might be taken ( l ) by the individual Mason as a citizen in his community, ( 2) by the several Lodges either singly or in combination, and ( 3)
by Grand Lodge on a state-wide basis.
By participating in a wide variety of organized activities available
to him in most communities, particularly in urban areas, the individual
Mason may find outlets for his personal efforts. as well as the opportunity for leadership in conceiving and developing constructive local
programs for youth. In applying to these efforts the tenets and tools of
the craft. it is likely that he will not do so in the name of Masonry as
such but rather in the discharge of those duties as citizen and individual
which are enjoined upon him on his first admission into a lodge.
It is well known that many of the brethren, up and down the state,
already are making valuable contributions and exerting their wholesome influence in the cause of juvenile welfare. Of such brethren we
have no census. and there is to our knowledge no inventory of their
achievements. But this report would be somewhat less than complete if it
did not record on behalf of Grand Lodge a grateful acknowledgement of
their services both to Masonry and to their communities.
Not only should their continued effort be encouraged, but every memb~ of the craft should be urged to give not merely of his means but of

298

299

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

himself in whatever ways, big or small, may be open to him on the local
scene to further these endeavors.
As for projects that California Masonry as such might undertake
through Grand Lodge and the constituent lodges, it appears to this
Commitee that a "recognition" type of program is most feasible. There
are several possibilities.
One proposal which has received a great deal of consideration would
involve speaking contests each year tied in with Public Schools Week,
Constitution Month Observance and the annual communication of Grand
Lodge. Under this plan, the contests on selected topics would start with
preliminaries in local schools, the winners in each round progressing to
the next, with state-wide finals being held as a special-events feature of
Grand Lodge Week.
In connection with this idea, several problems arise which would need
to be fully worked out before any attempt is made to put the plan into
effect.
First of all, the time schedule presents difficulties, in view of the
fact that summer vacation covers so large a part of the period which
intervenes between Public Schools Week and Constitution Month.
School is just getting underway again in September, and this may prove
to be a further complication.
Moreover, the annual communication as now scheduled comes in the
midst of Constitution Month Observances, so that the results of speaking contests in connection with this observance will probably not be complete in time to feature the finalists at Grand Lodge. If the plan itself
meets with general approval. perhaps upon further study the means
may be found or modi£ ications suggested which would make it workable.
Such a project would operate uniformly throughout the state in order
to give the young people interested an equal opportunity to participate.
To be successful, it would require close liaison between Juvenile Welfare, Public Schools Week and Constitution Month committees, both at
the Grand Lodge and at the local lodge or district level. as well as a
definite working arrangement with the school authorities in each locality.
The nature and amount of awards to be given at each level of competition, together with the source of necessary funds to pay for them,
will also need to be decided. Should each lodge or district make its own
determination on this point and be responsible for providing the awards
to winners up to the Grand Lodge finals? Would this result in an undesirable variation in the kinds and value of the awards? Should Grand
Lodge specify and finance all awards?
All aspects of this subject require thorough consideration.
We should note that a project of the kind above outlined would appeal to and stimulate the interest of a limited number of youngsters. Supplementary programs would be necessary on a broader front.

Essay contests on appropriate themes might be held among with, or
in place of, the speaking contest idea. But this, again. would tend to appeal to and provide an outlet for a comparatively small group of top
students.
We have thought that one of the constructive things we might do to
counter-balance the public attention given to delinquency and thereby
encourage good work on the part of youth, would be to devise a means
of giving recognition to worthwhile accomplishments.
Along this line, the idea of a "youth recognition week" is advanced as
having possibilities. The object would be to gi~e suitable r~co~nition at
public ceremonies in each community to 1:arbcularly mer1tonous conduct or outstanding achievement on the par~ of individual youngsters.
This kind of project would :h ave a broader s•ope, since elegibility for
recognition would extend to a wide range of activities and scholastic
ability would not be the sole or primary basis of selection.
Such a "youth recognition week", observed all over California with
colorful public ceremonies. could be made both dramatic and new~­
worthy in the finest sense. and might be timed in such a way as ~o av~1d
some of the problems mentioned in connection with the first pro1ect discussed in this report. Further study is desirable.
Scholarships have become a popular form of award, and while they
may be found to have a place in connection with whatever juvenile welfare program may be finally adopted, the Committee feels t~at t~e use
of scholarships should be considered with great care. There is eVldence
that the number and variety of scholarships being made available to high
school graduat6 and seniors of high scholastic standing is increasing at
su~h a rate that a number of them are going unused. The question has
been asked, how well it would serve our general purpose to enter into
competition with those now granting scholarships to the limited crop of
students at the top. It may be that other forms of recognition and awards
may fit in better with our purpose.
Some kind of juvenile welfare program could probably be •hastily inaugurated with some kind of immediate benefits. but since our objective
is long-range, the Committee believes that we should proceed only at a
pace consistent with thoughtful planning. While the beginning thus far
made are meager, they have perhaps served to "dear the site", so that
a successor Committee may build upon it the structure of a successful undertaking.
The development of a good plan, of course, is only the first step. To
carry it out will call for the help of many Masonic workmen interpreting
in action the designs that may be drawn upon the trestleboard.
We are con>fident that success awaits the effort.
In concluding this report, we recommend ( 1 ) that the special com-

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMIT TEE ON
MUTUAL AID ASSOCIA TIONS
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
At the last annual Communication of Grand Lodge your Committee
on Policy and General Purposes recommended that a special Committee
on Mutual Aid Societies be appointed by the Grand Master to investigate, evaluate, and make recommendations to the next Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, on all phases of the .problem of these associations to the end that a full understandi ng may be had before final action
is taken.
Your Committee concluded that it must first acquire all possible
factual data before any intelligent evaluation and recommendation could
be reached. Because of the independen t development of these mutual
aid societies throughout the state, the required information had never
been accumulated by Grand Lodge. Consequent ly your Committee disseminated questionnaires to all the lodges in the jurisdictions. The response was excellent, and we now have within our file a sufficiently
complete picture upon which to base an informed analysis. Much of this
information has been charted for easy reference by those concerned.
A general summary of the material gathered discloses the following
factual information.
( I ) The Methods of Operation.
The methods of operation of the associations are peculiarly uniform.
They are governed by a set of officers and a board of trustees. Upon
admission to membership, a small fee (usually about two dollars) is paid
the secretary of the association, and a small assessment (usually a dollar
and ten cents) is levied on the death of a member. The secretary retains
ten cents per levy for expenses and .p ays the the balance of the collections
up to a certain established limit (ranging from $100 to $10000 in the
various associations) to the beneficiary previously designated by the
deceased, or, if none, then to the next of kin. Most of the associations are
large enough to have sizable reserve funds. Some provide protedive
bonds, counter-signatures on checks and adequate audits. Others 1have

( 2) The Size or Extent of the Movement.
There are forty-six Low Twelve Clubs or Assistance Funds
reported. Four of the forty-six funds: namely, Mt. Vernon No. 517
Memorial Fund, Ione No. 80 Widows and Orphans Fund, Santa Ynez
No. 701 Club and James A. Forshay No. 641 Assistance Fund are not
mutual aid associations, but are strictly charitable funds, having been
accumulated by sporadic voluntary contributions, and distribution is
based on need.
Six of the Mutual Aid Funds reported have been recently dissolved
pursuant to \the Grand Lodge directive. They are Montebello Lodge
No. 451 Benefit Club, Damscus No. 648 Widows Benefit Fund, Charter
Rock No. 410 Widows and Orphans Retirement Fund, Amity Lodge
No. 370 Mutual Benefit Fund, Anaheim Lodge No. 207 Club, and
Covenant Lodge No. 527 Relief Club. Thus, there are thirty-six funds
of the mutual aid variety now in existence, but most of those recently
dissolved express a desire to re-establish. Not included in this report
are the mutual aid funds operated by the Sciots, Scottish Rite, Shrine,
and other relat~d bodies throughout the state.
The number of Lodges whose membership is involved in the associations reported is one hundred and twenty-two. The total reserves
of all funds of associations reported amount to $25.J,381.04. T 1he largest
association, the Long Beach Low Twelve Club, has a reserve fund of
$106,703.59, makes a beneficiary payment of $1000, and 1has distributed
$600.000 in the past thirty years.
The organization of these associations has been proceeding since
1908.
( 3) Degree of Involvement by Lodges.
Some lodges actually organize and operate the fund or association.
In some cases, though the association is separate in organization, the
Lodge officials are included on the association board. In some cases, the
secretary of the lodge is the secretary of the association. In some
instances, the association officers or board members are elected by the
lodge or appointed by the Master of the Lodge. The funds usually bear
the name o·f the lodge or Masonic District. In some cases, however, the
associations ·have completely separated themselves in name and or-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA
