ganizational set up from the lodges or districts they were originally
organized to serve. They do not allow officers of the lodge to serve
the fund in any capacity.
I? ~ost ~nstances, membership is limited to members of the lodges
or districts involved. However, in other cases, any master mason in
good standing residing within the jurisdiction may be a member. The
Long B~ach Club includes members of all lodges and related bodies
l~~ted m Long Beacih. In all cases, membership is voluntary and is
hm1ted to masons.
( 4) Proposed Methods of Dissolution.
T~e followi~g methods of dissolution have been proposed and, in
some msta.nces, 'h ave already been successfully applied by a vote of the
~embersh1p: (a) Pro-rata distribution based on individual contribub~ns: or on the ~u~ber of. years one has been in the fund. ( b) Pro-rata
dis~bution as indicated m (a) for those desiring the money, the remainder voted by a majority of the members to the Masonic Homes
!e~ple Committee, Blood Bank or lodge's general fund. ( c) A ma~
Jor1ty vote. t~ decide disposition to one of the funds named above. ( d)
The association be allowed to operate without forther collections until
all reserves are paid out, then to be discontinued.
There are two major questions presented to your Committee for
recommendation.
I. ~hould the Grand Lodge amend Section 333 of the California
Masonic Code, and thus permit the constituent lodges, as suc'h, under
ru!es a~d. ~egulations established by Grand Lodge, to engage in Mutual
Aid activities?

. It is t?e unanimous opinion of your Committee that the answer to
this question should be in the negative and we so recommend.
Masonry has always confined itself to charity in its truest form
and has never engaged in any type of mutual benefit program such as
h ave
t~ose characterizing other well-known fraternal orders. We 1
~iscourage~ the idea of financial self...:help as an incentive to membership
m a Masonic Lodge. Because of ill fortune and through no fault of their
own, brethren and th~ir widows ~nd 011phans may become impoverished,
and Ma~onry recognizes the obligation to extend to them charitable aid
and _assistance whenever needed. We feel. however, that it would be
detrimental to its hig<hest ideals to now convert this great fraternity into
a benefit group. As wa.~ so ap~ly s~ated by the Committee on Policy
and <?eneral Purposes, From time immemorial Masonry has been and
now is an association of friends and brothers bound together in lov
and .affection to disseminate knowledge, promote the welfare and
h~pmess of one another and to aid a distressed worthy brother, his
widow and orphans. It is a charitable association in its broadest meaning.

but it is not now, never has been, nor should it ever become an insurance
fraternity."
Furthermore. although mutual aid societies operated for the benefit
of masons have been in the process of organization in California for
almost 50 years, and until recently without discouragement. yet only
about 6% of the members of California Lodges now avail themselves
of this program. Thus if we officially adopt a mutual aid program. we
will fundamentally change our traditional concept of Masonic Charity,
when no widespread n.eed or desire •has been demonstrated.
II. There was a second and much more difficult question confronting
your Committee; namely, should this Grand Lodge prohibit individual
masons from :forming and participating in mutual aid associations
entirely disassociated by name, control. or other means from any lodge
or group of lodges, but catering only to members of the fraternity?
Masonry has always prided itself in insuring to its members a
maximum of freedom of conscience and action. Obviously mutual aid
associations do not fall within that class of business activities which
Masonry has prohibited to its members because of ethical or moral
considerations. There appear to be only two valid reasons for this
Grand Lodge to restrain the individual masons from participating in
mutual aid associations: first, that the association is operated or controlled, either directly or indirectly, by a lodge or group of lodges
contrary to section 333 of the California Masonic Code; secondly, that
these associations are operating contrary to State Law. Your Committee
has concluded many of these associations either now are operating or
by changes in their methods can operate without violating either Masonic
or State Law. •
For example. the Santa Monica Bay Low Twelve Club whose
membership is drawn from six lodges in the Santa Monica Bay area does
not exist under the name of a Lodge or Masonic District; the officers
and trustees are elected by the membership of the associations, and are
not designated by the various lodges; and there appears to be absolutely
no exercise of control. either directly or indirectly, by the various
lodges within the area. Your Committee has scrutinized this organization
in vain for any violation of Section 333 of the Masonic Code. Furthermore, the Santa Monica Bay Low Twelve Club has been approved by
the State Insurance Commissioner. and your Committee has within its
files a copy of the Certificate of Exemption issued by that office. In
determining whether these organizations are in violation of state law,
this Committee is properly bound by the legal interpretation of the duly
constituted state authority. Neither this Committee nor the Grand
Lodge has any province to otherwise determine the civil rights of
individuals.
We do believe the words "Low 12" should be deleted from the title
as they connote Masonic sponsorship.

305

PROCEEDINGS OP THB

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

Your Committee therefore makes the following recommendations:
I. That all existing mutual aid associations be given a period of six
months from the conclusion of this communication to comply with
Section 333 of the Masonic Code: i.e .• to amend their by-laws and take
all other necessary steps to completely eliminate any semblance of lodge
control or promotion including ( 1 ) the use of the lodge or district name
or the words "Low 12" or any other words in the organization title
which may indicate Masonic sponsorship. ( 2 ) any duplication of lodge
and association officers, ( 3 ) the selection of association officers or
directors by the Master. or by vote of the lodge ( 4) any attempt by
the lodge officers to recruit members or in any other way to indicate that
the association is a lodge activity or is existing under lodge sponsorship.
( 5) Any solicitation or the transaction of any association business
within a Masonic Lodge. II. That existing mutual aid associations take
all necessary steps within said six months' period to obtain a Certificate
of Exemption or other clearance from the State Insurance Commissioner who is the duly constituted authority having jurisdiction over
this type of business activity. Some contend that their association does
not involve life insurance and therefore should not require a Certificate
of Exemption. However. there can be no question but that under the
State Code. Mutual Aid Associations serving fraternal membership
fall within the broad general jurisdiction of the Insurance Commissioner. A clearance letter from the Commissioner would be easily
obtainable and will resolve all doubts as to the official interpretation of
the Code's applicability to these associations.
III. That at the end of said six months' period the inspectors of the
various Masonic Districts after having been given the necessary information report the status of mutual aid associations within their respective
districts to the Grand Master. and that those associations which have
not conformed to Masonic law and also obtained clearance from the
state officials as outlined herein, be dissolved. The methods of dissolution, as previously referred to in this report. seem satisfactory and have
been successfully applied.
IV. That the Grand Lodge Committee on Mutual Aid Associations
be continued during the coming Masonic year to assist in the enforcement of these recommendations.
In conclusion your Committee wishes to state that, as should be
expected among Masons, not a single case of dishonesty. corruption or
other makonduct was reported in this investigation. It was found that
in many instances those in charge of funds were not bonded or that
other routine precautionary measures for the safety of the members were
not followed. Inasmuch as this Committee opposes the official assumption of this mutual benefit program by Grand Lodge, we are not

proposing any regulatory rules. No doubt the State Insurance Commission will suggest, and the brethren engaging in this activity will
adopt, necessary safeguards. Your Committee has been impressed
with the sincerity and earnestness of those interested in this program.
It is a program which has extended over 50 years in this Grand
Jurisdiction and upon whic'h some of our oldest members have long
depended. These considerations have been carefully weighed by your
Committee. We firmly believe that the adoption of this report and its
recommendations will lead to a solution of the problem which will
definitely reaffirm our long established concept of true Masonic Charity.
and at the same time will not deal lightly or arbitrarily with the legal
rights and aspirations of the individual mason.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON LIBRARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Special Library Committee begs leave to submit the following
report.
There has been maintained in the City of Los Angeles for some
sixty years a Masonic Library owned and operated currently by the
Masonic Library.of Southern California, Incorporated. The support of
this undertaking has been and is presently being taken care of by some
of the local lodges.
During the year 1956 this library was offered to Grand Lodge upon
the following conditions:
1. That the library remain permanently in Southern California and
open to all qualified Master Masons.
2. That Grand Lodge obtain an adequate and convenient location
for the library in Los Angeles.
3. That Grand Lodge assume the responsibility for compensating
a full time librarian and make a reasonable fond available for
staff assistance and maintenance.
4. That the Masonic Library of Southern California be relieved of
all costs incidental to the acceptance of this offer.
Your committee has endeavored to obtain the answers to some of
the questions propounded by Committee on Policy and •General Purposes
and Committee on Finance as a result of this offer.
' It is estimated there are presently in the Library and in storage 7000
books. Of this number 1000 or 14.2% are Masonic Books on History.

3000 or 42.6% proceedings of Grand Bodies. with the remainder of 2800
or 40.4% miscellaneous sudh as History, Government, Religion, Philosophy. etc.
Mr. Lawrence Clark Powell, Head Librarian of the U.C.L.A. Library
was consulted and stated that such a Library should have a full time
Librarian. At present the Library is open ·five afternoons a week with a
volunteer Librarian in charge.
The Library at present is housed rent free in the Masonic Temple.
Pico Boulevard and Figueroa Street, in Los Angeles. While this is not
the most desirable location, it is convenient. The generous offer of
Hollywood Masonic Temple Association to give space to the Library
was examined. The space that could be allocated would be less than at
present and the location quite removed from the center of Los Angeles.
It is the feeling of your committee that if Grand Lodge were to undertake
this project, suitable quarters in a central location should be rented:
our estimate of such rent is $150.00 to $175.00 per month. It is our
further belief that a Grand Lodge Library should be housed in a building
owned and controlled by Grand Lodge. and if this be true, then you
get into an expenditure of thousands and thousands of dollars.

INVOCATION

0 God, Thou who art from everlasting to everlasting the Source of
our lives, the Guardian of their day on earth, and their Eternal Keeper
at the end of the pilgrim way: we beseec:h Thee to let Thy work appear
unto Thy servants and Thy glory unto their children. Grant that the
beauty of the Lord, or God, may be upon us in this sacred hour and
establish Thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our
hands, establish Thou it. Make us not afraid, but in Thy wisdom give
us understanding, as this mortality puts on immortality. Make us strong
in heart as we voice the faith that never fails:
"O God, our help in ages past,

Be Thou our guide w'hile life shall last,
And our eternal home!
Amen."

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Again we have reached the time when we pause to pay our tribute of
respect and affection to those who have been summoned to the Celestial
Lodge above during the past year.
Death is an inevitable experience for everyone. "Man that is born of
woman is of few days and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a Bower
and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow and continuet'h not."
Any organization with a membership as large as that of this Grand
Lodge must of necessity come up to its annual meeting with a long list of
those who have passed away during the year. Again the messenger of
the Eternal has called many of our brethren. Exactly three hundred of
our members have reached t'he end of their earthly toil and their liberated
spirits have winged their flight to the unknown world. Among these are
Past Grand Master Arthur S. Crites, an honored and beloved leader
among men. A fitting eulogy for Brother Crites will be presented by Past
Grand Master Leon 0. Whitsell. Clark H. Shaw, Assistant Grand
Lecturer: Oakley K. Morton, a former inspector and committeeman;
Alexander Douglas Potts, former inspector. and Grand Lodge officer;
Otho Stewart, Grand Bible Bearer in 1953-54: Dr. George A. Warmer,
Grand Chaplain in 1944: and Philip Stephan Cummings, former inspector.
Owing to the limitations of time it is obviously impossible to call the
roll of all who have left us. A complete list is appended to, and made a
part of this report.
Two hundred twenty-three of our lodges have lost past masters.
Two lodges, Eden Lodge No. 113 and King David's Lodge No. 209,
have lost four each. Nine lodges report the loss of three. Forty-five
lodges have lost two, and one hundred seventy-seven lodges have one
loss each.
CLARK HERVEY SHAW

On February 16th, 1957, Long Beach lost a distinguished citizen
and Masonry an honored and beloved leader W'hen Clark Hervey Shaw
passed away.
Born at Mansfield, Ohio, Brother Shaw came to Long Beac'h to live
in 1887, and continued to live in that city for the rest of his life. In 1900
he joined the Long Beach city staff as a civil engineer and remained in
the service of the city for over .fifty years-until his retirement in 1954.
He was superintendent of the City Water Department from 1921 to
1931, and since that time has handled oil leases and other important
engineering work for the city.
Brother Shaw had a long and illustrious career as a working Mason.
He was raised in Long Beach Lodge No. 327 in November, 1903, and

OAKLEY KENDALL MORTON

Death came suddenly to Judge Oakley K. Morton at his home in
Riverside about 7 a.m. on December 12th, 1956.
He was born at Crown Point, Indiana on August 2nd, 1891. He
graduated from Chicago University in 1914 and from Stanford Law
Sc'hool in 1916, fallowing which he went to Riverside to practice law.
After serving some years in the District Attorney's Office he was made
District Attorney in 1925, and was appointed Superior Court Judge by
Governor Young in 1928. He served until his death. He was a member
of the State Judicial Council since 1948.
Oakley K. Morton 'had a long record of Masonic service. Raised in
Lake Lodge No. 157, Indiana on January 29th, 1913, he affiliated with
Evergreen Lodge No. 259 in Riverside on May 1st, 1917. He was Master
of Evergreen Lodge in 1922 and served as Inspector from 1926 to 1935.
Appointed Chairman of the By-Laws Committee of Grand Lodge in
1935 he continued in that office until October, 1955.
Other Masonic bodies of which he was a member are Riverside
Chapter No. 67, Royal Arch Masons; Valley Council No. 27, Royal and
Select Masters; Riverside Commandery No. 28 Knights Templar, of
which he was a Past Commander. He was a member of Long Beach
Consistory, and the Supreme Council of the Scottish Rite conferred on
him its highest honor, the 33rd Degree. He helped to organize El Bekal
Shrine Temple in 1954 and was its first Illustrious Potentate.
His record of community service is imposing. Among many other
services in 1948 he became first chairman of the Citizen's University

Committee in Riverside which sought to encourage the development of
the University of California Campus at Riverside and now serves as
liaison between campus and community. He was later made Honorary
Chairman o·f that committee. He was a member of the Elks Lodge and
served on its service committees.
He is survived by his wife, May J. Morton, whom he married on
June 14th, 1917: a daughter, Mae Louise Morton of Riverside: and
three sons, Lt. Col. Oakley K. Morton, 2nd USAF, Colorado Springs:
Byron C. Morton, Attorney, of Riverside: and Macdonal d Morton of
Los Gatos.
Oakley K. Morton was a loyal Mason, a devoted public servant, and

ALEXANDE R DOUGLAS POTTS

Born in Scotland in 1898 Alexande r Douglas Potts received his public and high school education in Scotland and later studied at Edmonton
University, Alberta, Canada. He married Elma Thomas of Calgary,
Alberta in 1923. He was associated with banks in Canada and Salt Lake
City before moving to Honolulu in February, 1926. He continued to live
in Honolulu till the time of his death on May 23rd, 1957.
For a number of years he was with the American Mutual Building
and Loan Company of Salt Lake City, and in 1935 became President and
General Manager of the Finance Corporati on Ltd. which position he
held till he died.
A. Douglas Potts was a very active Mason. Raised in le Progres de
l'Oceanie Lodge No. 371 on October 21st, 1927, he served as its Master
in 1934. In 1935 he was. appointed Inspector and served in that position
until 1955. He also served as Grand Standard Bearer and on various
committees of Grand Lodge. Following December 7th, 1941, ihe was
appointed as the personal representative of the Grand Master in the
Hawaiian Islands, an assignment he held during t'he difficult years of
World War II.
He was a Scottish Rite Mason ( K.C.C.H. ): a member of Honolulu
Chapter, Royal Arch Masons: Honolulu Commandery. Knights Templar: Honolulu Council. Royal and Select Masters: and Aloha Temple
of the Mystic Shrine. Appointed by the General Grand Chapter, Royal
Arch Masons, he served as Deputy General Grand High Priest of Royal
Arch Masons in the Territory of Hawaii, and on January 3rd, 1957, had
conferred upon him the General Grand Chapter's Distinguished Service
Medal. one of t'he rarest honors in Royal Arch Masonry.
Alexande r Douglas Potts was a warm hearted family man and is
survived by his wife, Mrs. Elma Thomas Potts: two sons, Charles Douglas, and William Donald Potts, and two grandchildren, to whom our
sympathy goes out. He was a fine Christian gentleman who gave himself

OTHO STEWART

Otho Stewart, who served this Grand Lodge as its Bible Bearer in
the year 1953-54, was the finest type of working Mason. Born in Clay
Center, Kansas on December 30th, 1873, he passed away June 17th,
1957, aged 83 years and 5 months.
Brother Stewart was raised in Mission Lodge No. 169 on February
4th, 1899. Moving into the Pitt district while engaged in electrical construction work he helped to organize Fort Crook Lodge r,lo. 575 in 1923
and served as its Master for the first two years. In 1927 he was elected
secretary of his lodge and continued in that office for twenty-th ree years.
During those years 'he coached many of the officers of the lodges in t'he
district and many times was the Installing Officer for his lodge. In
March, 1946, he had the joy of raising his son, Homer E. Stewart in his
own lodge, and in December, 1952, it was his happy privilege to install
that son as Master of Starr King Lodge No. 3H. He was faithful in
attendanc e at Grand Lodge and as far as is known never missed an
Annual Communication since he became a member.
We pay our tribute to Brother Stewart for many long years of faithful service. It is such brethren as he who have made Masonry strong and
respected in this great jurisdiction.
GEORGE A. WARMER, Sa.

Dr. George A. Warmer, Sr., for forty-nine years a Methodis t
Minister, died at Pasadena on July 17th, 1957.
Brother Warmer was born in North Dakota on October 28th, 1882.
He graduated from the State University of North Dakota and studied
theology at Boston. He joined the Southern California Conference of
the Methodist Church in 1913, serving a number of churches in Southern
California. He completed his active ministry with a term as Superintendent of the Los Angeles District. For eight years, from 1940 to 1948,
he had a successful ministry at First Methodist Church in San Diego.
This was the church of which our late brother Claude Morrison was a
devoted member, and when Brother Morrison became Grand Master in
1943 'he appointed his pastor, George A. Warmer, as his Grand Chaplain. Brother Warmer served during the sessions of 19H.
Dr. George A. Warmer was an outspoken man of strong convictions
and 'his Church, the Lodge, and the State have been blessed by his
fearless and unselfish service.

who have gone. Everyone of our departed members has left "a vacant

EULOGY
ARTHUR SAXE CRITES

By Leon 0. Whitsell. P.G.M.
Arthur Saxe Crites was born on the Crites family ranch near
Caliente, California. As a youth he walked four miles to the little school
at Keene which his father was responsible in founding. At 16 years of
age he graduated from the Kem County Union High School in the
second class to receive diplomas from that institution.
·
While still in his teens he saw service in the Spanish American War
in 1898 with the California Volunteer Infantry, and he later served with
the National Guard.
During his youth he rode the range as a cowboy, pulled the jerk-line
over an eight-horse plow team, freighted on the Mojave desert, worked
in the hay ilelds on a baler and a thrashing machine, and cut and hauled
wood. Later in his early youth he was a bookkeeper for the Kern County
Land Company. He began his banking career as an errand boy in the
Kern Valley Bank. He was later to become manager and president of
t'he First Bank of Kern and also of the Security Trust Company. When
these two banks combined and were acquired by the Bank of America,
Crites continued to serve as an officer until he resigned in 1932.
For years his name headed practically every worthwhile civic
endeavor in t'he welfare field in Kern County. During World War II he
headed the 1942 Kern County War Chest Campaign and also the
U.S.O. drive.
For more than fifty years Arthur was a Mason and was honored
by the Masons of Kern County and of the State at a testimonial dinner
in 1951. He had joined Masonry as a member of the Masonic Lodge
No. 224 of Bakersfield on February 21, 1901, had become Master in
1906 and was treasurer of that lodge for many years. He was elected
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of California in 1923 when the
Masonic Temple was formally opened and he played a leading part in
encouraging its construction. He served on the Finance Committee of
Grand Lodge for 27 years and was chairman for 16 years.
He was elected Grand Commander of the Grand Commandry
Knights Templar in 1932. He received his honorary 33' degree in
Scottish Rite Masonry in 1939.
Brother Crites was the Most 'Illustrious Grand Sovereign of the
Order of the Red Cross of Constantine and had he lived but a few more
weeks would have presided over the 85th Annual Assembly of the
Grand Imperial Council of that Order which included not only the
United States, but Mexico and the Philippines. The 85th Assembly convened at San Francisco, May 18, 1957.
Recognition of Brother Crites' leadership in civic affairs was made
by Bakersfield Post American Legion which honored him as a dis-

318

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

tinguished citizen at a civic dinner in 1942 at which Chief Justice
Warren, then Governor of California, was one of the principal speakers.
Until he was incapacitated by illness he kept up his interest in political
and civic affairs.
His hobbies were many and varied. He hunted big game and had
trophies from Alaska and East Africa trips. Until recent years he made
annual pack trips into the Sierras.
Brother Crites had a remarkable memory and contributed to Kern
County's historical records. He was the author of "Pioneer Days in
Kern County" which was .published in 1951 and contained memories of
his early years in Kern County. Earlier he had written an account of
his hunting experiences and recently he had prepared a history o'f
Bakersfield Rotary Club, in which he was active and served as president
of the Bakersfield Club in 1929 and was also District Governor of the
old Second District of Rotary International which comprised California,
Nevada and the Hawaiian Islands in 1930. He was in regular attendance at the Club meetings until his recent illness.
He was a friend of the Veterans and was one of the contributors to
the Bakersfield Post American Legion building. He established the
Arthur S. Crites trophy for Armistice Day Parades.
He was a consistent backer of youth work such as Boy Scouts and
the YMCA. He maintained an interest in all worthwhile activities while
he was physically able.
Brother Crites was born on February 4, 1879 and .passed away April
28, 1957 in Bakersfield and was laid to rest in the family plot in Union
Cemetery. He was survived by his widow, Nellie, whom he married in
1904. He is also survived by a daughter, Mrs. Harry Conran; by a son,
Angus D. Crites; and by his grandchildren, Catharine McCuen, and
Angus D. Crites II.
As we survey the foll life and unusual activities of this truly remarkable man and .Mason we are forced to exclaim in amazement that one
life could encompass so prominent a part in almost every worthwhile
civic endeavor in the field of welfare and community betterment. Arthur
Crites, in all truth, has contributed immeasurably to the growth and
prosperity not only of Kern County, but also to the growth and prosperity of the great State of California as well.

ADDRESS OP

L. HAROLD ANDERSON, GRAND MASTER
ON THE OCCASION OP THE
CEREMONY DEDICATING PLAQUE IN
PORTSMOUT H PLAZA
MARKING SITE OP FIRST PUBLIC SCHOOL IN CALIFORNIA
SEPTEMBER 25, 1957

Ladies, Gentlemen and My Brethren:
We have gathered here this morning to commemorate an important
event in the early history of California. What happens here today, will
mark for future generations of Californians, the birthplace of the first
public school in California.
There is no place in California that is hallowed with more historical
events than the plaza in which we are now assembled. Here in 1835, the
Mexican Governor Figueroa, established the town of Y erba Buena;
here in 1846, the first American flag was raised in San Francisco; here
in 1817, the first public school in California was erected.
In order to feel the atmosphere of this historic Portsmouth Plaza
and to become sensitive to the ceremonies that are about to take place,

330

331

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

I would like to turn back·time and reconstruct the surroundings of this
park as they were one hundred and ten years ago.

ance of a growing city." In due time the "schoolhouse on the plaza"
received a coat of white paint.
Certainly this first little one room schoolhouse was not an architectural triumph, but its very presence in the center of San Francisco's
activities gave promise of the future educational and cultural development.
Much has been written about the early days of San Francisco and
California, but it is questionable whether any other frontier in all
history has spawned events that so completely range the breadth and
depth of human emotion. Most of the histories of California use the
Gold Rush as the theme and the energy of their writings, and most of
the ·historians record the deeds of men, their sacrifices, their defeats,
their triumphs.
But there is one California historian that found the soul of this
humble little public school that once stood where we stand today. His
words are as plain and as humble as the little schoolhouse itself. but
they express an understanding of the things that make tradition and
history, and make them as important as our great heroes, so I shall
quote from the "Annals of San Francisco", published in 1854 and
written by the great pioneer historian, Frank Soule.
In his description of the "little schoolhouse on the plaza" he has
this to say: "lnsigniJkant as the building appears, it was destined to
subserve more useful purposes than any that has been erected in the
city, and it should have been preserved as one of San Francisco's most
important relics. Its history was almost an epitome of that of the curious
people who built it. Every new enterprise found here a heating oven to
warm the egg iiito successful hatching. Here churches held their first
meetings, and here the first public amusements were given. It was the
assembly room of the early gatherings of benevolent associations: and
a universal public hall for political. military, and almost every other
description of meeting. It was dignified as a court house under Judge
Almond, designated as an institute at another period, and at length
became a police office and station house. Not a vestige of the old relic
now remains and its site is only recognized by a thousand cherished
associations that hover like spirits around its unmarked grave."
He goes on to describe how the school prospered until it received a
sudden and unforeseen check when, and I quote, "the accounts from the
interior had lately been of the most favorable character, rumors of
immense and rapidly acquired fortunes, but above all the exhibition of
specimens of precious ore drove the whole .population to such an intensity of excitement that it resulted in a stampede of men, women and
children for the "mines", leaving the teacher minus pupils-trusteeseven a town council. He therefore locked the schoolhouse and, shouldering his pick and pan, himself started for the "diggins", and in the general scramble for gold, the school enterprise was for the time forgotten.

This is October ..11. 184 7-this is the plaza-this is San F rancis<:o.
It is a nondescript little settlement of 375 people, 247 men and 128
women, which includes the 56 boys and girls between the ages of 5 and
15 years. There are seventy-nine buildings. described as shanties and
.tenements. Since_1844. there has been a little customhouse in the southwest corner of the "plaza. The United States flag flies over the customhouse: it was placed there by a Marine detachment from the U. S. S.
Portsmouth, under the command of Captain John Montgomery.
The town's limits are not far away, just three blocks to the north, on
what is now Broadway: two blocks west, on what is now Powell: one
block "south on what is now Sacramento: and bounded on the east by
Y erba Buena Cove, a muddy sweep of shoreline of San Francisco Bay
that starts at Clark's Point, three blocks west and north, at what is now
Broadway and Sansome, cutting inland sharply to two blocks northeast,
at what is now Jackson and Montgomery: and then sweeping in a long
curve to where Bush Street now meets Market. There is a little finger
of Y erba Buena Cove that extends beyond Montgomery Street and
almost reached the far corner of the plaza on Kearny Street, where the
Presidio trail takes off over the lower hills of San Francisco. This is the
plaza: this is San Francisco in October 1847.
Since January of this year there have been constant reminders in
the weekly newspaper, that "What this town needs is a public school."
San Francisco has a fiery little newspaper called the "California Star",
and it is owned and edited by a very independent, progressive, loyal and
outspoken citizen by the name of Samuel Brannan. Sam Brannan was
a member of the Craft, and he played a very important part in every
constructive program that ·helped to build San Francisco and the West.
If this historic Portsmouth Square is properly called "The Cradle of San
Francisco", then it was Brother Sam Brannan that rocked the cradle
because his hand is to be seen, and his voice is to be heard in every
community enterprise that took place in early San Francisco.
. Finally, yielding to a public demand that had been inspired by Sam
Brannan's weekly editorials, Washington Bartlett, the Mayor, appointed a committee on September 13th to take measures for the establishment
of a public school. This committee consisted of William A. Leidesdorff,
William Glover and William S. Clark. These gentlemen lost no time in
putting their .plans into execution. They contracted for a schoolhouse
to be built in the plaza and in less than a month, on October 11th, the
first public school in California was started and on its way.
The irrepressible Sam Brannan wrote another editorial criticising
the "stark simplicity" o.f its unpolished redwood, and suggested a "coat
of paint, and some other decoration, more in keeping with the appear-

.. The Masons of California are very proud of the honor and recog~
mbon that allows them to provide and dedicate this historical landmark.
Deeply rooted in the landmarks of our ancient and venerated Craft in
California is an unselfish and vigilant interest in our public schools.
Deeply rooted in the traditions of our fraternity are those principles of
freedom that find their fullest expression in the American free public
school system. !hey are the great melting pot of a great America,
temples of learnmg that take children of nations, all colors, all races and
all c~eeds and mold them into useful and devoted citizens, striving only
to give .each of them an equal opportunity to become enlightened and
responsible leaders who can and will perpetuate and strengthen our
great American heritages.
It is these traditions and these principles that bring the officers and
members of the Grand Lodge of California, Free and Accepted Masons,
to th~ plaz~ tod~y, not to make history, ~ut to preserve history and to
unveil a~ h1ston~al marker of California s first public school. and with

ADDRESS OF CHARLES ALBERT ADAMS
Fellow Citizens:
I so address you because although the Grand Master of Masons
and other officers of the Grand Lodge are clad in the regalia of their
respective stations, as is, of course eminently proper, they also appear
as to all of us here assembled as citizens of the State of California,
with representatives from practically every one of its 57 counties, to
participate in the setting of a monument which will mark the location
of the first public school in California - the establishment of a land~
mark - a landmark not only in the history of this state, and that of
this city, but a landmark also in that long and steady, though sometimes
slow march of Education from its beginning ages and ages ago when
there was nothing like a school of any sort, and when its nearest
approach was a sort of apprenticeship by which there was passed on
to the youth of succeeding generations, by their parents and other
adults, such knowledge and skills as they possessed, and the folkways,
tribal customs, and ethical concepts were imparted and preserved by
tribal ceremonies and rituals - from that time, thousands of years ago,
to its advent here on this spot:
And that the Grand Lodge of Masons of California has been
accorded the privilege of presenting this monument to the City of San
Francisco, and to take an active part in the ceremony, will not seem
strange to those who know that the establishment of landmarks, and
their strict observance, have been from time immemorial, intimately
associated with the history, philsophy, and ritualism of Freemasonry:
and that Amefican Masons are earnest and active champions of our
system of public education and unqualifiedly subscribe to the belief
announced by one of its earliest advocates, that an educated and
enlightened citizenship should be the first great care of a progressive
state: and that upon the public schools will depend the hope for the
perpetuity of a free and untrammelled democracy.
Now, before I say anything else, and to relieve your apprehensions,
I want to assure you that although I know that you would be delighted
to listen to everything I should like to say, no matter how long it would
take, I have in mind that you are not seated in comfortable chairs and
able to take a little nap which you could explain as "not asleep, only
just resting my eyes": but that you are all standing. perhaps on one
foot and then the other, hoping-, if not expecting. that I will know
what you may think is a good stopping place-and avail myself of it.
I shall not, therefore, attempt to even ske~chily describe that long
march of Education to which I have referred, with the institution by
the Greeks of what we know as a School---or say anything about the
medieval schools and their accomplishments. I shall not even remind you
of what you must have many times heard or read about-the "Old

334

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Deluder Satan Act," and the earlier legislation which made it compulsory for householders to provide education for the children of the
community, and which resulted in what are generally regarded as the
Colonial beginning of our system of free, tax-supported public schools~xcept to say that while there was in Colonial times the germ of the
idea, the schools of that day, and of even a much later time down to
about the middle of the 19th Century. were as different from the modern
public schools as were medieval schools from them. The colonial school
was a semi-private, semi-religious institution. Its curriculum was limited
to reading, writing, and ciphering, and religion. Indeed it was for religious reasons that there was that insistance on education-so that all
might be able to read their Bibles and that there might be a supply of
properly-trained ministers. It was essentially a period of middle-class
education in accordance with English traditions. and followed the
customs of those Eurepean schools with which the Colonists were
familiar. It was very far from being a free, tax-supported public school
as we know it.
There is, however, one thing which all school systems supported,
either entirely, or in part, by taxes, have in common; and that is that
they have come into existence and have survived only after more or
less opposition and in spite of the criticism to which they have been
subjected-and it is with respect to this I purpose using the time I feel
warranted in taking.
If there is one single Institution in our way of life which more than
any other is purely and essentially American, it is our system of free
tax supported public schools; and it is one of our most cherished. It
reaches every boy and every girl in the land. It is for the sons and
daughters of the rich and of the poor. It offers to all the children of all
the people an education suited to their needs, desires. and capabilities,
and which commences in the kindergarten and ends only in the university. Its ultimate purpose and the only real justification for its existence is the creation of that enlightened citizenship without which a
democracy can not exist.
As I have intimated, the system came into existence and was
preserved only after a long and bitter opposition was overcome. By
some of the objectors, it was deemed a fantastic idea which would upset
all social order and stability and that a citizen without any children
should be taxed for the education of his neighbor's child. was deemed
highway robbery.
A story attributed to one of the early advocates of the public school
is about a neighbor of his. a farmer, who insisted that it would be as
sensible to propose to take his plough away from him to plough his
neighbor's fteld as to take his money to educate his neighbor's child.
It would appear that that was the attitude of a large proportion of
the people down to a time as late as 1844.

The latest instance of widely publicized criticism of our
public
schools which has been broug ht to my attention, (but of a

It is in two parts, because there are two answe rs to the questi
on.
One parent answe rs "No," and assert s that ·public school

young minds by feeding them insipid lessons in social confor
mity and
"living skills" instea d of furnishing intellectual challenge
to develop

en from a

at a cost of

The other parent s answe rs "Yes. " a1.1d he declares that ~e.

privat e schools in equipping young sters to meet the ~eman
d~
. of the

~iting the

338

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

youngsters outscored the private school applicants in both aptitude
tests, and in all subjects in the Achievement Test except English competition, French, and Spanish-and quotes the Director of Admissions
of a major Ivy League College as saying (among other things favorable
to the public school) "on the average, graduates of public schools
perform academically better than do the boys from the private schools."
He says further, "my wife and I have heard all the criticisms: we have
investigated and have found them basically without truth.''
This parent has a boy of 13 and a girl of 10 in a public school and
says that he and his wife intend to keep them there. He says they want
the best education possible for their children and believe that they are
getting it: that they are lucky enough to be able to afford any school
they might choose: and that they choose a public school.
I wish I had time to tell you more about this article and detail the
different points of view. I hope that every one of you interested in the
subject will read it: and that if you have already done so, you will read
it again-keeping in mind what I have said about the purpose of, and
the only justification for, a free tax-supported public school.
In the last analysis, we have in this article a discussion of that old
question "What Should the School Teach" by two well-informed
parents.
Of course, everyone is entitled to have, and to express, if an opportunity is presented, an opinion of his own as to what the schools teach:
and I now close this all too scattering, I fear, talk by telling you, and I
hope with due modesty. what I as a layman believe are among the most
important things a public school should teach and bearing in mind that
in the last analysis the tax-supported public school came into existence
and has been preserved not for the benefit or aggrandizement of the
individual child, but that all the children of all the people, according
to their capabilities might make their respective contributions to an
enlightened citizenship.
I believe that every child should be taught how to become, and
remain, a good citizen: how to live and how to make a living for himself
and those dependent upon him and how to conserve his own physical
well being and to contribute to the health and safety of those with whom
he must live. and play and work: how to make a wise use of his leisure
time, as a child and as an adult; how to be happy by being the cause
of the happiness of others in the intimate relations of life and to believe
in, and be loyal to our form of government, not because he has not
learned about any other, but because he has and believes ours is better;
and he should learn and demonstrate by his own conduct that democracy
is not only a form of government but a mode of life where no one wil1
claim for himself a right or privilege he will deny the other fellow, and
that with every right and privilege there go corresponding duties and
responsfbilJtJes. There, I believe, are among the things every boy and
girl should learn and what the schools should teach.

RESPONSE BY
MAYOR GEORGE CHRISTOPHER
ACCEPTING THE MARKER AND PLAQUE

339

This ceremony is most significant. As we unveil this monument in
honor of and depicting the first public school in California, we are
reminded of the great strides education has made in this state. This
building was a single classroom but now our multi-storied public school
buildings are in every section of this great city.
In spite of all this there is much to do, not the least of whiC'h is to
eliminate classes which must presently be held on a part time basis. To
meet this ever growing need San Francisco passed a 27 million dollar
bond issue for education, and just a relatively few years ago passed a
similar bond issue in the amount of 48 million dollars.
We are all concerned about the cold war which is being carried on
with Russia, and well we might be concerned with it for we never know
when it may become a hot war. There is, however, another cold war
being carried on with Russia and one of which all too few are conscious.
I refer to the cold war in the field of education. Of all the students in
schools in Russia 50% go to colleges and the emphasis is on science and
engineering. The reason for this is perfectly obvious, and when we
remember that there is a great shortage of competent scientists and
engineers in the United States today we wonder if perhaps we are not
losing this phase of the cold war.
Public education and its support are traditional in San Francisco, and
I am glad to say that we are self-supporting. We are entitled only to a
minimum of the state allocation for education, and are entitled to no aid
from the State Board of Equalization. There is not only nothing wrong
with this theory, but there is much to commend it, and I hope that all the
metropolitan areas and cities of larger 1population would concur, because it is the traditional American way of supporting public education.
The future of our city, state and nation depends upon our free.
public school system because the foundation of every state is the educa·
tion of its youth.

We therefore offer the following resolution:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In Trial Record No. 865 J.B.F., a member of America Lodge No.
475, was expelled in 1935 for conviction of a violation of the Corporate
Securities Act. He applied for restoration in 1938 but was refused. He
has again applied for restoration. He is now 73 years of age and has
no blot on his record since his expulsion and has several good letters
of recommendation. We recommend his restoration.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved that the petition of J.B.F. for restoration be granted and
that he be restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1157
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In Trial Record No. 1157, H.R.D. was expelled by Downey Lodge
No. 220 in 1948 after he had been convicted of lewd and lascivious
conduct with children and committed to San Quentin prison. He has
petitioned for restoration. He has several letters of recommendation
from persons in his present home town in the state of New York.
However we do not feel we have enough evidence of his conduct
since his release from 1prison to justify a recommendation for restoration
at this time. We desire to know more about him than the present letters
show.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved that the petition of H.R.D. for restoration be continued to
the next annual communication of Grand Lodge and that further facts
of ·his life since leaving prison be furnished and no further notice need
be given.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1305
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In Trial Record No. 1305 J.M.P., a member of a Michigan lodge,
was expelled by Grand Lodge in 1952 after he was convicted of grand
theft in Fresno County. He had been given a county jail sentence only
in the state court, which made the crime a misdemeanor under state
law, but it was a "crime classified as a felony" and justified the automatic expulsion. It appears that overuse of liquor was the problem of
the accused, and 1he seems to have conquered the habit. He applied
for restoration in 1956 but we recommended a year's delay and Grand
Lodge ·so ordered. During the past year his record has been clear and
he has a number a One letters of recommendation from prominent
persons in Fresno. We recommend his restoration.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1386
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In Trial Record No. 1386 V.W.M. was expelled by Grand Lodge
in 1954 after suspension by Alhambra Lodge No. 322. He had pleaded
Guilty in Municipal Court of immoral conduct with another man
and had been placed on two years probation without imprisonm~nt.
After his probationar y period expired he was allowed to go mto
court and withdraw his plea of Guilty and plead Not Guilty and the
case was dismissed to clear his record. This is the proceeding provided
in the California Penal Code to clear a record after a successful probation.
The accused then demanded of Alhambra Lodge that he be restored
and raised the point that the withdrawal of plea of Guilty and dismissal
of the charge in the state court proved his innocence. He also asked
that the lodge publicly apologize to him for suspending him. In spite
of his original plea of Guilty at a time when he was duly represented
by counsel •he now takes the position that he has been greatly wronge~.
He also assumes that the completion of his probation requires automatic
restoration in the lodge. We feel that his attitude is such that restoration
is not warranted.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved tliat the petition for restoration of V.W.M. be denied.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1477
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
In Trial Record No. 1477 an acquittal of an accused was reversed
by Grand Lodge in 1956 and the matter sent back to the Lodge for a
retrial. This has not been held. The Lodge · asks to be relieved of the
burden of retrying this case as some investigation ·had shown that a
conviction of the accused would not be possible. We have seen no
details of the alleged investigation which the Lodge feels justifies this
relief. We talked to the Master and explained to him that proper
charges are before the Lodge stating unmasonic conduct, and they
should be disposed of by a trial. H the charges are properly tried and
the evidence available fully presented. and if it does not justify a
finding of Guilt of the accused, he should be acquitted. but not otherwise.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved that Park Lodge No. 449 be directed to proceed with
the retrial in Trial Record No. 1477 as ordered heretofore by this
Grand Lodge.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1514
To the Most Worshipfu( Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances makes the following report concerning Trial Record No. 1514:
Accused L.R.M. a member of Metropolitan Lodge No. 646 was
charged with unmasonic conduct in that on or about July 17, 1953,
he committed grand theft of property of a value in excess of $200.00
belonging to the estate of Charles S. Anderson, deceased, and Helen
Schwartz, administratrix of said estate.
The evidence consisted of a certified copy of a judgment of the
Superior Court of Los Angeles County and extensive excerpts from
the testimony taken in the Superior Court trial. The judgment showed
that accused and his attorney, one Reynolds, were. on January 18,
1956, convicted of grand theft by a judge, sitting without a jury. The
Judge placed accused on 5 years .probation with a fine of $5,000.00
as a condition thereof. Accused took an appeal from this judgment
and subsequently dismissed ·his appeal.
Accused was the president, general manager and majority stockholder of a building and loan association. There were a total of 750
shares of stock of this association issued and outstanding. The Estate
of Anderson owned 110 shares of this stock. Reynolds was accused's
personal attorney and also on occasions performed legal services for
the building and loan association. Upon Anderson's death Reynolds
became attorney for Mrs. Schwartz, deceased's sister, a resident of
Ohio, and procured her appointment as administratrix of the estate.
Reynolds, acting as attorney for both Mrs. Schwartz and accused,
persuaded Mrs. Schwartz to sell the Anderson stock to accused for
$350.00 a share or $38,500.00. T•his stock was worth about $2,000.00
per share or $220,000.00. Reynold's fee from accused for arranging
this sale was $5.000.00. Prior to the consummation of the sale of the
Anderson stock to accused, accused entered into negotiations with
one Shaw for the sale of all of the stock of the association. As a result
of these negotiations accused sold the stock for $2,800.00 per share.
Under the law before a director of a corporation buys stock of such
corporation, he must make a full and fair disclosure of all .pertinent
facts concerning such stock to the prospective seller. His failure to
do this makes the transaction fraudulent. To meet this legal requirement
accused and Reynolds arranged for a court reporter to take down and
transcribe a statement •purporting to be a full and fair disclosure of all

348

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

pertinent facts concerning the stock to Mrs. Schwartz. The evidence
shows that this statement was not a foll and fair disclosure of all the
facts. In addition, no information was given to Mrs. Schwartz prior
to the consummation of the sale of the Anderson stock concerning
the pending negotiations with Shaw. When Mrs. Sc'hwartz found
out what had happened ·she changed attorneys and under the threat
of suit accused paid to the Estate of Anderson the difference between
the $350.00 tper share already paid and $2,800.00 per share, or
$269.500.00.
Notwithstanding accused's conviction in the State court and the
foregoing facts, the Trial Commission found accused not guilty.
Your committee is of t'he opinion that the evidence clearly establishes
accused's guilt.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the Trial Commission's finding of not guilty in
Trial Record No. 1514 be and it is hereby disapproved and set aside:
that a finding of guilty of the specification and of unmasonic conduct
is hereby supplied by this Grand Lodge: and that accused be and he is
hereby expelled from all the rights of Masonry.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1.517
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1517, reports as follows:
This trial involves a question of considerable import relating to trial
procedure, and in view of the earnest contention of the Trial Commission that the verdict of "Not Guilty" should be affirmed, your
Committee deems it advisable to briefly review the proceedings.
Morning Star Lodge No. 68 F. & A. M. at Stockton was designated
as the Lodge where the Masonic trial of the accused, a member of
Woodbridge No. 131, should be held.
Morning Star Lodge No. 68 F. & A. M. convened at 7 :45 o'clock
p.m. on September 27, 1956, for the purpose of conducting the trial of
J.D.T .. the accused, on charges preferred by t'he Junior Warden of
Woodbridge Lodge No. 131 F. & A. M.
At this meeting, held on September 27, 1956, Trial Commissioners,
seven in number, were nominated and elected. Brother Hubert H. Briggs,
the Trial Master, then .proceeded with the trial. He appointed a reporter and the trial •proceeded. David E. Kellar, Junior Warden of
Woodbridge Lodge No. 131, appeared as accuser, without counsel.
The accused did not appear. The Trial Master ordered two Brethren
of Woodbridge Lodge No. 131 to search the "temple and area in and
about it to see if the accused could be found: if so, to conduct him to

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

349

this Lodge." A five-minute recess was declared. Diligent search was
made wit'hout effect, thereupon the Trial Master ordered the trial to
proceed. The Secretary stated that the charges with the summons had
been duly served upon the accused, and in his certificate of service
stated that same was served by registered mail on September 27, 1956,
the very same day upon which the trial itself was ·held.
In an effort to support the contention of "due service," a letter,
purported to have been written by accused, was read into the record,
addressed to Donald L. Stewart, Secretary of Morning Star Lodge,
in which !he stated:
"I have at •h and a copy of charges against me .preferred by David
Kellar, Junior Warden of Woodbridge Lodge.'' and he requested a
continuance and for the .place of trial to be moved to Sacramento. This
letter was dated September 25, 1956, two days before the Trial Commission was even elected and trial held. The original of this letter is
not in the record.
This letter could not be construed as legal service of the summons
and specifications.
Section 707 of the California Masonic Code reads in part as follows:
"Service of Summons.
"H the accused be within the jurisdiction of the Lodge, the summons
and copy of the charges shall be issued and served upon the accused
at least ten days prior to the day appointed for the trial . . . If he be
without the said jurisdiction, but within the state, and his 1'esidence be
known, they shall be issued and served upon the accused at least thirty
days before the day of the trial, and shall be forwarded to his address
by the Secretary by mail . . . and service shall be complete from and
after depositing the same in the mail upon due proof thereof ..."
The only proof of service of the summons and specifications
offered in the entire record is the Certificate of Service of the Secretary ·
of Morning Star Lodge, which on its .face shows that service was
made on accused on the very same date upon which the trial was
·held.
Nowhere in the entire record is there any proof or showing that
there was any compliance with Section 707 of the California Masonic
Code.
It is the opinion of your Committee that the Trial Commission had
no jurisdiction to proceed with the trial of this case.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved, that the Trial Commission's finding of "Not Guilty" be
reversed and the matter be remanded back to Morning Star Lodge
No. 68 F. & A. M. for retrial.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECO RD No. 1519
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1519, reports as follows:
It appears from the file that H.R.M. •petitioned California Lodge
No. 1 and was elected and received two degrees. The lodge then learned
that H.R-M . had been convicted of a felony prior to the time he
petitioned the lodge, and had been sentenced and served a term at
San Quentin prison.
Based on this conviction, automatic expulsion proceedings were
commenced. The accused did not demand a trial. Therefore, in accordance with the provisions of Sec. 732, California Masonic Code,
the accused was eJ1Cpelled.
The ·felony conviction upon which the proceedings were commenced occurred in 1939, long before the accused .petitioned for the
degrees. Grand Lodge has previously held, in Trial Record No. 1191
( 1950) and Trial Record 1327 ( 1953). that automatic expulsion
should not be used in connection with convictions suffered before the
accused became a Mason. The proper procedure is to file charges
against the accused. Your committee therefore offers the following
resolution:
~ESOLVED: That the automatic expulsion of H.R.M.
by California Lodge No. 1 be reversed and set aside; and that the lodge file
appropr iate charges against the accused.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECO RD No. 1521
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1521, reports as follows:
L.L.M., a member of Hesperian Lodge No. 264, was charged by
the Junior Warde n of being a full-time, regular bar-keeper, dispensing
alcoholic beverages over the bar to any and all customers, at a cafe
in the City of ~anta Maria. The accused was duly served and appeared
at the trial without counsel. He admitted that he was acting as a
bartend er for a period of approximately 13 months. In addition, there
were two witnesses ~ho testified that ·he had so acted as a bar-keeper.
Accused further testified that he had accepted this type of employment because he was unable to get a job in his regular line of work
as an oil field construction worker.
In connection with the question of whethe r this cafe was a bona
fide restaurant, the accused testified that the food which was served
was not very substan.tial, ~ing "sandwiches and eggs and, well, of
course peanuts and pickles. T·he trial commission found the accused
not guilty by a vote of 4 to 3.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

351

An appeal has been filed by the Junior Warden . the accuser, on
the ground that the accused 'had not shown that the bar was a bona
fide restaurant, and in view of the accused's admission that he acted
as a bar-keeper, the verdict ·should have been one of Guilty. We feel
that there is much merit in the appeal and the ground s set forth therein.
The cafe probably served enough food to comply with the then requirements of the Board of Equalization, but clearly was not a bona
fide restaura nt according to standar ds determined in previous Masonic
trials dealing with this question. In addition, the accused testified that
he worked as a regular bar-keeper. Under Sec. 513 of the California
Masonic Code and the innumerable decisions under said Section,
the accused was guilty of unMasonic conduct. Your committee therefore offers the following resolution:
RESOL VED: That the finding of Not Guilty of unMasonic conduct in Trial Record No. 1521 be and the same is hereby vacated and
set aside; that by action of this Grand Lodge, finding that the accused
L.L.M. is guilty of the specification charged and of unMasonic conduct
is made herein; and that the penalty therefor be fixed by this Grand
Lodge at expulsion."
Adopted.

TRIAL RECO RD No. 1525

To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was reiferred Trial Record
No. 1525, reports as follows:
T •he accused F.M.M . was automatically expelled after he plead
guilty to violating section 288 of the Penal Code of the State of
California, a felony. He was subsequently confined.
Two errors appear in this record which requires a reversal.
·First: No certified copy of the final judgment of the conviction of
the accused appears in these proceedings.
Second: The accused was not given 60 days notice.
Both are required by section 732 C. M. C. and Grand Lodge has
consistently held that the proper notice to the accused is jurisdictional.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
That the automatic ex1pulsion of F.M.M . be and the same is hereby
reversed and set aside, and the matter be referred back to the lodge
with directions to proceed in accordance with section 732 C. M. C.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECO RD No. 1527

To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1527, begs leave to report as follows:
The accused E.K.B., a member of Pacific Grove Lodge No. 331,
F. & A. M .. was charged in •his Lodge with unmasonic conduct as set
forth in the specifications as follows:

352

353

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

"That duril'lg the time he was serving as a Representative of the
People of the 13th Congressional District of California, in the Congress
of the United States, •he did commit payroll fraud during the years
1948 to 1954 and was convicted in fue Courts of the United States of
such charge."
The accused was present at the trial, and in answer to the C'harge
in said specification entered a plea of "not guilty."
The Trial Commission then proceeded to hear the testimony. and
at the conclusion of the hearing the accused was found guilty.
The accused has 'filed his appeal from this verdict of "guilty" by
the Trial Commissioners. The accused also appeared in person before
tlie Grievance Committee.
In his letter of appeal, filed with Grand Lodge, and in t'he presentation of his appeal in .person before the Grievance Committee, it was
the contention of the accused that the evidence presented before the
Trial Commission did not "substantiate the charge" and that the
"proceedings were irregular." The accused stated that he testified
before the Commission for two hours in presenting his defense and
that the evidence presented in his defense was suflkient to sustain a
verdict of "Not Guilty.''
The Trial Record discloses that the proceedings were not reported
by a qualified reporter. An examination of the proceedings discloses
the following:
"The accused offered the following testimony:
A.fter being duly sworn his testimony consisted of letters which
he read and of which photostatic copies have been made and attached
with this transcript.''
The Secretary did not write out the oral testimony in full and
certify the same, as required.
Section 715 of the California Masonic Code provides in part as
follows:
"All oral testimony, direct and cross, will be written out in full
by the Secretary or stenographer, and certified as correct.''
Your Committee is of the opinion that the very nature of this
appeal requires a review of all of the evidence had and taken before
the Trial Commission. This cannot be done for the reason that the
Trial Commission failed to make a proper transcript of the testimony
as required by the aforesaid Section 715 of the California Masonic
Code.
In view of the serious nature of the charge against t'he accused
and the failure of the Trial Commission to make a full and proper
transcript of the testimony, it is the opinion of your Committee that
the verdict of "Guilty" be reversed and the matter remanded back to
Pacific Grove Lodge No. 331, F. & A. M., for retrial, and that a

proper record be made of all oral testimony as required by Section 715
of California Masonic Code.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved, that the Trial Commission finding of "Guilty" in Trial
Record No. 1527 be reversed: and said matter be remanded to Pacific
Grove Lodge No. 331, F. & A. M., for retrial.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1529

1

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances, to which was referred Trial Record
No. 1529, reports as follows:
The accused D.Y.I. was charged with on-Masonic conduct in a
specification alleging in substance tliat on or about November 5, 1955,
at and in the County of Los Angeles, he did wilfully, unlawfully and
feloniously offer to give a bribe to one G.A.R., a police officer of the
City of Los Angeles, with intent to corruptly influence said officer in
respect to arresting accused on a charge of bookmaking, all in violation
of section 67 of the Penal Code of the State of California.
The accused was .found not guilty of the specification and not guilty
of on-Masonic conduct.
The record shows that at the time of his trial in Superior Court
the accused was represented by able counsel; that he waived his right
to a jury trial and submitted his case on tlie testimony taken at the
preliminary ihearing, reserving the rig•h t to submit additional testimony.
The accused elected not to testify nor submit additional testimony
and the matter being so submitted the accused was found guilty, fined
$750.00 and placed on probation.
While we do not have the transcript of the testimony given at the
preliminary hearing, it appears from the probation report that at that
hearing the police officer testified that on the morning of November
3, 1955, he met the accused in Lafayette Park; that accused mentioned
his bookmaking activities and offered him $300.00 if he would "lay off"
accused; that he met the accused aga:in the following evening and
sifter some discussion accused gave •him $300.00, whereupon accused
was placed under arrest. The officer further testified that during all
of the time he was talking to accused ·he was under observation by
_other police officers and that he carried transmitting equipment on his
person for the purpose of recording his conversation with the accused.
The accused testified that he paid the oflker nothing and at the same
time claimed the defense of "entrapment." The two are inconsistent.
l£ he paid the officer nothing no crime was committed and •h e could
not be "entrapped.'' H he was entitled to the defense of "entrapment"
it meant that he paid the police officer a bribe but that the idea was

354

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

placed in 1his mind and he was induced to do so by the officer. In other
words that the idea of paying a bribe did not originate with him.
The accuser was not represented by counsel. The accused was
represented by counsel and the record discloses that his counsel, who
was a Mason, either deliberately or through ignorance mislead the
trial commissioners on many material matters. The following instances
will serve to illustrate.
Counsel for accused told the commissioners that certain evidence
could not be brought out at the Superior Court trial because "it
would be in violation of the Cahan case." Such statement was false.
He told them that the accused "was never given a trial" whereas he
was given a trial of his own choosing. He further stated that accused
"never had a chance to testirfy" at his criminal trial, whereas in truth
and in fact accused had reserved the right to produce additional testimony and had he desired he could have testified and also had others
testify in his behalf. In view of the fact that the police officer had a
recording device on his person it is understandable that the accused
did not elect to testify.
In addition to misleading the trial commissioners counsel for the
accused made many statements which were improper and wholly irrelevant to the issues involved.
We, therefore, offer the following Resolution:
Resolved: That the findings of the trial commissioners finding the
accused D.Y.I. not guilty of the specification and not guilty of unMasonic conduct be and the same are hereby reversed and set aside;
that the case be remanded to the lodge for re-trial with instructions to
obtain a certified copy of the transcrilpt of the testimony given at the
preliminary hearing, and that the Grand Master be requested to appoint a trial master and an attorney for the accuser.
Adopted.

ADDITIONAL TRIAL RECORDS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Grievances ·feels that the publication in full
in the proceedings of Grand Lodge of the reports in the following trial
records would either fomish no point of Masonic law or would put
into print matters which might better be left unpublished because of
the nature of the cases. We therefore offer the following resolution:
"Resolved that Trial Records Nos. 1508, 1509, 1515, 1520, 1522,
1531, 1536, 1546, 1547,1551 and 1552 be not published in full in the
proceedings of this annual communication."
No. 1508-A member of North Hollywood Lodge No. 542, findings of
guilt affirmed and penalty raised to expulsion.
No. 1509-A member of La Mesa Lodge No. 407, findings of guilt
affirmed and penalty raised to expulsion.

Petitions for Restoration in Trial Records Nos. 1333 and 1483
have been filed but the notice to the respective lodges was given less
than sixty days before the convening of Grand Lodge. It is to be noted
that such notice to a lodge is not effective until the stated meeting at
which it is read to the lodge and should therefore always be given
sufficiently long before the annual communication that the stated
meeting of the lodge next after the giving of the notice to the secretary
will be a full sixty days before said annual communication.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
Resolved that the petitions for restoration in Trial Records Nos.
1333 and 1483 be continued to the next annual communication of
Grand Lodge, but that no further notice need be given. Further evidence
in support of or opposed to the petitions may be filed if desired.
Adopted.

COLUMBIA BRICK SCHOOL HOUSE RESTORATION

Another matter receiving widespread support from those in California who are continually interested in public schools is the project now
under way to restore, at Columbia, the first brick public school house in
California. This is largely under the sponsorship of the California
Teachers Association and the California Retired Teachers Association.
We are informed that the school children of the state have raised about

It has been recommended that this Grand Lodge contribute $500 to

In view of the fact that the Endowment Fund, owned by the Masonic
Homes Corporation, is the sole beneficiary of the flne results Which are
accomplished for the Fund under the leadership of their board, it
appears logical that the expenses of the Endowment Board should be
defrayed by the Homes. Commencing with the current .6.scal year this
procedure will be followed. Your Committee appreciates the cooperation
of the Homes Board in putting it into operation.
The Endowment Board is a constitutional board of Grand Lodge.
In line with the accounting recommended by our auditors, we are
including in appropriations the sum of $12,000 for expense of this Board
and an equal amount in Estimated Income as refund from the Masonic
Homes for this purpose.

CAPITAL ADDITIONS AND REPLACEMENTS

Our auditors have expressed the opinion that, in future, the amounts
expended by Grand Lodge for furnishings and equipment which become
the property of Grand Lodge, should be capitalized and carried on the
balance sheet of Grand Lodge as an asset. There have been very few
expenditures of this nature in t'he last several years, but with the removal
of the Grand Lodge offices to the new Memorial Temple, there will be
substantial expenditures in this category and it is felt that now is the
time to adopt the proper accounting procedures with respect to such
expenditures.
It is our recommendation, therefore, that all items of a capital nature
be excluded from the regular expense items and set up separately in the
budget. Accordingly, we have included a new caption entitled "Capital
Additions and Replacements" under which we will report and recommend appropriations to be charged to the capital account of Grand
Lodge to cover all expenditures of this nature which are referred to the
Finance Committee or otherwise approved.
We estimate.that there will be expenditures in this category for the
current year totalling $33,796.76 and have included this amount under

RETIREMENT PENSION IPLAN FOR 'GRAND loDGE EMPLOYEES

The necessity of obtaining legal opinions on tax questions has
delayed the integration of employees in the Grand Lodge ofBce under
the Masonic Homes Retirement Pension Plan. Tihis action was ap- ·
proved by Grand Lodge to be effective January 1, 1956.
Satisfactory opinions have been rendered and we are now ready to
proceed.
.
Our actuaries estimate the cost for the current ·fiscal year to be
$19 ,500. We have included this in the budget. We call your attention
to the effective date of January 1, 1956. The above amount, therefore,
covers the two-year cost of current service under covered payroll and
the minimum annual payments required to fond prior credits earned.
The above action relates only to those individuals directly employed
in the Grand Lodge office. At the last Annual Communication, on the
recommendation of this committee, Grand Lodge approved the integration under the Masonic Homes Pension Plan of certain individuals
outside the Grand Lodge office such as those employed by the various
Boards of Relief. Employment Bureaus and University Clubhouses.
It seems clear that these individuals are employees of the agencies
involved, just as is the case with the Masonic Homes, and not direct
employees of Grand Lodge.
Therefore, it now becomes the responsibility of the boards of the
University Clubhouses and those of the several Boards of Relief and
Employment Bureaus to determine if action is to be taken, and, if so, to
take the necessary steps looking to the integration df their employees
under the Masonic Homes Pension Plan.
Subject to a future review of any exceptional case, the plan is limited
to full time employees of the agencies involved. Payments to fund prior
credits earned shall be limited to the minimum payment necessary to
fund such credits.
Based on the employment data of a list of such employees, our actuaries inform us that it will require approximately $12,815 to defray the
cost of covered payroll and the minimum annual payment to fund prior
credits earned. We have included a lump sum appropriation in this
amount. When we have further experience in the matter, it should be
possible to allocate the appropriation in the correct amounts among the
various agencies.
In view of the fact that this is action still to be determined by the
various boards, for the sake of uniformity we recommend that in every
case the effective date be January 1, 1958.

BUDGET

BUDGET FOR FIRST QUARTER 1958-59 FISCAL YEAR
ONE QUARTER~}ULY

Your Committee .feels that it is proper and necessary to bring to your
attention a condition in Grand Lodge finances which confronts us
annually and causes some concern.
At this Communication, as in the past, Grand Lodge will adopt a
budget for the fiscal year, currently ending June 30, 1958. But expenses
will continue to run and bills will have to be paid during the succeeding
three months interval until the next Communication of Grand Lodge
in September 1958. Expenditures during this interval have, in the past,
been approved by the Grand Master.
However, to the extent that such expenditures are approved, they
are being taken from the budget of the succeeding year, and when the
succeeding Grand Master takes office he faces the fact that one-fourth
of his budget-and sometimes more-'has already been spent, over
which he had no control.
This situation is presented to you as a statement of fact and not as a
criticism of the results whic'h obtained in any particular year.
The second point is this: Your Finance Committee, the Grand
Treasurer, and certain members of the Jurisprudence Committee have
felt that it was sound practice for such interim expenditures approved by
the Grand Master to be reported to and given final approval by Grand
Lodge. Although we have followed this procedure for the last two years,
it is an expedient, not a correction of the condition.
After considerable thought and consultation, we have decided to
recommend to Grand Lodge that, in addition to the regular budget for
the current fiscal year, you adopt a One-Quarter Budget to cover this
three-month interval, July 1 to September 30, 1958.
This procedure will serve the purposes that all monies thus spent will
be under the prior approval df Grand Lodge. By realistic planning and
budgeting we think the necessity for the approval of excess expenditures
will be infrequent and for emergencies only.
We present no estimate of income for this Quarter. The budget to be
presented to you at our next Annual Communication will be for the full
year 1958-1959 and will include the actual results of this first quarter.
At that time we will report to you on this new ,p rocedure and make sudh
recommendations for the succeeding year as seem advisable.
