DEas10N No. 3
On Grand Master's Decision No. 3 your Committee reports as follows:
In Whittier Lodge No. 323 a candidate received the Entered Apprentice Degree in May, 1946, and the FeUow Craft Degree in October of
the same year and then disappeared until August, 1956, when he contacted the Master and requested completion of his work. The Lodge
never gave the Candidate the notice required by Section 546 of the Code
or otherwise. The Master appointed a committee to investigate the candidate's delinquency and on receipt of its report ruled that the candidate
could not proceed to the Third Degree and ordered forfeiture of his fees
and contribution. This was error. The correct and required procedure is
prescribed by Sections 542, 5i3 and 544 of the Code. The candidate

368

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

being a Fellow Craft is a Mason and as such is entitled to all of the
safeguards of our law.
Forfeiture is a penalty and in Masonry it must not be invoked except
in strict accord with the conditions prescribing it.
The Grand Master's decision to the extent that it is in tune with this
report is approved.
Adopted.

On Grand Master's Decision No. 4 your Committee reports as follows:
The applicant, a single man, resided in Santa Ana for many years and
was Street Inspector in said city from November, 1946, to May, 1948,
when ·he became an employee of the Arabian American Oil Co. and was
transferred to Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. He returns to Santa Ana several
month.s each year and claims and has claimed his brother's home at 2535
Spurgeon Street, Santa Ana as his permanent residence for 20 years but
he files his income tax return as a nonresident.
The Grand Master held that the application could not be received on
the ground that if a man claims nonresidence for income tax purposes he
cannot be considered a resident of the community.
The Grand Master's decision is correct but his reason is subject to
doubt. Under civil law it is quite proper for a resident who spends 18
months or more in a foreign co1,mtry to file his income tax return as a
nonresident without disturbing his permanent residence. Under Masonic
law residence generally is a matter of intention. Prolonged absence of
one on business or pleasure for years accompanied by an intention to
retain . and return to his permanent address will not disturb rights and
privileges when he does return. However, an applicant for the degrees
must in fact have resided in this jurisdiction in the manner and for the
time required by law immediately preceding the date of his application.
(517-cC.M.C.)
Adopted.
DECISION No. 18

A brother who visited a Lodge so impressed the Master with his
personality that the Master there and then invited him to become a plural
member of his Lodge. He was given a petition for membership; he signed
it, but he did not fill in the blanks. The petition was not read by the
Secretary.
Two months later the Master declared the brother elected, after an
investigating committee had reported. Applicant never returned to the
Lodge, nor signed its by-laws, nor paid any dues.
Under the facts stated, applicant was not a member of the Lodge, and
the Grand Master's order declaring his election void is right.

FORM OP APPLICATION FOR DEGREES

Several resolutions, some of them in the alternative, are suggested by
Brother P.G.M. Paulsen and Brother Ross, having for their purpose
clarification as to the effect of conviction of crime on eligibility to apply
for the degrees in Masonry, and as to the effect on a Mason of nondisclosure by him of the fact of such conviction in or in connection with
his application for the degrees. They have received careful consideration
and your Committee reports as follows:
Not a little confusion has been due to the use in the discussions of the
word "felony," definition of which differs greatly under the laws and
decisions of the courts of the United States and of the various states.
With the great influx into this jurisdiction of men from other states and
countries the questions and problems incidental thereto have recurred
with increasing frequency, and the need for clarification :has become more
pressing.
The present form of application for the degrees contains no question
which speci·fically requires disclosure of conviction of crime. The only
question therein which even remotely suggests such disclosure is the
following : "12. Do you know of any physical, legal. or moral reason
which would prevent you from becoming a Freemason? State particularly any physical deformity or defect."
An applicant is not, of course, charged with knowledge of our
Masonic law. He may, therefore, be of the opinion, from his standpoint,
that the fact of such conviction is no reason for preventing his becoming
a Mason, and answer "No" to Question 12.
Furthermore, it has been decided that a Mason who had been convicted of crime before applying for the degrees, and had failed to disclose
the fact in or in connection with his application, cannot be found guilty
of a Masonic offense unless the evidence shows that the non-disclosure
was wilful and with actual fraudulent intent to conceal the fact.
It seems, therefore, necessary that the direct and specific question be
asked and answered, so that false answer will leave no room for doubt
that the non-disclosure was wilful and fraudulent.
Conference with Brothers Paulsen and Ross has resulted in their
concurrence that amendment to the form of application by adding the
specific question will go far to correct most of the evils sought to be cured
by their suggestions. They urge. however, and your Committee agrees,
that to avoid the confusion arising out of the word "-felony" it is neces-

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
POLICY & GENERAL PURPOSES
MUTUAL AID ASSOCIATIONS
The report of the Special Committee on Mutual Aid Associations
having been referred to the Committee on Policy and General Pwposes,
we report as follows:
We have considered said report and concur in the matters of
policy contained therein. We present the recommendations of said
Committee in almost the identical language used in the report of the
Special Committee.
We move that all existing mutual aid associations be given a
period of six months from the conclusion of this communication to
comply ·wUh Section 333 of the Masonic Code: i.e., to amend their
by-laws and take all other necessary steps to completely eliminate
any semblance of lodge control or promotion including (a) the use
of the lodge or district name or the words "Low 12" or any other
words in the organization title which may indicate Masonic sponsorship, ( b) any duplication of lodge and association officers, ( c) the
selection of association officers or directors by the Master, or by vote
of the lodge, ( d) any attempt by the lodge officers to recruit members
or in any other way to indicate that the association is a lodge activity
or is existing under lodge sponsorship, ( e) any solicitation or the
transaction of any association business within a Masonic Lodge, and
That existing mutual aid . associations take all necessary steps
within said six months' period to obtain a Certificate of Exemption
or other clearance from the State Insurance Commissioner who is
the duly constituted authority having jurisdiction over this type of
business activity, and
That at the end of said six months' period the inspectors of
the various Masonic districts report the status of mutual aid associations within their respective districts to the Grand Master, and that
those associations which have not conformed to Masonic law and also
obtained clearance from the state officials as outlined herein should
dissolve.

Your Committee has considered the Edict of the Grand Master
relating to the Royal Order of Caritas and the Amaranth Foundation.
Inc. and reports as follows:
The Grand Master found:
1. That the Royal Order of Caritas is a fraternal organization
recently incorporated in the State of California, and Masonic affiliation
or related Masonic affiliation is a requirement for membership therein;
2. Said Royal Order of Caritas was promoted, formed and organized by a dissident group who are or were members of the Order
of Amaranth;
3. One of the prime purposes of said Order of Caritas is to take
over the control and sponsorship of a purported charitable organization
known as the Amaranth Foundation, Inc., a self-perpetuating corporation;
4. A judgment of the Superior Court of this state, now final,
favored the Order of Amaranth and permanently enjoined said
dissident group;
5. Much bitterness, discord and strife exist among and between
Masons by reason of the foregoing facts, and said schemes are misleading and questionable, and the good name of Masonry and the
peace and harmony which should exist among Masons is thereby
seriously jeopardized. and a continuance thereof would be injurious
to the Grand Lodge of California and the Craft generally.
Wherefore, the Grand Master on May 18, 1957, issued an edict
enjoining Masonic membership in the Royal Order of Caritas and in
the Amaranth Foundation, Inc. Said edict also forbade aid and
assistance, directly or indirectly. to said Royal Order of Caritas and
to said Amaranth Foundation, Inc. by any Mason.
..Your Committee concludes that said edict was a valid exercise
of prerogatives and powers of the Grand Master and presents the
following:
RESOLVED:
That the edict of the Grand Master relating to the Royal Order
of Caritas and the Amaranth Foundation. Inc.• be approved and confirmed as a permanent Edict of Grand Lodge.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
Policy and General Purposes
Adopted by 5/6 Vote.

EDICT ON EL ZARAA SHRINE CLUB AT SAN JOSE
Your Committee has considered the Edict of the Grand Master
relating to the proposed El Zaraa Shrine Temple at San Jose and
reports as follows:
The Grand Master found:
1. That a group of Shriners were attempting to form and establish
a new Temple ( El Zaraa) at San Jose:
2. That members of said group or some of them in attempting to
secure other members threatened economic reprisal, boycotts and other
injury and did actually boycott, coerce and slander Masons who refused to join them, thereby in8icting injury and distress upon such
Masons. their business and families: and
3. That said course of action was u1.tethical. unmasonic and resulted in bitterness, Masonic unrest and brought discredit upon
Masonry.
Wherefore, the Grand Master issued an edict enjoining Masonic
membership in said group. This edict was limited in its application
to the specific group and was predicated upon the unmasonic practices
of that group. Said edict did not purport to bar any other movement,
consonant with Masonic precepts, by any other group to form a new
Shrine Temple.
Your Committee concludes that said edict was a valid exercise of
prerogatives and powers of the Grand Master and presents the following:
RESOLVED:
THAT the edict of the Grand Master relating to a group of
Shriners who were attempting to form and establish a new Shrine
Temple (El Zaraa) at San Jose be approved and confirmed as a
permanent Edict of Grand Lodge.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
Policy and General Purposes
Adopted by 5/6 Vote.
EDICT ON SHRINE CIRCUSES
Your Committee has considered the Edict of the Grand Master
relating to Shrine Circuses and reports as follows:
The Grand Master found that Shrine Circuses are commercial
ventures: that tickets are sold to the public on basis of good names
and reputation of Shrine and Masonry: that high pressure solicitation
is condoned: that ticket sales to the public far exceed actual seating
capacity and that such conduct violates basic Masonic law and tends
to bring discredit upon Masonry.
W:herefore, the Grand Master on December 6, 1956 issued an
Edict reading as follows:

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

379

"It is my order and edict, effective immediately, that no Mason in
California or under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California
shall directly or indirectly engage, take part, or participate in sponsoring. holding, conducting, or operating any circus or like commercial
venture or event which is sponsored, conducted. or operated, directly or
indirectly, by any organization of prerequisite Masonic membership or
temple, club, committee, or agent thereof. and for which public support
is requested or for which tickets, programs, or other items are sold to
the public. A violation of this order and edict will be considered a
violation of basic Masonic law and, therefore, unmasonic conduct
and wil' subject the offending Mason or Masons to expulsion from
the fraternity."
Your Committee concludes that said Edict was a valid exercise of
prerogatives and powers of the Grand Master and presents the
following:
RESOLVED:
That the foregoing Edict of the Grand Master be approved and
confirmed as a permanent Edict of the ·Grand Lodge.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
Policy and General Purposes
Adopted by 5/6 Vote.

'

USE OF PHOTOSTAT OF CHARTER AT
INSTALLATION S
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes submits the
following report and recommendation concerning a resolution to amend
Section 313 (a) so as to strike out the requirement that the original
charter of a Lodge must be used at the annual installation of officers. As
the Section now stands, the installation of officers is the only ceremony at which the original charter must be used: on other occasions
a certified photostatic copy of the original may be used.
The resolution was submitted by Past Master William C. Kunz, of
Far West Lodge No. 673. The resolution recites that the present
requirement for the use of the original charter at the installation of
officers, "seems to serve no real purpose and at times can be a real
inconvenience."
Your Committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted.
While it may sometimes be slightly inconvenient to produce the original
Charter from a safe deposit box, the actual transfer of the original
Oharter from the out-going Master to the incoming Master at the latter's
installation. is a very real symbol of the transfer of the authority from
one Master to the other. In our opinion it is far better to exhibit the
original Charter to the assembled brethren than a mere photostatic
copy. Many of the young members of the Lodge would seldom if ever
have an opportunity of seeing the original Charter of the Lodge if
this resolution were adopted. We believe that the Original Charter itself

385

RECOMMENDA TIONS OF
COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
The Committee on Segregation has referred to the Policy and
General Purposes Committee the recommendation of the Grand Master
relative to the employment of a Property Management Consultant _to
assist the various Masonic Temple Associations to conduct their
financial affairs.
We have presently a well in.formed and thoroughly competent
committee which through the years has performed outstanding service
and has acquired a complete working knowledge of our various
Masonic Temples.
Section 200, C.M.C., now requires all Masonic Lodges and Temples
to annually report their financial condition to the committee.
Because of the background of the committee in this field, and the
fact that they have all of the necessary financial information at hand,
we are of the opinion that the present Committee on Lodge Financing
is the proper vehicle to accomplish the purpose outlined by the Grand
Master.
We recommend that our law be implemented by adding to Section
200, C.M.C., a clause authorizing the Committee on Lodge Financing
to advise and recommend on matters relative to property management.
Whereas, a review of financial statements submitted pursuant to
Section 200, C.M.C .• indicates the almost universal subsidization of
prerequisite and other organizations through reduced rentals or no
rentals at all, and
Whereas, no specific Grand Lodge Ordinance is now in effect

PUBLIC RELATIONS COMMITTEE

EXPENDITURE S FOR ATHLETIC EVENTS
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which has been
referred the resolution to permit Constituent lodges to expend monies
from the refreshment fund in support of athletic events, submits the
following report:
This same question was resolved in 1955 by a ruling of Grand
Master Clausen against such permission, which was approved by Grand
Lodge. ( 1955 Proceedings, Page 51-Decision 15.)
The only reason given .for again bringing this matter before Grand
Lodge is that Grand Master Clausen's reasons were not practical. His
view was that because of the limited number who might participate it
could not be considered a matter of fraternal intercourse. We heartily
agree with his reasoning and not with the arguments of the proposer of
the resolution. We feel further that athletic programs, as commendable
as they may be are not within the general scope of activities for which
refreshment funds are intended.
In order to get the matter before Grand Lodge the Committee therefore moves the adoption of the resolution and recommends a "NO" vote.

COMMIT TEE TO SURVEY PROPOSI TIONS AND
CANDIDA TES FOR OFFICE
The resolution requesting the Grand Master to appoint a Committee
to survey propositions and Candidates for office and give their findings
to the Inspectors and Masters of the Jurisdiction for the information of
the Craft has been referred to the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes and the Committee reports as follows:
Ever since the action of the Grand Lodge in 1875 which action is
set forth in the California Masonic Code, Section 16 annotation f, it
has been the inflexible rule of this Grand Lodge not to interfere or
meddle with political matters at home or abroad.
The Grand Lodge at that time approved the statement that "its
members may represent all shades of political opinions, but when they
are assembled in subordinate or Grand Lodges, they cannot so much as
discuss such opinions. Masonry has its own proper objects and purposes
and those must be considered by us to the absolute exclusion of all
others, and particularly of such as would certainly arouse contention
and confusion."
It is our responsibility as individual citizens to intelligently evaluate
the men we vote into office, and by diligent search and study of the
propositions as they appear on the ballot, exercise our right to vote as
our conscience and good judgment dictate.
Your committee recommends a "No" vote on the resolution.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
Policy and General Purposes
Resolution was not adopted.

TWELVE MONTHS RESIDENCE
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes submits the following report and recommendation concerning a resolution to amend Section
517 of the California Masonic Code so as to require that a petitioner for
the degrees must have been a resident within the jurisdiction df the
Lodge for twelve months next proceeding the date of his petition, instead
of the six month period now required by the Section.
The resolution was submitted by Past Master Reinmiller of Canby
Cross Lodge No. 679. The reason advanced for the proposal is, "that six
months are not sufficient to determine if an applicant is truly a good man
and eligible to receive the degrees."
Your Committee recommends that the resolution be not adopted. If
a Lodge feels that a candidate has not lived in the Community for a
sufficiently long period for his qualifications to have become established
and known, that Lodge can discourage his premature presentation of a
Petition, and if he or his sponsors insist on presenting it---can decline to
receive the petition, which does not constitute a rejection ( C.M.C .•
523-f). Furthermore , in our opinion the adoption of this resolution
would prevent or postpone indefinitely the presentation of petitions by
eligible and highly desirable men who in six months have proved and
demonstrate d their qualifkation s to the brethren of their respective
communities, but whose occupations and careers might make it necessary
for them to move before twelve months had elapsed. We believe that
any subordinate Lodge is capable of determinin g-as to any particular
candidate-w hether his petition is presented too soon after the expiration of the six month minimum period of residence.
The Committee therefore moves the adoption of the resolution but
recommends a "NO" vote.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
Policy and General Purposes
The resolution was not adopted.

LIMITATION ON CHARTER MEMBERS
The Committee on Policy and General Pur:poses :has reviewed the
resolution introduced by Past Master Eugene R. Conly of Lodge No.
717, and others recommending a change in Part 2, Artide l, Section 301
of the Ordinances, which if adopted would effect removal of the present
membership limitation of not more than 50 on the original petition for
dispensation for a new lodge.
Your Committee feels that the financial problems of new Lodges, as
well as the possibility of undue drain on the membership of neighboring
Lodges, was adequately considered when the limitation of 50 on original
memberships was established.
Analysis shows that of the new Lodges receiving dispensations during the last year, less than one-third had 50 petitioners, whereas nearly
half listed 40 or fewer. We .feel that, in the light of experience, a change
is not presently warranted.
We, therefore, move the acceptance of the resolution but recommend
a "No" vote.

al, your Committee (Jurisprudence) reports as follows:

the words in t:he second line thereof reading "and not more than fifty"
and substituting therefor the words "or more."

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RECOGNITION
OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES

4. On February 16, 1957, the delegates from 14 of said 'Lodges
assembled in Tokyo, organized the convention, passed a number of
resolutions ,and adjourned to March 16, 1957. The Secretary of the
Convention, on February 20, 1957, in pursuance of a resolution adopted
at the convention, sent a letter with enclosure reporting its acts, purposes, and next meeting date to the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of the Philippines. Said letter in rpart reads as follows:
, "It is believed, that Masonry in Japan has made sufficient progress
to justify a Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons in Japan,
and we therefore earnestly request that favorable consideration will
be given for the formation of this Grand Lodge in Japan."
Our comment: (Under Masonic law and custom this letter and
report were not required but they indicate marked fraternal courtesy
on the part of the convention.)
5. On March 16, 1957, the convention reconvened and there were
present duly elected delegates representing 12 of the Chartered Lodges
under the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of the Philippines. The
GRAND LODGE OF FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS OF
JAPAN was then and there erected, a Constitution and Bylaws adopted
and Grand Lodge Officers elected. Dr. Carlos Rodriguez-Jiminez, Past
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Venezuela, was elected Grand
Master. On the above date the Secretary reported the transactions of
the convention by letter to the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
the Philippines.
6. On March 29, 1957, M. W. Brother Carlos Rodriguez-Jiminez,
Grand Master-elect, wrote to the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge
of the Philippines explaining, with due consideration and courtesy,
the facts and applicable law respecting the formation of the Grand
Lodge of Japan and requesting recognition of the new Grand Lodge
at the next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, to be held in April, 1957. At said Annual Communication,
April 23-25, 1957, petition for recognition was presented and referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence, which reported and recommended
that said Grand Lodge of Japan be not recognized. Grand Lodge accepted the report and ordered a committee appointed "to further studr,
the case during the incoming year and report to the Grand Master.
Such committee has been appointed. Said Committee on Jurisprudence
in its report listed reasons for nonrecognition, as follows (our comment
thereon is enclosed in parentheses) :
a. That the Grand Lodge of Japan was irregularly established,
although it was organized by a majority, more than three, of Philippine
chartered Lodges in Japan. (The latter clause would appear to negate
irregularity.)
b. Philippine Lodges in Japan were composed almost entirely of
transient members belonging to the U.S. Security Forces.

396

Most Worshipful and Members of Grand Lodge:
Your Committee has given consideration to matters o'f foreign
relations and petitions for recognition which have come to attention
during the current year and reports as follows:
GRAND LoDGE OF SANTA CATARINA

A petition for recognition has been received from the Grand Lodge
of Santa Catarina of Florianopolis, Santa Catarina, Brazil. This Grand
Lodge was founded April 25, 1956, but we have been unable to obtain
sufficient information upon which to make affirmative recommendation.
Said petition will therefore be held for further consideration next year.
GRAND LoDGE OF VIENNA

Information recently reached us indicating that this Grand Lodge
had some years ago filed a petition with us for recognition. Said
petition apparently reached the hands of Past Grand Master William
Rhodes Hervey, who was chairman of this Committee at that time,
and said petition has disappeared.
We have written the Grand Lodge of Vienna requesting appropriate information, which has not been received. Further consideration
will be given to this matter during the ensuing year.
JAPAN

The documented petition for recognition by the Grand Lodge of
Japan reveals and confirms the following facts:
1. As of January, 1957, the country of Japan, Masonically speaking,
was open territory; that is, no Grand Lodge existed in Japan and
no Grand Lodge held or possessed territorial jurisdiction in that
country.
2. As of the said date there were 20 Lodges in Japan-13 chartered
and 3 under dispensation by the Grand Lodge of the Philippines with
a membership of 2500, 2 by Scotland, 1 by England and 1 by Massa~husetts.

3. On January 16, 1957, Moriahyama Lodge No. 134, chartered
by the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, unamimously adopted a res~
lution calling for the organization of a Grand Lodge in Japan, and the
Master of said Moriahyama Lodge, in pursuance of said resolution, on
January 17, 1957, sent a letter with copy of said resolution enclosed
to the Masters of the other 15 Lodges chartered and under dispensation
by the Grand Lodge of the 'Philippines requesting Lodge approval of
said resolution; election of delegates and attendance thereof at a
convention to be held in Tokyo on February 16, 1957, for the purposes
specified in said resolution.

have liberally established, particularly our Masonry for the Japanese

That the District Grand Master in Japan, appointed by the Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, refused to obey the
Grand Master's orders and resigned: that when his successor, appointed by the Grand Master, left for Manila in January, 1957, the
actual planning of the new Grand Lodge began.
That the resolution calling the Convention to form a new Grand
Lodge was signed by a Mason who had been raised to the degree of
Master Mason barely 2Yi years and was Worshipful Master of his
Lodge. (This reason is self-effacing.)
(It is natural perhaps for a mother to criticize a grown-up child.
This happened also when our Grand Lodge was formed. Missouri
chartered one of the three Lodges upon which our Grand Lodge was
formed. The Grand Master of Missouri, at the opening of his Grand
Lodge in May, 1950, in speaking of California remarked-Cal if. Proc.
1851, rp.102:
"I received a communication from a Master Mason in that distant
land, who informed me, as a friend, that the ties of Masonry even,
appeared to him to have lost much of their binding force in California:
that gold, and the thirst for gold had dried up the fountains of Brotherly
Love and Relief in that country. That such is the case is not astonishing.
Wherever that raging thirst for Mammon seizes a fellowbeing here
with us, even, the channels of fraternal feeling become dry; the finer
sensibilities of the heart become diseased, and at length cease to operate
on his conduct, because he has ceased to call them into action; and
his sensibilities and the charities of his nature become dead for want
of being used. In such a bosom no sympathy for Freemasonry, no sympathy for others' woe or weal can be found.")
c. No Lodge of Master Masons was opened for the purpose of
conducting the two conventions to organize the Grand Lodge. (Such
was not required. No Lodge was opened to conduct the convention
when the Grand Lodge of California was formed. 1950 Proc. ipp 3-20.)

d. As authority for its decision the Committee on Jurisprudence
cites California law: Ross Digest Sec. 586: Proc. 1875, p. 112, and
Masonic Code Sec. 16r reading as follows:
"When Lodges owing allegiance to one of more foreign Grand
Lodges unite in the formation of a Grand Lodge, as in Prince Edward
Island or the Province of Manitoba, we recognize the right of the
Mother Grand Lodges to maintain jurisdiction over their own subordinates, and the duty of the subordinates to obtain consent before
severing their allegiance. T ·his Grand Lodge should not recognize Grand
Lodges so established until they have been recognized h~ the Gran?,
Lodges from which the constituent Lodges hold their charters.
(Italics supplied.)
(The italic words limit the application of the law to cas~s
where the parent Grand Lodge held territorial jurisdiction in the area m
which the new Grand Lodge was established. In this case the Grand
Lodge of Canada actually held and exercised jurisdiction over the
Provinces in which the new Grand Lodges were formed as well as
jurisdiction over the Lodges themselves. In this case our Grand Lodge
said:
"This Grand Lodge would urge upon the mother Grand Lodges
the propriety of giving consent that their subordinates might in ..all
proper cases join in the establishment of new Grand Lodges, • . · ·
This was quite unnecessary because 3 months prior thereto the
Grand Lodge of Canada ·h ad done the honorable thing by. giving its
consent to the new Grand Lodge [Calif. 1876 Proc. 492]. Smee Japan
was open territ9ry at the time, this California law was and is not in
point.)
7. ~he Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Japan, under date of
May 14, 1957, issued a Manifesto in which he reported as follows (our
comment respecting same is embraced in parentheses) :

401

8. The Grand Lodges of South Carolina and Venezuela have recognized the Grand Lodge of Japan.
CONCLUSION

The California law upon this subject is embodied in the first paragraph of Sec. 16r of our California Masonic Code ( 1956) reading as
follows:
"In the United States it is universally recognized as the law
of Masonry that whenever there are three chartered Lodges in any
state or territory in which no Grand Lodge has been established. those
Lodges have the absolute right to meet in convention and organize
a Grand Lodge for such state or territory: that when a Grand Lodge
is once regularly established in any state or territory. it has exclusive jurisdiction over all Masonic Lodges and Masons within such
state or territory. and that no other Grand Lodge or grand body can
establish a new Lodge within the territorial jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge so organized, or can maintain jurisdiction over a Lodge therein
to which it may have granted a charter. From the moment of the
organization of the new Grand Lodge its jurisdiction becomes absolute
over the entire territory, and all Lodges and all Masons there must
acknowledge it and yield obedience to it, and their allegiance elsewhere
ceases.
We find that the Grand Lodge of Japan was regularly erected
upon more than three regular Lodges holding valid charters from
the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, and that said Grand Lodge of
Japan fully meets our tests for recognition. It is true that the mother
Grand Lodge has considered but delayed recognition in order to further
investigate the f>etition and will perhaps take further action at its
next Annual Communication in April 1958. While recognition by
the mother Grand Lodge is not a condition precedent to our recognition.
we do believe that fraternal courtesy dictates that we should withhold
recognition until the Grand Lodge of the Philippines, which we
sponsored, has an opportunity to consider the subject further at its
next Annual Communication.

..

We therefore present the following:

RESOLVED:
That our recognition be held in abeyance and that the Grand Master
be authorized to recognize the Grand Lodge of Japan on or subsequent
to June 1. 1958.
Respectfully submitted.
JOHN R. MOORE
CHESTER H. WARLOW

Adopted.

ARTHUR M. WARREN

POINT WITHIN A CIRCLE

We have pointed out on prior occasions that there is no authority in
our law or regulations for so-called officers' aprons, and no regulation
governing color, design or insignia to be placed on them. They exist in
contradiction of the instruction given to candidates to the effect that the
white lambskin apron is the badge of a Mason. If we are to adopt an
amendment to section 554 to prescribe the practice with respect to
aprons, we should first adopt a regulation specifying the color, design
and insignia to be placed thereon.
There is neither law nor precedent for the contention that the apron
belongs to the instaIIed officer. It is merely part of the equipment belonging to the Lodge, just as is the jewel with which the officer is formaily
invested at installation.
The officer who is selected to act in any station or place is selected
by the installed Master, but nevertheless, for the purposes of the degree,
he is the officer of the Lodge which has been convened to confer the
degree. The Junior Warden acting as Master in a Lodge of Entered
Apprentice Masons is for all purposes the Master of that Lodge. He
must be addressed as Worshipful Master. He wears the Master's jewel.
He wears the Master's hat and he wields the Master's gavel, which is
the distinct emblem of the Master's authority. These are all surrendered
to him without question. So also, we think, must the apron be surrendered, if it designates the office.
If the installed Master is to sit on the sidelines with the Master's
apron, then by the same token 'he should retain the hat and his gavel.
It requires very little reference to our ritual to demonstrate that the
officer occupying the station or .place is the officer of the Lodge as thus
convened for the degree. These references obviously cannot be written
in this report.
If the rule suggested in this resolution were adopted, the result would
be confusion, because if the installed Master or other officer only could
use his apron, half the officers conferring the degree might be clothed in
officers' aprons and half of them clothed in white aprons.
We recommend that the resolution be not adopted, and suggest that
since it purports to amend section 554 of the Ordinances, its adoption
would require a five-sixths vote of Grand Lodge.
In order to conform to the required procedure we move the adoption
of the resolution and recommend the No vote.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
Ritual
The Resolution was not adopted.

The resolutions submitted with reference to the Point within a Circle
have been referred to this committee, whic'h reports as follows:
These resolutions are based upon a misunderstanding of the position
of the Grand Lecturer and Ritual Committee, which would have been
pointed out to the proponents if they had sought a hearing before the
Committee.
The Grand Lecturer has not ruled that the point within a circle may
not be present in the lodgeroom. There is nothing whatever to prevent
any lodge from having physicaily represented in its lodgeroom any
monitorial emblem.
What the Grand Lecturer has taught is that the emblem cannot be
used as a part of the ritual by pointing or calling particular attention to
the emblem. The work as taught in this jurisdiction does not include
·such use of it. As declared by Grand Master Clausen in 1955, the work
is taught and should be con.ferred without the use of charts or "props."
( C.M.C., Sec. 554v.) It is communicated only by the instructive tongue
to the attentive ear, and any other method is positively forbidden. (Proceedings 1908, P. 120: Ross Dig .• Sec. 502.)
The resolutions are unnecessary, so far as the physical representation
is concerned, and we therefore recommend that they be not adopted.
In order to conform to the required procedure we move the adoption
of the resolution and recommend a NO vote.
Committees concurring:
Jurisprudence
. Ritual
The resolution was not adopted.

OFFICERS' APRONS
The Ritual Committee to which was referred a resolution of several
Masters of lodges at Bakersfield to amend Section 554u of the C.M.C.
to provide that aprons indicating an officer's rank are to be worn only
by the installed officer himself, reports as foIIows:
~he practice adopted and taught by the Grand Lecturer and Ritual
Committee is that an officer vacating his station or place shall surrender
to the person occupying it not only the jewel but the apron, if it bears
insignia indicating the office.
Several years ago the Ritual Committee became aware that two
differing practices prevailed in this jurisdiction with respect to this
matter, and the practice adopted was to make uniform one practice
throughout the jurisdiction. The Committee was unanimous that the
correct practice was the one it adopted and that it was taught in the
greater number of areas in the State. Furthermore, it conforms to the
practice of the Grand Lodge officers at Grand Lodge ceremonies, at
which the man filling the office customarily wears both jewel and apron
indicating the office.

Gentlemen:
We have examined the Balance Sheet of
MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNI A
(A California Non-Profit Corporation)
as of June 30, 1957, and the related Statement of Revenue and EX'pense for
the eleven months then ended. In connection therewith we also examined
the Balance Sheets of the Permanent Endowment Fund and the other
Endowment and Trust Funds of the Masonic Homes of California as of June
30, 1957, and their !!:'elated Statements of Revenue for the eleven months then
ended. Our examination was made in accordance with generally accepted
auditing standards and accordingly included such tests of the accoun·t ing
records and such other auditing procedures as we considered necessary in
the circwnstance s.
The annual financial statements of Masonic Homes of Califomia have
been prepared for many years past on the cash basis of accounting and the
attached financial statements are prepared on that basis. Under 'the cash
basis of accounting, revenue and expense are recorded upon the books of
account and reflected in the financial statements when received and paid
without regard to the period to which they apply.
The Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes of California on March 30
1957 changed the annual accounting period from a fiscal year ending July 3i
to a fiscal year ending June 30 to conform with the fiscal year of Grand
Lodge, F. & A. M. As a consequence of this action, the period covered by
this report is the eleven months ended JU!l'l.e 30, 1957.
The total revenue ·received by Masonic Homes of California during the
eleven months ended June 30, 1957, amounted to $690,440.56 as shown on
$730 075 69
Exhibit E. Its operating expenses for the year amounted

expense over revenue, including capital gains, of $24, 795.66 as shown on
Exhibit E. Included .in the operating expe~es o_f $730,075.69,' is the sum of
$39,673.69, representmg the voluntary contribution s to the Masonic Homes
~f California Retireme!1t 1!1come Plan. The total amount paid of $39,673.69

the plan . and of a contribution fo_r the first .six months of 1957 of $13,454.65
as an estimate of the amount due m that period.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

Exhibit A

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

Balance Sheet, June 30, 1957

June 30, 1957

ASSETS

1. The financial statements herewith have been prepared on the cash basis
of accounting under which basis accrued receipts and expenditures are
not reflected in the financial statements until received and paid, respectively.
2. Under date of October 4, 1955, promissory notes to six San Francisco
banks, totaling $3,000,000.00, were signed by the officers of California .
Masonic Memorial Temple. These notes are secured by a first deed of
trust on the temple site real property and the improvements thereon,
and are to be further secured by a chattel mortgage on the furnishings
and equipment of the new temple. Prior to June 30, 1957, the original
loan commitment of the banks of $3,000,000.00 had been reduced by
$240,000.00, representing an amount equivalent to two annual instalments of $20,000.00 to each bank, and during the eleven months ended
June 30, 1957, advances of $300,000.00 were received on the notes reducing the balance of the total commitment on the notes to $2,460,000.00
at June 30, 1957. Interest at 4% per annum is rpayable semi-annually
April 1 and October 1 of each year on the amounts advanced by the
banks on said notes. The principal advanced on the notes is payable in
annual instalments of $20,000.00 to each bank beginning October 1, 1958
and annually thereafter until October 1, 1965, on which latter date all
sums of principal and interest then unpaid shall be due and payable.
The amount of the banks' commitment under the notes and repayment
to the banks of advances thereon are subject to the provisions of the
banks' commitment letter. Below are shown the amounts advanced
under the notes and the balance of the banks' commitment at June 30,
1957:
Advances to
Balance of
June 30, 1957 Commitment
